Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What does being depressed feel like?
Answer: It feels like nothing. And everything at all. Every day seems like another giant to be slain, in a never-ending battle. You just survive each day, hour, minute at a time. And sometimes it takes everything you have just to do that. I have not talked about this in detail, but the last 3–4 months have probably been the worst time of my life. I still don’t feel like talking in detail about the exact issue, but it’s a very integral part of my life that is seemingly falling apart. And it has taken me more than 100 days just to make some sense of it, to seemingly come to terms with the situation, and start fighting back. There were a few really dark weeks back in the latter half of December and the first part of January where there seemed no hope - just a world shrouded in darkness, a descent into the bottomless pit of despair with nothing to break the fall. No straws to clutch on to, no end to the grief. I didn’t get out of bed for days on end, neglecting my physical health and personal hygiene. I didn’t eat, couldn’t sleep, had to force myself just to get water. It felt as if my body was being weighed down by invisible chains, my mind drowned out by a barrage of thoughts and memories, my soul beaten, bruised, and defeated. You don’t feel like doing anything. You just can’t muster up the energy to do anything. What used to excite you no longer does. It’s an emotional roller-coaster where you are laughing one moment watching a random funny video, and breaking down sobbing the next because something triggered (and you don’t know what). It took me 2–3 hours in the morning just to get myself together. Like an antiquated PC struggling to reboot itself. And then I would try to fill in my waking hours with anything to take my mind off of the situation. I would immersed myself in work. Drown out my senses with loud music. Head out in the dark for a walk just to feel the slightest semblance of what being alive felt. And in all of it, I was trying to do it alone. It never occured to me to seek help, until one day it did. And I reached out. I opened up to people I trusted. They listened. I felt good. Like a sepsis eventually bursting and oozing out and the poison that had built up over the years finally found a release. I blabbered on for hours. And these wonderful souls listened. Some of them came over from other cities just to let me know that they are there. Some even offered to fly across half the globe. I started opening up about it. I started writing about it. Primarily on Instagram and Twitter — I still did not have the energy and the perseverance to sit down and write anything more than a couple of paragraphs. More people reached out — a lot of them in the same boat. Everyone fighting their own invisible demons. And I opened up to complete strangers. And they opened up to me. It felt better. I am still in touch with about half a dozen folks and we all are each other’s support structure. Another lost, falling soul just reaching out in the dark and finding another hand, seeking some solace in company. After all “misery loves company”. But not in Schadenfreudig way, but just to ask for some more hope, a little bit of strenght. To make inappropriate jokes about the situation, to vent out our feelings, anything that helps us hold on for a few more moments. I have been reading about depression, anxiety, and mental health and wellness. I have been trying out many things — journaling, focusing on small tasks, meditation and mindfulness, rewatching my favorite movies and TV shows, getting back to my old hobbies. And it is getting better. Even if the situation is still the same, I am coping better. I have had time to think and analyze and I believe I have made peace with what is happening and all eventual outcomes from it that could come to fruition. I have set small personal goals for myself, because I am going to prioritize my own happiness from now on. To anyone going through a "rough patch", "emotional distress", "bad day", know you are not alone. I am here. You can talk to me. I might not have any advice to give, but I promise to hear you out. This is a fucking monstrosity but you don’t have to go alone. Talk. Embrace what you are feeling. Express your emotions because then they start making some sense. Be gentle on yourself. It's fine to feel amazing at the start of the day and be absolutely devastated by nightfall. It's cool if you don't do anything. Ir's perfectly okay to discard your personal or social obligations. None of that matters if your mental health isn't fine. Prioritize your own well-being first. Do whatever helps you deal with it. And just to reiterate, hit me up if you want a sympathetic ear, a human pillow to scream into, or just someone to virtually hug you and say "there, there!"

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What is the importance of books in our life?
Answer: In today’s “instant gratification” world, marked by a never-ending pursuit of the next big thing, the simple act of reading a book holds a timeless significance. Books are more than just a source of knowledge; they are gateways to other worlds, repositories of wisdom from people no longer on this planet, companions for solitary times, and catalysts for personal growth. The importance of reading cannot be overstated. It shapes our perspectives, broadens our horizons, and instills a sense of empathy and understanding. When we immerse ourselves in the pages of a book, we step into the shoes of its characters, experience their joys and sorrows, and see the world through their eyes. Even fictional characters have their roots in reality, they are after all the intellectual offsprings of their creators. This simple act of vicarious living enriches our own lives, making us more compassionate and open-minded individuals. Consider, for instance, the profound impact that Harper Lee's "To Kill a Mockingbird" has had on generations of readers. Through the innocent yet perceptive eyes of Scout Finch, we confront the harsh realities of racial prejudice and moral courage. The lessons learned from such narratives stay with us, subtly influencing our thoughts and actions long after we've turned the last page. Yet, one might argue, we don't retain every detail from the books we read, so why even. True, but the essence of what we read lingers in our subconscious, shaping our values and beliefs. As the renowned author and educator Mortimer J. Adler said, "The mark of a good book is it changes every time you read it." This speaks to the evolving nature of our understanding and how the messages from books become interwoven with our personal experiences and growth. In the words of Ralph Waldo Emerson, “I cannot remember the books I've read any more than the meals I have eaten; even so, they have made me." Moreover, the very act of reading—a solitary activity that demands focus and attention—serves as a sanctuary from the chaos of modern life. In a world where we are constantly bombarded with information and distractions, sitting down with a book allows us to disconnect and find peace. It is in these quiet moments that we can reflect, dream, and explore ideas that might otherwise be drowned out by the noise. Quotes from literary giants further underscore the importance of books. Franz Kafka famously said, "A book must be the axe for the frozen sea within us." This metaphor highlights the transformative power of reading, how it can break through our emotional and intellectual barriers, revealing truths we might not have discovered otherwise. Books also play a crucial role in education and intellectual development. They are the foundation upon which knowledge is built, offering insights that are often more nuanced and comprehensive than those found in other media. The depth and breadth of understanding that come from reading extensively cannot be replicated by quick online searches or skimming through summaries. In the words of the celebrated American author Mark Twain, "The man who does not read has no advantage over the man who cannot read." This quote serves as a reminder that the true value of reading lies not just in the acquisition of knowledge but in the continuous process of learning and growth. In conclusion, books are invaluable treasures that enrich our lives in countless ways. They expand our horizons, shape our perspectives, and provide a refuge from the world's distractions. While we may not remember every detail, the underlying messages become a part of us, guiding us subtly yet profoundly. As we navigate the complexities of life, the wisdom and experiences gleaned from books become our steadfast companions, helping us to become more thoughtful, empathetic, and well-rounded individuals.

Question: Should the sex trade be legal?
Answer: If it is legal to perform an activity of your own accord, it is logical that it should be legal to to perform it in exchange for money. Legally, I can write. I can also write in exchange for money — I can charge a fees for a guest post, I can be fully employed in the capacity of a writer at a firm, I can write books, or ghost-write them for someone. Legally, I can work out to achieve a splendid physique or to become stronger. I can also participate in body-building championships where I can flaunt my bulging, oiled to perfection muscles for everyone to admire in exchange for money. Or I can become a strongman, a powerlifter, or a wrestler where I put my body on the line everyday, pushing myself to physical extremes in exchange for money. Why should “sex work” be any different? It is mind-boggling — the entire taboo around prostitution, despite it being one of the oldest recorded profession in the world.[1] Humans have exchanged money and goods for sex for thousands of years, and indeed it seems that any society that begins to develop material wealth soon develops some form of prostitution. The Bible depicts many Israelites as having large numbers of concubines, who could be viewed either as prostitutes or as wives of a lesser status. According to 1 Kings 11:3, King Solomon had “700 wives … and 300 concubines.” In ancient Rome, it seems you could hand over a token at a brothel in return for a specific sexual favor. However, the common image of prostitutes as a special group of outcasts walking the streets may not have arisen until the Victorian era, when health officials blamed them for the spread of venereal diseases. In the 21st century, prostitution occurs across cultures and political systems, even operating in socialist societies. It is not even specific to humans. ...but there’s evidence that some kinds of animals engage in a form of prostitution. Female chimpanzees living in the Ivory Coast have been observed to trade sex for meat. In one experiment capuchin monkeys were taught to use silver discs as a sort of money (they could be redeemed for grapes), and it wasn’t long before one monkey exchanged one of the tokens for sex. Dr. Fiona Hunter, a researcher at Cambridge University, observed female penguins in Antarctica trading sex for stones and pebbles. Adélie penguins need rocks to build their nests, and some females—though they already had a mating partner—would have sex with a single male while away and then take some of his stones. While the females may have had other motives than gathering pebbles, Hunter noted that “stones are the valuable currency in penguin terms,” and penguins are usually very protective of them. Some penguins engaged in the behavior over and over, but she said, “It’s probably only a few percent.” There is no reason for it to be illegal, except imaginary moral/theological frameworks posited by religions all over the world. Criminalizing sex work is actually a violation of the fundamental rights of an adult human being. It is the government telling you what you can and can not do with your body. It should be treated in the same vein as criminalizing abortions and publicly chastised in the same vein as slut-shaming women. By criminalizing sex work, women who partake in that profession are left at the mercy of local goons and enforcers, of middle-men and corrupt officials. They are subject to public humiliation and ostracization. The Sonagachi Red Light District in India or GB Road in New Delhi or Kamathipura in Mumbai are prime example of how widespread prostitution in India is and at the same time, it sheds light on the plight of the sex workers because of the legal status of prostitution in India. And in most cases it is usually men (who have benefited from centuries of patriarchal control) who design and implement these laws. The positive impacts of legalized, regulated sex-work are widely researched and documented. Key findings from the study show that there were 31 percent or 824 fewer reported rapes and a decrease of approximately 2000 cases of gonorrhea during the seven years indoor prostitution was decriminalized. The authors note that the results suggest that “decriminalization could have potentially large social benefits for the population at large — not just sex market participants.” The research, published in journal PLOS Medicine, reviewed data from more than 130 studies on 33 countries - from Britain to Uganda - published in scientific journals between 1990 to 2018. It found sex workers who had been exposed to repressive policing like arrest or prison were three times more likely to experience sexual or physical violence by clients, partners and other people. It is high time sex work should be legalized, regulated, and treated the same as any other vocation.

Question: What’s the best excuse for missing class in college?
Answer: There is only one legitimate reason for missing class in college and that is if you truly believe it will not add any value to you. That could be either because the subject doesn’t interest you, the professor is not good at teaching and you would rather spend the same time learning it from other online options, or you already are an expert in it. As someone who graduated from a college with a “zero attendance policy” and abused it liberally for the entire 4 years (because I could), I highly recommend against it. A simple thought experiment. Any good UG college in India costs about 4L/annum in tuition. ~3 classes per day for about 160 days a year (excluding holidays, vacations, and exam days), implies you are spending about INR 1000/class. Is what you are doing with the time worth more than that? Are you building something cool? Learning a new skill? Working on your career goals? Networking? If not, why even enroll in the first place? If you think (like I did) that you are too good for college, you are in for a rude awakening later in life. College is a fun time, but it is not a fully-paid 4-year vacation. It is the right time for you to figure out who you are and what you want. It is the opportune period of life to try out new things and see what sticks. It is a crazy-ass part of life that decides the trajectory of the rest of your existence. You are not fooling anyone by bunking classes. It won’t magically make you the coolest kid in towm. So don’t be a tool.

Question: How can people read 5 books in a week?
Answer: 99.9% of the people cannot read 5 books a week. Consider that the average books has 80,000–100,000 words. And that the average person reads at a speed of 250 wpm. That basically translates to 5–6 hours required per book. Or about 25–30 hours required every week to read 5 books. Considering that the average person also holds a job and/or has other commitments, taking out ~4 hours everyday for reading is a huge ask. However, some people do read more than that. A case in point is Maria Popova of The Marginalian (previously, Brain Pickings). Maria is a voracious reader and an exceptional writer, who has been churning out 2 articles a day consistently for years now. And here’s how she does it. She’ll then start her day in her Brooklyn apartment with a 15-20 minute meditation session and a workout — 20 chin ups, 50 push ups, then a series of planks and stretches — before heading to the gym where most of her long-form reading is done while she’s on the elliptical. As part of her research for Brian Pickings, Popova consumes a staggering amount of content every day. She discussed her consumption habits to Kelton Reid in 2013, “I do most of my long-form reading at the gym (pen and Post-Its and all), skim the news while eating (a questionable health habit, no doubt), and listen to philosophy, science, or design podcasts while commuting on my bike (hazardous and probably illegal).” But Maria’s an oddity, an extreme outlier — someone with a strong affinity towards reading, a robust system for cataloging and documenting excerpts, and growing up in a household that promoted reading from the start.[1] Ms. Popova traces her discipline to her upbringing behind the Iron Curtain. Her parents met as teenage exchange students in Russia and had her almost immediately. Her father was an engineering student who later became an Apple salesman; her mother was studying library science. “We’re not very much in touch,” she said of her parents today, “but recently we were on Skype, and this whole library science thing came up. I realized a lot of what I do is organizational, almost like a Dewey Decimal System for the Web. My mother got so emotional. It was very funny, and kind of moving.” Her paternal grandmother was a rabid biblio and had a collection of encyclopedias, Ms. Popova said, and she credits the act of randomly opening volumes and happening upon entries for her passion to discover old knowledge. “The Web has such a presentism bias,” she said, with Facebook updates, tweets and blog entries always appearing with the latest first. By contrast, flipping through the encyclopedia was “an interesting model of learning about the world serendipitously and also guidedely.” However, not everyone can be Maria. And you don’t even have to be. Reading isn’t about numbers and targets. Reading is about exploring the world around you through the lenses of others. It allows you the chance to gaze into the minds of others, to relive the experience of people who lived before you, to broaden your horizons. It should be something that helps you grow, provides comfort in times of need, and overall enriches your life. You could be reading a book a month or a book a day, it does not matter. What matters is what you read and how it impacts you in your daily life. I normally try and read ~2 books a week. And with my long history of reading, I have been able to improve my reading speed to ~500 wpm. So an hour of dedicated reading every day is enough. Here’s how you can do it too.

Question: What is moonlighting? Is it ethical to do more than one job in India?
Answer: moonlighting, verb. have a second job, typically secretly and at night, in addition to one's regular employment. I am not sure of the legalities of moonlighting in India, but there should not even be a debate about the ethics of it. The contract between an employer and an employee has a very simple “give and take” — the employee works for a certain # of hours (30–45 per week) for the employer and in turns get compensated for the same. What they do outside those hours is not the employer’s fucking concern. You can get a second job, and a third one. Or you can choose to idle away the time doing nothing but binging on Netflix. Doesn’t fucking matter. The same employers who are creating this whole hullabaloo about moonlighting are the ones who don’t pay their employees their due and treat them as bonded laborers. In India, the organized labor market till recently has been very lopsided, with corporations holding power over people. Prior to COVID, employees could not even work from home even when they were under the weather, or had some personal commitments. I remember Mumbai being totally submerged during the monsoons a few years back, and people were still asked to come to office. Now all of that is changing. People realized that they can work from the comfort of their home in a remote village in Kerala or Assam, and still deliver the same impact as they would from office. Companies are desperate to attract and retain talent, which is suddenly in huge demand. If the output and timeliness of someone’s work is not impacted, how does it matter if they have 3 different jobs or 12? If Elon Musk can be the CEO/Founder/Head of 5 behemoths, all the while brain farting on Twitter and raking in billions every year, why can’t a normal person have a second job? All of the ongoing nonsense is just to retain the status quo — keep the people oppressed and they will stay poor. And the cycle of corporations abusing cheap labor will continue. Fuck that! Go get a part-time gig. Go rake in all the money you can. Go wave both your middle fingers to every fucking millionaire/billionaire that says moonlighting is unethical/theft.

Question: What are the topics we need to talk about in India these days?
Answer: The hidden epidemic that is mental health. Last year, India witnessed the largest number of suicides ever. Various estimates put the percentage of Indians suffering from some form of mental health issues from anywhere between 14%[1] to a staggering 43%[2] (Image source: Our World In Data - Mental Health) And for a country that houses 1.4 billion people, this is a seriously staggering numbers. Especially in light of the utter lack of awareness about it and the absence of the infrastructure to remediate it. We are talking about hundreds of millions of people silently fighting these invisible demons, not knowing what to do, not sure who to talk to, unaware that they can (and should) reach out for help. In India, depression, anxiety, and other mental health issues are treated with an apathetic frivolity. Families do not understand any of it (“you seem perfectly fine!”, “There is nothing wrong with your life, just take a vacation.”) Colleges and universities do not provide counselling/therapy. Employers do not have any provision for wellness days. We do not even have a robust infrastructure to provide care for people with mental health issues. [3] According to National Crime Records Bureau 2015, the entire mental health workforce, comprising clinical psychiatrists, psychologists, psychiatric social workers and psychiatric nurses, stands at 7,000, while the actual requirement is around 55,000. In the last couple of years of reaching out to and interacting with people fighting these invisible demons, I have had personal experience about the depths of this hidden pandemic. People are unhappy in their marriage, fighting profound grief stemming from broken relationships, suffering from an overpowering feeling of inadequacy at the workplace, students reeling under the pressure of intense academic rigor, and the FOMO arising out of constant social media exposure. And the COVID years have exacerbated the situation. It is high time we, as a collective (family and friends, employers, institutions, and governments) take cognizance of the situation. Else we will end up like Japan in a few years, a composite of broken people.

Question: How long does it take to get over severe heartbreak?
Answer: You do not get over a heartbreak, you get through it. There’s a beautiful couplet by Jigar Moradabadi. ये इश्क़ नहीं आसाँ इतना ही समझ लीजे इक आग का दरिया है और डूब के जाना है which roughly translates to Heed - this journey of love isn’t easy, A river of fire; to be crossed submerged. To be honest, you never “completely” get over someone. Just like the half-life decay of radioactive elements, you never truly reach a state where the heartbreak ceases to exist. But the good news is that it gets easier. With every single passing day. With every word of validation from friends and family. With every new person you meet who rekindles the hope of finding love again. With every moment of self-reflection and self-acceptance. I ask that you read this Twitter thread - one of my favorites ever since I stumbled across it fortuitously at my lowest last year. Your healing journey is your own. No one can tell you how to get over a heartbreak. That is something you have to figure out on your own. I won’t tell you what to do. Just what I did. And hope that it helps you figure out your own path. The first thing I did was get ride of the self-blame. For a long time, I was angry at myself - for the mistakes I had made (inadverently), I chided myself - “should have done better”. Until I realized that such thoughts do not help. No one is perfect; people make mistakes. And sometimes they get second chances, but other times they don’t. Next I let of the anger and the resentment. I offered her the same courtesy I did to myself. We both were human, we both made mistakes. Finally, acceptance. I realized that life is complicated and unpredictable. And often, despite your best efforts, it doesn’t go the way you had planned because there are a lot of externalities at play. You can’t fight an earthquake, you can’t outrun a storm. All you can do is find shelter till it passes away. And then salvage what you can from the ruins and rebuild. Think of healing as an actual, physical journey. You’ve been thrown into the wilderness with no preparation. The first few days are excruciating. You feel lost, desolate, overpowered by despair. But the only way is through. All you can do is start walking. Your feet blister, your legs hurt. The thickets cut you, the sun scorches your skin. And every single day, you have to fight the urge to give up. But you need to persist. Your stamina increases. You figure out the navigation. You unlock the balance between continuing and resting. The blisters heal. The scars start to fade. One day you realize you are at the prescipice of the forest and you finally step out. While the tumultous journey is over, it stays with you. You get the occasional nightmare. But eventually you accept and embrace the experience. Another facet of life. The scars now part of your identity.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why are so many decent people single nowadays?
Answer: Relationships demand work - conscious, relentless work. The nature of human life has changed dramatically over the last couple of generations - in a good way, but that has also had some unexpected impact on the way relationship dynamics function. In earlier generation, people used to refer to their husband/wife as their “better half”. An endearing term for sure, but one that also indicates that neither of them is a “complete person”, dependent on the other for some aspect of a complete life. That equation is changing. As more and more women enter the workforce, they are no longer financially dependent on a man. They can very well provide for themselves. Parallely, men now realize that household chores and parenting is their responsibility too. Now we no longer have two incomplete people seeking their complementarty halves. What we have is two independent people, each with their own personality, ambitions, and interests. As such, relationships now are not a matter of convenience, but one of fulfilment. They’ve now moved up a couple of rungs on the Maslov’s Heirarchy of Needs. Then there are other external factors that have “complicated” the situation. The globalised nature of the current world means that even a seemingly small disconnect between two people in terms of their life goals (one might want to stay back in their home country, while the other gets an opportunity in a far away land that they can’t refuse) becomes insurmountable. The internet has brought people closer - allowing you to get in touch with other people with similar interests easily. As such, you are no longer dependent only on your spouse for emotional or recreational support. And finally, the advent of online dating has made finding casual dates or hookups quite simple. People are choosing to stay single because it is rather convenient. At least easier than the alternative. If you want something fixed or delivered, you can do it online. If you want to share your heart out, you can reach out to friends. If you want physical intimacy, just start swiping. The nature of relationships has to evolve in line with how everything else has. They should no longer be about finding someone who complements you, but someone who elevates you. They should no longer be about obligations, but the conscious choice to stay together. They should no longer be restricting and adjusting, but liberating.

Question: Is the Darwin Platform Group of Companies company fake or real?
Answer: It is a real company. You can find their incorporation details on the MCA website.[1] That doesn’t mean it is genuine. I came across this company due to their huge billboards on the Mumbai-Pune highway. I was intrigued. But a cursory look at their website shows that it is a scam masquerading as a company.[2] Their MD is this guy (who also is the face of their numerous billboards). He holds a 99% stake in the company. The kind of language used in the writeup reads more like a “cult” than a corporate setup. “under his directorship & guidance” “leadership of Mr. Ajay Harinath Singh that has capatulted its vision into its presaent growth trajectory and stature at this moment”. “charismatic leader” “despite his busy schedule” The grammatical errors are a dead giveaway too. Go to their “about” section. Tell me what they do. Their Beverages section[3] writeup reads as follows. Which beverages? No fucking clue. But they “look good and taste even better”. They reiterate their belief in “conducting ethical business”. But as Tywin put it, Let’s look at the guy though. He is astute. Always present at awards (that you can buy). Has profiles of him on websites like ToI[4] (clearly bought once more). Ajay Harinath Singh- The Prince of Sultanpur and the descendent of the Ikshvaku clan. He comes from Lava (The Son of Lord Rama) lineage. Lava belongs to the Ishkavaku clan or Suryavanshi Dynasty of Kshatriya in ancient India and Ajay Harinath Singh’s caste, Suryavanshi claims their descent from Lava. With a glorious lineage, Ajay Harinath Singh is passionate about nation-building through strong and innovative models. The ultimate aim of DPGC’s businesses and initiatives in India is to boost the economy. He was recently honoured with the Times Men of the Year 2020 award for being an ‘Innovative Multipreneur’. And this piece in Forbes India. Notice the disclaimer at the end. (Definitely not a cult leader). Still not convinced? Well, the company has a huge history of cases of fraud against them. Lenders of Jet Airways are examining past allegations of fraud against the founder of Darwin Platform Group Company, which has offered to infuse ₹14,000 crore in the airline. At least four cases had reportedly been registered against Ajay Harinath Singh, the founder of Darwin, which claims to have a net worth of ₹24,000 crore from businesses across different verticals. The company, however, denied the charges and said the cases had been resolved. But top sources close to the lenders said that every aspect will be evaluated to make sure the wrong money does not come into the company. According to a 2015 report in The Tribune, the Uttarakhand police had registered a case against Singh in the State and in Uttar Pradesh for allegedly duping the residents of ₹100 crore, posing as an investor. However, in response to BusinessLine’s email query, a spokesperson for Darwin said: “All legal cases (against Darwin founder) have been closed in Uttrakhand, Delhi and Rajasthan and no cases in any part of india are pending on him. No evidence was found and the FIR in Uttrakhand was fake and fabricated” In another case, reported on February 2018, the Cyber Cell of the Delhi Crime Branch arrested two people for allegedly duping people of ₹7,50,000, by luring them to invest in a Russia-based company, ‘Rosneft Hedge Fund’. In the same case, Singh’s name was associated with the two people who perpetrated the fraud. The company said: “We are the victim here. Our statement has been recorded by the Delhi police and we have been given a clean chit in all the cases.“ These guys misused our company’s name, made a proprietor firm, and cheated the public. They earlier were allegedly into Insurance too, but since then seem to have shut that business now, after a scathing notice by IRDA.[5] A former CM, Babulal Marandi, also warned in 2020 that the company was scamming people by using the likeness of the current CM, Hemant Soren.[6] Jharkhand BJP chief Babulal Marandi warned chief minister Hemant Soren against the possibility of chit fund companies using his face to cheat innocent people of the state. Marandi wrote to Soren on September 13 after he noticed a picture published in the handbook of a Mumbai-based non-finance company, Darwin Platform Group of Companies, in which chief minister Hemant Soren has been shown shaking hands with the company’s chairman, Ajay Harinath Singh. Marandi said CBI was probing a Rs 25,000-crore scam involving a dozen of chit fund companies in the state. Hence, the chief minister should think twice before shaking hands with senior officials of any non-finance company as the company may use the picture to lure innocent people for investment to dupe them later. There is a special investigation going on against them in Haryana.[7] During the investigation being done by the Special Investigation Team constituted in the case of fraud of crores of rupees in the name of investment in Darwin Company, it came to light that the accused profit sharing partners used to get people to invest in the form of referral traders. When the investment was high, he was shifted to another company. The special thing was that transactions worth lakhs of rupees kept happening from the accounts of the investors and they did not even realize it. When an investor asked for the money back, he was brutally beaten up. At present, the names of 30 different companies have come up in the investigation. Police have issued search warrants in search of people wanted in the fraud case. Caveat Emptor!

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Are you pro-life or pro-choice? Why?
Answer: I am pro-choice because the “pro-life” section is a bunch of hypocritical bastards. Firstly, let’s address the nomenclature. “Pro-life” is a marketing gimmick. These folks are just “anti-choice”, or even more accurately “anti-abortion”. They do not care about the life of the child after it is born. They are not out there advocating universal healthcare, free/safe childbirth, actual fucking paternity/maternity leaves, social service, enhanced standard of living. They just want control over women’s bodies. The same people who claim they are “pro-life” seethe at the sight of a homosexual couple adopting children. They would not campaign for promoting sex education or advocating for vasectomy for men. Their entire identity is tied to child birth and their crusade ends when the newborn emerges into the world. Abortion rates in US are now lower than they were prior to Roe v. Wade in 1973.[1] This isn’t the only significant statistic that has gone down since. Women dying due to unsafe abortions has decreased drastically. But women’s life is not the “life” “pro-life” people are hinting at, isn’t it? Let’s do a quick thought experiment. There’s a sick person with a rare blood disease. The only way they will survive is if you consent to attaching them to your body for 9 months. This way they will get the blood required (you are the only viable match because you share a specific genome marker with that person). The process is relatively safe. However, you won’t be able to drink or smoke or consume caffeine in any manner. Your movement is restricted and you suffer from perennial fatigue for the duration of the procedure. However, it is a small price to pay to save a life, isn’t it? There is however some residual risk of you dying due to various complexities that can arise. Will you do it? How would you feel if the government forced it? You really don’t like the idea of the someone else regulating your body, do you? That’s the essence of pro-choice. Our body is probably the only thing we have control over. But for women, this is not even the case. Take Ireland’s example. What it took to spur the nation to legalize abortion was the tragedy of Savita Halappanavar.[2] Halappanavar arrived at hospital on October 21, 2012, complaining of lower back pain that had lasted for around 12 hours. She was 17 weeks into her first pregnancy at the time. After examination, doctors found that Halappanavar's pregnancy was inevitably going to fail due to complications and she was admitted that same day. On October 22 her water broke but the fetus was not expelled. On October 23, Halappanavar and her husband asked whether her labor could be induced since they did not want to wait longer than necessary if the pregnancy was to fail anyway. They were told by a consultant that this was not possible under Irish law—they had not identified adequate risk to the patient. Over time Halappanavar's condition worsened and she was diagnosed with sepsis on October 24. That same day she miscarried and delivered the fetus. She was admitted to an intensive care unit on the morning of October 25, and her health continued to worsen. Halappanavar died on Sunday, October 28. The cause of her death was documented as multi-organ failure following sepsis and E. coli infection. Imagine being in her shoes. Imagine carrying a dead fetus spurring a life-threatening sepsis inside your body. Imagine feeling so fucking helpless in the face of death. This is what “pro-life” people stand for. They would rather a woman die than abort. They would rather a rape victim be forced to live with the trauma of rape for 9 months to birth the offspring of her rapist than abort. They disgust me. And that is why I am “pro-choice”.

Question: Why some people don't like IPL even though it is entertaining?
Answer: I am not a big fan of the IPL. It has its merits, I must admit. It has allowed many players to pursue Cricket as a career which might not have been possible earlier when there were only national teams. It has also allowed India to better catch upcoming talent at a young age and groom them. However, it is not as much Cricket as it is a series of 4-hour long corporate endorsements with Cricket peppered in between. Look at this highlight reel from 1985. The focus is on the game and not who is the “title sponsor”, no one is calling the sixes “DLF Maximum”, there is no “CEAT timeout”. Just this list of sponsors for IPL tells you that this is nothing more than a glorified cash-grab: IPL Sponsors List 2022. Look at how pervasive ads are in IPL now. Question: Is it true that when you reach your 30s, you will stop caring about what other people think?
Answer: 30s isn’t a magical milestone when you wake up one day to the glorious revelation that allowing other people’s opinions to affect you or control how your life plays out is just not worth it. It can happen right now. In your teens. Or your early 20s. Or it can happen later. When you are four decades wise. There’s this Bollywod song that goes, “Kuch to log kahenge, logon ka kaam hai kehna. Chhodo bekar ki baaton mein, kahin beet na jaaye raina”, which translates to “People will always tell you one thing or the other, that is what they do. Ignore this nonsense lest this night goes to waste.” And tell you what, that is a bloody-good philosophy. At the bare minimum, there are 100s of people you love, are friends with, or at least interact in a personal or professional capacity. And most of them will have their opinions, some very likely in conflict with one another. If you decide on the pursuit of appeasment, it is a never-ending road. You will spend your days and nights changing yourself, making sacrifices, and destroying your inner peace. Frank Zappa put it quite strongly, “If you end up with a boring miserable life because you listened to your mom, your dad, your teacher, your priest, or some guy on television telling you how to do your shit, then you deserve it.” So do not wait for your 30s. You’re welcome to the IDGAF side anytime. We have delicious cookies, interesting conversations, and a revigorated mental fortitude 😊.

Question: How do I stop being ashamed of everything I do and step out of my comfort zone?
Answer: I read this quote a few years back and it really helped put things in perspective. “You probably wouldn’t worry about what people think of you if you could know how seldom they do.” ― Olin Miller We aren’t really afraid to fail. We are petrified that people will remember our failures for eternity. However that is not really the case. Try it! Try and think of something embarassing someone you know did last year. It’s hard to recall. And even if you do recall something, you will realize that you had to actively focus on remembering it. You will also realize that you don’t think lesser of them because of their failures. We give ourselves too much credit. We might be the main protagonist in our story, but in everyone else’s, we are either a supporting character or worse an extra in the background. 😊 So go! Unleash yourself. Push your limits. Venture far out of your comfort zone. Fail spectacularly. And laugh about it along with everyone else. Rinse, repeat, live!

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Is it possible to live with little and be happy?
Answer: Life isn’t a sum total of all that you possess, but rather a culmination of all your experiences. In the last few years, there has been a drastic shift from consumerism to an “experience economy”.[1] Recent research from San Francisco State University found that people who spent money on experiences rather than material items were happier and felt the money was better spent. The thrill of purchasing things fades quickly but the joy and memories of experiences, from epic adventures to minute encounters, can last a lifetime. Next time you're feeling a bit down or lacking in some way, before you go out and buy things remember these five tips for evaluating your spending and decide to have experiences instead of just accumulating stuff. I recently spent a good deal of money traveling through Goa and Shillong. Both of these experiences have stayed with me for months now, and I find myself going through pictures of my stay there and reliving my favorite moments. I also got a new phone last week, and I haven’t thought about it much after setting everything up. The net happiness derived from traveling for me has proved to be far greater than acquiring another material possession. “Minimalism” and “decluttering” might sound like some of the new-age buzzwords of the Instagram generation, but they are two very radical, effective ways of living to increase your life satisfaction. Popularized by author Marie Kondo in her book “The Life Changing Magic of Tidying Up”, they offer a fresh perspective on a post-consumeristic life. After the Industrial revolution, access to goods became easier. People started accumating more and more possessions because it was something novel for that time. But having more doesn’t mean much after a certain point of time (the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility). A few starrling statistics were complied by Becoming Minimalist that prove the same. 1. There are 300,000 items in the average American home (LA Times). 2. The average size of the American home has nearly tripled in size over the past 50 years (NPR). 6. British research found that the average 10-year-old owns 238 toys but plays with just 12 daily (The Telegraph). 8. The average American woman owns 30 outfits—one for every day of the month. In 1930, that figure was nine (Forbes). 9. The average American family spends $1,700 on clothes annually (Forbes). 10. While the average American throws away 65 pounds of clothing per year (Huffington Post). 13. Some reports indicate we consume twice as many material goods today as we did 50 years ago (The Story of Stuff). 18. Women will spend more than eight years of their lives shopping (The Daily Mail). 19. Over the course of our lifetime, we will spend a total of 3,680 hours or 153 days searching for misplaced items.The research found we lose up to nine items every day—or 198,743 in a lifetime. Phones, keys, sunglasses, and paperwork top the list (The Daily Mail). 20. Americans spend $1.2 trillion annually on nonessential goods—in other words, items they do not need (The Wall Street Journal). We no longer buy because we need stuff, but because we can. Incomes have risen and good have become cheaper. Add to that the insane power of targeted advertising and marketing, and we end up buying stuff we didn’t really need. But that era is in its final throes. Now we are headed in the subscription+experience economy. People do not own movies or music anymore — they stream/rent it. Same goes for books and comics. You don’t need to own a car, you can call an Uber. No need to purchase a holiday home, you can book a new one everytime on AirBnB. Everything from electronics to clothes to furniture can be rented in most countries. As such, living with little might be the way forward. I recently spent 3 weeks on the road, spending time at my parents’ place and shacking up with a bunch of friends. All I had with me was a backpack and a luggage trolley. I weirdly did not miss anything I possess back home (in my rented apartment). I have also started the “one thing a day” decluttering practice, where I plan to discard or donate one item (book, clothing, utensils, electronics, and all manners of oddities) every single day of 2022. And it is a calming experience. Bhutan’s GDP is just a tad over $3200 per year, ranking about 150th in the world. However, it is one of the happiest countries in the world. That is quite the empirical evidence that economic growth and happiness do not really go hand-in-hand. So next time, you feel the impulse to buy something, shelve it for a day. If the next day, you still feel the urge as strongly, go ahead. You will realize that in most cases, you decide to not buy the thing.

Question: What are some ways to cope with living by yourself?
Answer: The biggest mindshift you can start with is by redefining the question itself. If you think of living by yourself as undesirable, something you have to “cope with”, it’s already a tough road ahead for you. Further paraphrase “living by yourself” to “living with yourself”. You are not alone, you are in your own company. So we basically end up with a radically shifted viewpoint. “What are some ways to enjoy living with yourself?” This is one of the things everyone should experience at least once in their lifetime. Very rarely do you get the chance to be completely with yourself. As a kid, you stay with your parents. Then you’re off to college where you’d be sharing a room or dorm with other students. You start working and its economically the prudent choice to share an apartment with other working professional. Then you get married and share your space with your spouse. Then your kids. Where in all this is the time to truly figure out who you are? They say “you are the average of the 5 people you spend the most time with”. And if none of those 5 is your own self, you risk becoming an amalgamation of various personalities, a derivative being. Living with yourself gives you a chance to discover who you truly are. Pay attention to how you are when there is no one around and you don’t need any filters or masks. Get in touch with your deepest thoughts. Notice how you spend your time. I have been living on my own for 1.5 years now and it can be a really pleasurable and introspective experience. That said, it is not easy (nothing ever really is!) There are times when you feel lonely, when you desire the comfort of companionship, when you feel the urge to talk to someone. However, all of that can be remediated. Because we live in the era of instant connectivity, you can call up your family or friends and see them. You can get on a bunch of dating apps and find someone to have a conversation or a casual encounter with. Boredom, similarly, can be worked on. You need to figure out your hobbies. Create your own personal mini-verses in the house. A comfortable sofa and comfoter so that you can just snuggle up and watch the latest movie or re-runs of your favorite show. A cozy nook for reading. A quiet breezy corner where you can meditate. You can join interest groups and find interesting people to form new connections with. Go hiking. Volunteer at an animal shelter. Head out alone and explore the city on weekends. Plan a solo trip. Pick up the guitar and strum. Paint. Sculpt. Enroll for online classes. Have a teleparty. The avenues are endless, it is up to you to reach out and give them a try. Godspeed stranger!

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Does it get better? I’m 22 and I think that I’m at my lowest.
Answer: No one can know for sure. There’s an age old saying that “it’s darkest before the dawn”. But can you really tell when the darkness is at its peak, except for in hindsight? This isn’t to put you down, or say that what you are going through doesn’t feel like hell. It is but a reminder that things can always get worse; life is a bitch that way. There is no limit to the amount of misery a human can experience. Consider this, you’ve just lost your job and can’t service the mortgage on your house, so it gets repossesed by the bank. You’re now effectively homeless and have zero savings. Feels like rock bottom, doesn’t it? But you’re a resilient one, so you start working on getting a new job, consolidating your debt, declaring bankruptcy and so on. You aren’t gonna give up that easily. However, life has other plans and you come down with a sudden prolonged illness. That is your new “darkest”. Till now. A lot of other things could go wrong too. And if Murphy is to be trusted, they most likely will. Losing a loved one. Being dumped. A natural disaster completely outside your control. Fucking World War 3 because Putin is a total douche. What I am trying to say is that whatever you are facing right now, it could get worse. But it eventually does get better. After all, there is only so much a pendulum can swing one way. Every season is finite. And the only constant in this universe is change. Relentless, gradual change. All you can do is embrace the uncertainty that is the defining characteristic of life and this universe. Be prepared to deal with whatever may come. Keep your head down and your feet running. If you keep pushing, it does get better. Maybe not tomorrow, or the week after. But eventually. The hard part is to keep pushing. Every single day.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Is Raj Thakre right in his opinion on the loudspeaker noise of Azaan?
Answer: Ignore Raj Thackerey for the time being. Ignore what any religious text says. Ignore any other “whatabouteries”. Give me one good objective reason why Azaan should be played on loudspeakers. There is none. Over the years, I have had debates with many people on this issue and I have never received any logical justification to this practice. Any form of noise is a nuisance. There are strict laws around the use of loudspeakers in India. As per the The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000[1] (1) A loud speaker or a public address system shall not be used except after obtaining written permission from the authority. [(2) A loud speaker or a public address system or any sound producing instrument or a musical instrument or a sound amplifier shall not be used at night time except in closed premises for communication within, like auditoria, conference rooms, community halls or during a public emergency.] [(4) The noise level at the boundary of the public place, where loudspeaker or public address system or any other noise source is being used shall not exceed 10 dB (A) above the ambient noise standards for the area or 75 dB (A) whichever is lower; (5) The peripheral noise level of a privately owned sound system or a sound producing instrument shall not, at the boundary of the private place, exceed by more than 5dB (A) the ambient noise standards specified for the area on which it is used.] Explicit written permission is required for use of loudspeakers and there are decibel restrictions on the same. However, in India none of these are enforced. Imagine living in a densely populated residential area and being woken up at 5 AM due to Azaan from multiple mosques nearby. Despite the prolonged lockdowns in 2020 and first half of 2021, noise levels in Indian metros were far higher than the prescribed norms[2]. Noise pollution is a huge issue for a developing, overly populated country like India. And this issue is not even specific to India. Loudspeakers are banned in many developed and developing countries. Even in Saudi Arabia, an Islamic nation, the government had restricted the loudspeaker volume to one-third of its maximum.[3] Azaan is a call to prayer. And even Propher Muhammad was never in favor of using bells or horns to call devotees.[4] Azaan is the Muslim call to prayer, made five times a day from a mosque, for believers to join the congregational prayer. Prophet Muhammad instituted this practice after he migrated to Medina, and built a mosque there. As to the method of calling people to the mosque for the five periodic prayers, he deliberated the issue with his companions. Some suggested ringing a bell, some blowing a horn, and some lighting a fire. But, under divine inspiration, the Prophet decided on the human voice, and chose a manumitted Black slave, Bilal, for making the call. The human voice, even if it were the baritone of Bilal, couldn’t be as loud and couldn’t go as far as the mechanically produced sound of a bell or a horn. Yet, the Prophet chose the low-decibel human voice over the high-decibel mechanical sound. Clearly, there is a lesson in it for his followers who should consider whether the mechanically amplified sound of a loudspeaker remains the human voice that the Prophet might approve of. They would also do well to reflect on whether attaching religious import to the use of such a contraption amounts to a reprehensible novelty called bid’at, — that is, an innovation which distorts the religion. Sadly, now the use of loudspeakers is just another means of “showing-off” and forcing ones beliefs on others. Loudspeakers have become prominent in the last few years and is more like a “dick-measuring contest” between various mosques. The ubiquity of loudspeakers in the mosque is of fairly recent origin. In the 1970s, it started becoming pervasive. First, it was installed as a bauble of superficial modernity to reflect the self-esteem of the local community, which, in its growing affluence, couldn’t be seen lagging behind the neighbouring Muslim community, which had already fitted their mosques with loudspeakers. However, it was always met with much scepticism and some resistance because it was not only seen as an intrusion of modernity in the timeless space of religion, but the blaring sound was also regarded as shaitani awaz — devilish sound — which was not fit for the sanctity of a mosque. But all of the above is probably lost on India’s extreme Left who would bend over backwards to “appease” the minorities.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What will you do if you are made Finance Minister of India and given complete autonomy?
Answer: Crackdown on tax evasion. India has a notoriously poor system for monitoring taxes and applying stringent penalties to the defaulters. Even though GST has streamlined indirect taxes to a large extent, there is still massive tax evasion that happens. Then there are corporations abusing global tax loopholes. India is losing more than $10.3 billion (around Rs 75,000 crore) in taxes every year due to international corporate tax abuse and private tax evasion, according to a report by the State of Tax Justice. It’s high time to relook at DTAA (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement) treaties that India has in place with various nations to ensure that they are not being abused. The income tax collections are the most suspect due to the informal nature of the economy and the fact that unlike in the US, there are rarely any IT audits that happen. And no one abuses this system more than the already uber-rich.[1] Few would contest that India’s tax system leaves a lot to be desired when it comes to checking evasion, but lo and behold: there could be some 68,000 individuals in the country earning above Rs 5 crore a year when the official I-T returns show only 5,000 people with such income. Similarly, the number of people with taxable income between Rs 1 crore and Rs 5 crore could actually be 10 times what the I-T database shows and in the Rs 50 lakh-Rs 1 crore income range, there could be 11 people tucking themselves away from the taxman’s gaze for every individual reporting such income. FE has juxtaposed the I-T data for FY16 with the Household Survey on India’s Citizen Environment & Consumer Economy (ICE 360° Survey), conducted by the People Research on India’s Consumer Economy (PRICE) for the reference period, April 2015 to March 2016, to bring to light these astounding facts. Some quick back of the envelope calculations shows that 63000 additional people paying 1.5 crores of median tax (with income over 5 crores) would net the coffers 100,000 crores in tax. Between 1–5 crores of income, there were about 1,40,000 returns filed in 2019. FE claims that this number is under-reported by about 90%, implying 11,00,000 people not paying their due. Median income of 2 crores would yield about 50–60 lakhs in taxes, pointing to evasion to the tune of 6 lakh crores. Finally farmers and religious institutes in India are exempt from taxes which translates to many rich farmers not paying taxes, corporations claiming agricultural tax exemption and the uber-rich exploiting this loophole too. In a reply to a question in Lok Sabha[2], it was revealed that many major corporations have availed benefits of the tax exemption amounting to hundreds of crores. Total income declared for exemption was Rs 9000 crore. And this is just the declaration — a lot of folks in rural areas do not even file tax returns. Taxing the income would ensure many things: A lot of the farmers have very small land holdings and can only produce enough to feed themselves. That is one of the key arguments for exempting farm income from taxation. And it should be the case. Plus even for folks that sell their products, there is always the question of the “cost of production” which cannot be easily estimated — money paid to contract laborers, equipment cost, fuel, seeds, irrigation, etc. However, the same can be mitigated to an extent by considering the extension of the formal banking system to a large chunk of the population, and by devising a different tax structure for farmers. A 2015 report[3] by Prof Ranganathan found that almost two-thirds of the farmers own less than 1 hectare of land. Let’s assume that one hectare is just sufficient to feed the family and have some extra cash for other expenses. As such, farmers with declared lands of less than one or two hectares would directly come under exemption. For the rest, the same tax slabs could be applied with deductions allowed (on reproduction of proper bills, just like the way HRA and other deductibles work) up to a certain extent. There should also be classification based on what is being produced. There was a recent report[4] that a few select farmers were earning in excess of 3 lakh/acre by growing herbs etc which would translate to 7.5 lakh/hectare, which even after input cost deduction would easily come under the lowest tax bracket. Assuming half the population is in farming, and an average rural farming household has 5 people, we have about 12 crore families. As per the above data, 10% have land holdings above 2 hectares, implying 1.2 crore eligible taxpayers. We currently have 2.8 crore taxpayers (including the ones with zero tax liability). Even if their average tax liability is lower than the current taxpayer population, let’s say 50%, it would effectively mean adding another 0.6 crore taxpayers, increasing total income tax collection by about 20%, or about 2 lakh crore. The same should apply to all religious institutes who need to be run like a firm. Although some services provided by them have been brought under the ambit of GST — food tariffs, sale of cds, books etc — tax on income is still not applicable. If you have religious trusts earning hundreds of crores a year, you need to pay taxes just like everyone else. Salaried individuals pay taxes on their income and then pay GST on stuff they buy. Such huge religious institutions should be mandated to follow proper accounting principles and be taxed under the corporate law. The Tirupati temple[5] alone earned more than 2800 crore in 2018 as income. Assuming a paltry 20% profit margin, it would have netted 500–600 crore in profits and should ideally have paid 150–200 crore as tax. An article in Deccan Herald[6] noted that the state had 171 temples earning more than 20L (and hence under the ambit of GST). It seems even gods cannot exempt themselves from GST, as 171 temples in Andhra Pradesh above Rs 20 lakh income have come under the new tax regime. There are 23,834 temples in the state, of which 45 temples come under the Rs 1 crore income category, 63 temples up to Rs 25 crore and seven temples with more than Rs 25 crore annual income, including Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), the country’s richest. Sum up and you get ~Rs 4000 Crore as the total income. Assuming 20% EBITA, the total taxable income should have been Rs 800 Crore, leading to about ~250 Crore in taxes. Andhra is home to about 4% of Indian population. Assuming uniform distribution of temples as per population, the total tax collection would have been 25x, or about Rs 6000 crore. Add Gurudwaras, Mosques, and Churches, and the government can net up to Rs 10,000 crore annually. If you sum up all the major numbers: GST - 93,000 crores Global tax evasion - 75,000 crores Income tax evasion - 7,00,000 crores Farmers - 2,00,000 crores We are essentially talking about increasing India’s tax collection by over 50%. It is high time the governments and the IT department formalize some draconian measures to curb such rampant stealing.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What lessons do people in their 30s know that they wish they'd known in their 20s?
Answer: But Mouse, you are not alone, In proving foresight may be vain: The best-laid schemes of mice and men Go oft awry, And leave us nothing but grief and pain, For promised joy! – Robert Burns, “To A Mouse” I have always had a blueprint for my life. I like to plan things, down to the most minute details. I love creating checklists and detailed processes for every single task. So it is natural that I also had my life figured out — fell in love at 17, graduated at 23, got married at 25. Had a well-paying, stable job. A bunch of hobbies to keep me entertained. I knew how much I had to save for a comfortable retirement. I knew where I wanted to settle down. I had planned the kind of house I wanted to build. And all was fine and dandy until an unfortunate evening in the penultimate month of 2020. I haven’t talked about what transpired then. I don’t think I can even put it into words; recapping that episode for the therapy sessions itself is a daunting task. Needless to say, that day the first domino fell, kickstarting a personally catastrophic chain reaction that drastically changed the trajectory of my life, altered the very basic fabric of my personality, and shaped the way 2021 turned out to be (it was horrible btw). Every single plan of mine came crumbling down. And in a very long time, I felt absolutely clueless. Fearful of a future that seemed rife with uncertainty. I became a broken, shattered visage of the man I used to be, who couldn’t even figure out how to get through the day, let alone plan the next few years. It took more than a year of suffering and perseverance, the unyielding support of my family and some amazing friends, therapy and counselling to claw back some semblance of the previous sanity and stability. So, “What lessons do people in their 30s know that they wish they'd known in their 20s?” That life is nothing more than a butterfly effect that we live through, albiet one that we have some degree of control over. But every now and then, it just picks you up and shakes you down just to let you know who’s the ultimate boss. It breaks you down and picks you apart. It disperses every single piece of you in random directions making you scramble for them. You find some, some are lost for eternity. And by the time it is done, you are left with nothing but with shattered remains of your previous self and a choice — to either buckle down and accept your fate, or to buckle up and rebuild, knowing very well that life isn’t done. With every year that passes, the probability of you encountering such uncontrollable, transformational episodes increases. It could be anything — a heartbreak, the loss of a loved one, failing health, financial losses, or just plain old innui. Just make sure you are prepared. Equipped to deal with the aftermath. Be adaptable. Be open to asking for help. Be willing to let go. Be resilient enough to weather these inevitable storms. And ensure you figure out who you are at the core of being. That is the only thing that will stay with you.

Question: Some people are saying that Hindus should boycott “Halal” certified products in India. Do you agree with this?
Answer: The recent controversy around Himalaya products being Halal certified despite branding themselves as purely herbal is a good starting point. India is a Hindu-majority country. And most Hindus are pure vegetarians. They abstain from all meat and meat-related products. Hence the demand for the “herbal” segment. Someone leaked an email response from the firm on one of their products. Imagine a capsule that is branded “Pure Herb” containing byproducts of meat, and that too of cow. Hindus revere cows as holy animals. Just like Muslims abstain from anything remotely containing pork, Hindus would never consume anything containing beef. But this firm that has been calling itself Herbal and has branded itself after the pious Himalayas has been secretly adding cow remains to their products. This is consumer fraud. Then there is the second angle to the entire Halal certification market. Only a Muslim man can slaughter the animal. In many texts, it is also mentioned that if Jews and Christians slaughter the animals following the rest of the steps (Halal procedure), the meat is halal as per the Islamic dietary laws. The Quranic verse must be read while slaughtering the animal and is known as Tasmiya or Shahada. Meat is only considered Halal if slaughtered by a Muslim while reciting specific Quranic verses. And the certification is provided by specific Halal committees that comprise mostly Muslims. This is a form of economic discrimination against non-Muslims. The simple chain of events is: Most firms are taking this route since there is no alternative demand in the market. Do you remember the Indian Mutiny of 1857? That happened because the cartridges, which had to be bitten, were smeared with cow and pig fat, hurting the sentiments of both the Hindu and Muslim soldiers. If the mutiny was acceptable, a boycott surely is since it follows the same principle of respecting the religious beliefs of everyone.

Question: What was the worst part of The Batman (2022), and what was the best part?
Answer: The best part of Matt Reeve’s Batman was the fact that it truly explored the “detective” side of Batman and gave us a peek into the raw, unpolished, “Year Zero” version of the Caped Crusader. Although Nolan’s Batman also showed us his origins, this version always was well-trained and ready to kick-ass even when he was just starting out. However, Reeve’s Batman is clearly a young PTSD billionaire orphan that just decided to don a kevlar suit and makeup to fight the bad guys. The lack of any formal fight training is evident in the fights where he struggles against any large group. Having the Riddler as the main villain was just the perfect choice to bring out the detective. After all, when you are against someone whose primary forte is his mind, you can’t be challenging him to a fistfight. The worst part of Batman was the Joker tease in the final act. The Joker is one of the greatest fictional villains of all time. But we already have gotten more than enough renditions of him in the last few years. Ledger’s Joker brought “the chaos”. Phoenix’s Joker brought the tragedy and the pain. Monaghan’s Joker brought the unhinged psychopath vibes. Leto’s Joker brought….er…something (?) It’s time to put the spotlight on some more villains. The Batman has one of the most elaborate rogue galleries of any superhero and there are so many underutilized characters that deserve a silver-screen treatment. And a lot of them would really fit with the whole detective thriller angle that Reeves is going for. If the movies progress and encompass more of Batman’s facets, Mr. Freeze and Poison Ivy could (and should) be introduced to the ReevesVerse.

Question: What does it make sense to spend money on?
Answer: Anything you use for extended periods of time on a regular basis. A good mattress You are going to spend a third of your life sleeping, so it makes sense to invest in a good-quality mattress. Not getting proper sleep (quantity and quality) causes drowsiness, issues with concentration and performance, and long-term back pains. Appropriate shoes I have had slight flat feet (overpronation) since childhood. It has now started causing pain in my left leg. A quick visit to the ortho confirmed that “regular” shoes are not appropriate for people with this condition (~30% of the population). Invest in shoes (and footwear) designed specifically to help with this. Workstation Most people work on laptops and computers nowadays. The increasing adoption of WFH means that you need to have a proper workstation. A chair that provides the right level of support for your back and neck and an adjustable table to ensure the screen is at eye height. High-quality headphones/earphones If you take a lot of calls or listen to music/podcasts frequently, do your ears a favor and get some good quality headphones/earphones. They allow for proper noise-cancellation allowing you (in a noisy world) to better focus, high-quality sound leading to a better, more immersive experience, and are easier on your ears.

Question: How can suffering be an opportunity to transform yourself and the world around you?
Answer: The Holocaust was one of the darkest periods that humanity has witnessed and endured. Over the course of years, tens of millions of Jews were hunted, imprisoned, tortured, and killed. If you read through the memoirs of the survivors of concentration camps, you will come across amazing tales of human endurance and how these survivors later channeled their sufferings into meaningful pursuits. In his magnum opus, Man’s Search for Meaning, Dr. Viktor Frankl describes how the same horrifying experiences can lead to starkly different reactions and changes in people. “A human being is not one thing among others; things determine each other, but man is ultimately self-determining. What he becomes - within the limits of endowment and environment- he has made out of himself. In the concentration camps, for example, in this living laboratory and on this testing ground, we watched and witnessed some of our comrades behave like swine while others behaved like saints. Man has both potentialities within himself; which one is actualized depends on decisions but not on conditions.” The same sentiment is echoed in the Cherokee fable “The Two Wolves”.[1] Every experience – positive or negative, depressing or reassuring, exhilarating or deeply painful – leads you to a crossroads. Some people let success get to their head, some imbibe the core learnings from it and chalk out the path to even greater achievements. Some people stay embittered after being hurt by others, harboring feelings of resentment towards their perpetrators, while others eventually choose to forgive and move on. Everyone is capable of both, it’s the choice they make that matters. There’s the Indian legend of “The Mountain Man”, a man with both the metaphorical willpower of mountains and the literal ability to move them. Dashrath Manjhi lived in a remote village in Bihar, India. When his wife met with an accident, he could not get her in time to the nearest doctor (~100 kms away) because of the serpentine mountainous terrain. His wife succumbed to the injuries. Any other man would have been broken, resentful. But Dashrath channeled his grief and suffering into a monumental quest that lasted more than 2 decades. Armed with just his hands and a “stone-age” hammer and chisel, he started chipping at the same mountain that had been in the way of his wife getting the required treatment. Eventually the immovable object surrendered to Manjhi’s sheer unstoppable willpower. Manjhi carved out a 110 m long tunnel, reducing the distance between his village and the next by 40km.[2] He took a hammer, chisel and nails and started hammering the hill, working day and night for almost 22 years. People considered him mad, but he still continued with his exemplary efforts and carved out a 360 feet long, 30 feet high and 25 feet wide passage through the Gehlour hills, which reduced the distance between Atri and Wazirganj from 55 km to 15 km. When Gautam Buddha, the royal prince, saw the suffering of human around him (despite concerted efforts from his father to shield him from such), he set on a search for enlightenment, culminating in the foundations of the religion and philosophy of Buddhism. When Malala Yousafzai was shot in the head by the Taliban at the age of 15, she not only survived, but intensified her campaign against the Taliban, inspiring millions across the world. Of course that is not always the case. Men like Manjhi are rare. And not eveyone is expected to transform the course of the human race. But you can always transform your personal life. The weightlifter, Matthias Steiner, lost his wife in 2007. For some time, he could not even train, let alone compete. However, he had made a promise to his late wife that he would one day be the Olympic champion. So he persisted. Things during the competition also did not go according to plan. After the Snatch, he placed 4th in the rankings. In his final attempt for the Clean and Jerk, he had to best the leader by 10 kgs if he had to win that gold. And he did. “That was the great thing, I didn’t have to wait for everyone else to fail at their attempts. I just could go out on stage and finish it myself. I felt I could have lifted anything that day, whether I actually could have is a different matter.” In the end, he stood there on the podium, having fulfiled his promise, and holding a picture of his wife, knowing she was watching. His journey, in his own words, is a testament to how humans can find courage and strength even in the bleakest of times. “It’s hard to describe. You think you’ve got your life figured out, I was completely focused on the Olympic Games, my wife was studying, she had her career in front of her. Then, one day it’s just over.” “I had to make a decision, whether to just stop or to carry on weightlifting. I realized that even if I stopped, what had happened was not going to change. It’s going to stay with me for the rest of my life.” And this should be the key takeaway. Whatever has happened, is in the past. The unmutable, unchangeable past. You can not go back and make a different decision. But that does not mean that you cannot change the future trajectory of your life. This is best illustrated by Tim Urban from “Wait, but Why?” in this gorgeous graphic.

Question: Who's side will India take in the Russia-Ukraine war?
Answer: In the ongoing Russia-Ukraine crisis, India is going to be one of the few major economies that will carefully tread the thin line called bureaucracy. Firstly, let’s get one thing straight: Russia is the clear aggressor here and most of the world (rightly) is supporting Ukraine. That includes Indians too. But the Indian government is in a precarious spot - the humanitarian choice is to support Ukraine and impose sanctions and trade bans with Russia to hurt them financially. However, Russia has been India’s closest ally, especially when it comes to matters of the military. Two-thirds of Indian military imports are from Russia, and it makes up for a third of Russia’s military exports. [1] The Indian Army's main battle tank force is composed predominantly of Russian T-72M1 (66 per cent) and T-90S (30 per cent), it said. The CRS said the Indian Navy's sole operational aircraft carrier is a refurbished Soviet-era ship, and its entire complement of fighter and ground attack aircraft are Russian-made or produced in India on license. The Navy's fighter fleet comprises 43 MiG-29K/KUBs, it said. "Four of the Navy's 10 guided-missile destroyers are Russian Kashin class, and six of its 17 frigates are Russian Talwar class. The Navy's sole nuclear-powered submarine is on lease from Russia, and eight of the service's 14 other submarines are Russian-origin Kilo class," it said. "Finally, the Indian Air Force's 667-plane FGA fleet is 71 per cent Russian-origin (39 per cent Su-30s, 22 per cent MiG-21s, nine per cent MiG-29s). All six of the service's air tankers are Russian-made Il-78s," CRS report said. During the Kargil war of 1999 with Pakistan, the US, which has always shielded and funded Pakistan, denied India access to GPS, severely limiting the ability of the Indian forces to carry out a proper offensive.[2] When Pakistani troops took positions in Kargil, one of the first things Indian military sought was GPS data for the region. The space-based navigation system maintained by the US government denied India access to vital information. On the other hand, Russia’s help was instrumental in India winning the 1971 war. While the US, UK, and the West was aligned with Pakistan, it was the former Soviet Union that sent all the help they could.[3] It is well-known that when the Americans and British sent their navies into the Bay of Bengal (task force 74 and task force Eagle respectively) the Soviet navy confronted them. Under Admiral V Kruglyakov, the Soviet navy deliberately let its nuclear submarines surface, to be picked up by American satellites, to threaten the American surface fleet. The Soviets also organised a flotilla of cruisers and destroyers under task force 40 to help Admiral Kruglyakov's much smaller force. Faced with these twin threats, the US and British task forces withdrew from the Bay of Bengal and could not interfere with Indian land operations in erstwhile East Pakistan now Bangladesh. Finally, India is also heavily dependent on Russia for fertilizer imports, which for a primarily agrarian economy like India are supercritical. The world right now is no longer “bipolar”. It is split into 3 factions - the Western bloc comprising of the US, Canada, and the EU nations, China and all the countries it has “financially conquered” and the trio of India, Russia, and Israel. And although Putin here is clearly the warmonger, the Indian government will never publicly chastise them. This is the extent of what we can expect.
