Question: Why should I read books if I go back to being my "same old self" forgetting what I learned from it after a few days?
Answer: One of the greatest essayists and lecturers to have ever lived noted, “I cannot remember the books I've read any more than the meals I have eaten; even so, they have made me.” (Ralph Waldo Emerson) And therein you have your answer. Reading has many purposes, but memorization isn’t one of them. One reads to escape the humdrum of the real life. Or to explore a fascinating part of human history, in a different era and a different area. We look up to books for comfort, for knowledge, for inspiration. Anything you read stays with you, even if you might not be able to exactly recollect lines from it. I read the Alchemist a long time ago, I barely remember a couple of lines. But the central theme (“we are in control of our destiny”) stays with me. The same goes for To Kill A Mockingbird. I still think/find that my thoughts and actions are influenced, ever so slightly, by the wisdom of Atticus Finch, or the innocence of Scout. Harry Potter taught me the value of bravery and friendship (and how the two are interlinked). Enid Blyton’s Famous 5 was a great childhood companion and I cherish every morning, afternoon, and evening spent in their company. RK Narayan’s narrative set in the rustic town of Malgudi was the perfect nostalgia trip. And not all books even need to have a lasting impact - if they manage to provide you an escape for the duration of your read, rile up your emotions, or make an otherwise gloomy day brighter, it’s all worth it.

Question: What do you think about Naomi Osaka withdrawing from the French Open?
Answer: “Her body, her rules”, right? Then why isn’t it “her mind, her rules”? Osaka is currently the most successful and highest-earning female tennis star who roped in $55 mn in match winnings and endorsements last year. She had made it clear that she cannot do post-match interviews at the start of the Roland Garros.[1] The message couldn’t be clearer. Press conferences are useless. You just have the same fucking stupid questions lined up that the players have addressed multiple times. And this isn’t the first time the current champion has been vocal about it. Just a couple of days after defeating Serena Williams in that frazzling US Open final in September, Osaka said of the mental health challenges facing elite athletes: "You can easily get depressed. You think your whole world is over." Last April, having won her biggest title to date at Indian Wells, Osaka revealed: "Yesterday I woke up and I was really depressed, but I don't know why. Like, I'm so sad right now." What people fail to understand is that mental health issues do not crop up only when you’re losing. There is no set formula to predict how your mental health is going to pan out. There are these subtle subconscious events that can trigger a breakdown. And what’s the fucking use of press conferences anymore? Athletes have open access to their fans and followers through social media. If Osaka wants to say something, she can tweet it out. Why subject players to a pandemonium of journalists barking at them like rabid dogs? And especially after they have been through a grueling match just before that? My mental health has been in the doldrums over the last half a year. And I can personally vouch for how fucking debilitating it is. There have been days where I dreaded even the smallest, most casual interaction. Weekends where I didn’t leave the house and switched off my phone because I just could not bear to see or talk to another human being. I know the effort it takes to maintain one’s sanity. It’s a continuous ongoing battle and you cannot let your guards down. And another thing people don’t understand that physical and mental wellness is interconnected. I recently got my first covid jab and I was down with fever and bodyache for 2 straight days. While my mental health over the entire month of May was as good as it could be, those 2 days were horrible. The pain in my body translated to mental stress and fatigue and I could sense my brain spiraling out of control. I have immense respect for Osaka for sticking to her guns and for prioritizing her mental health over a fucking tournament. She already has earned more than she needs and if sports are going to continue to be as rigid and demanding, I hope they die off. Players should be judged based on their on-field performance, not their speeches or their interviews.

Question: Should we blame the Indian government for the second wave of covid-19?
Answer: Oh, abso-fucking-lutely! Indian government massively fucked up when it comes to handling the second COVID wave in India. Just to be clear, others are at fault too. As soon as we saw the daily numbers dwindling in Dec-Jan, the public dropped all precautions. Everywhere you could see people not wearing masks, flocking to supermarkets and malls just for fun, and disregarding all manners of social distancing. Companies started calling people back to office, with such hurry that you’d have thought they’d die out if their employees didn’t start working on premise. Never mind the fact that the same companies survived for almost a year with people working remotely. I just have no fucking clue what the rush was. But all of that aside, the majority of the blame for where we are lies with the government. In the first quarter of 2021, the central and state governments did fuck all to prepare for what was an inevitable second wave. All they needed to do was to look at Spain and Italy and the US to see that just because we weathered the first attack, didn’t mean jackshit. All they needed to do was to listen to experts who’d modeled and predicted the behavior of pandemics to an eerie degree of accuracy to see that the second and third waves would be deadlier as the virus mutated and adapted. All they needed to do was not lower their guard and use the period of the relative lull to fortify the nation’s defenses. But what did we get? JACK SHIT! - Vaccine manufacturing wasn’t ramped up. We knew SII could only produce ~80 mn doses every month at maximum capacity for the complete population. And Bharat Biotech just about 10 mn. Why weren’t other pharma companies looped in for vaccine manufacturing? Why wasn’t SII granted funds to increase capacity? Why did we not negotiate deals for vaccine import to prepare for a rapid surge? - The entire Kumbh fiasco should never have happened. It’s not even about the fact that 50 mn people attended a religious gathering, every person coming into close contact with thousands of people, and then going back to various parts of India as superspreaders, but about the overall signaling. You see that shit happening and everyone assumes that things have normalized. They hadn’t. - The PM is not just an administrator or jansevak as he so often calls himself. He is a role model (for better or worse) for millions. When you see him hold rallies in Bengal and Assam, the false feeling of security that everything is alright now is amplified. More caution thrown to the wind! - No enhancements were done to ensure that our medical infrastructure was propped up to support the inevitable tsunami of cases. In Feb, a parliamentary panel had warned of Oxygen shortage. The industrial producers should have been asked to start stocking up oxygen for medical use. Empty buildings and railway coaches should have been prepared as isolation wards. Hospitals should have been stocked up with essential medicines, other supplies, and medical equipment. Again, nothing was done! We are a country where 600 million people cast their vote in just under 2 months. We have run multiple massive polio inoculation campaigns where hundreds of million doses were administered in just days. Imagine, 110 million doses in just 3 days. And our COVID vaccination rate is 2 million per day. We had the infrastructure to vaccinate the entire population in just 2–3 months. All the government needed to do was to prioritize the fight against the pandemic. Instead, we saw a total disregard for the common man when the state elections rolled out. Question: It has been almost a year since the lock-downs started around the world. What did you do in these 12 months and what are your plans for the future?
Answer: The last 12 months have been such a wild ride. The entire world has changed and things from before the pandemic feel so weird now. And my personal life has mirrored this insane global metamorphosis. I switched jobs for the first time ever. Came out of my shell and ventured into unknown territories. I also moved out of Mumbai after 7.5 years of a wonderful stay there. Sometime, around the halfway mark of the pandemic anniversary, my life started to turn upside down. I went through probably the toughest period of my to date. I firsthand experienced how truly debilitating depression can be. In my 3 decades on this planet, I have always been physically and mentally healthy. But all of that changed during the last two months of the travesty that was 2020. For a time I tried fighting it all alone, believing relying on other people to be a sign of weakness. And then I couldn’t. I started spiraling deeper into a bottomless pit of despair. I stopped reading. I stopped writing. I could not even sit still and watch something for 5 mins. Which is weird because all I was doing physically was staying still. I didn’t go out, didn’t meet others. I stopped picking up calls from friends. The only thing I would do was work. Eat only when I was truly famished. The house was a mess, in a way reflecting what my head looked like. I had to decide soon. Make a move. Fight against it to save me. And I did. I decided to fight it again, this time with a different, better plan. I started opening up. I talked to some of the people closest to me. Made myself completely vulnerable, terrified of how they would react. Made a quick checklist of things I wanted to do every day. Small tasks like making the bed after getting up, doing the dishes first thing in the morning. Putting on my shoes and going out even if for a few minutes. I started working out. Forced myself to laugh. Found comfort in my favorite movies and books. Eventually, I began being vocal about my mental health issues. Started reading about it. Sought therapy. Every day, someone new approached me. Strangers came, with words of comfort. Someone offered to lend an ear and I took up that offer. We ended up talking every day. Developed a bond, that usually takes years, in less than a month. Tried helping a young man navigate his professional rapids. I ended up making more “best friends” in the last 4 months than I have in the last decade. Slowly the bad days started becoming less frequent. Like a “red ball in a box”. I moved to a new place. Decided to start over in a sense. Been pouring myself into work, frantically trying to do everything. And it helps stay shielded from the demons hovering over me. Started a bit of gardening. Being in proximity of nature is so soothing. I also started journaling on the advice of a friend. I do it first thing in the morning and it helps calm the pandemonium of thoughts in my head. In all of this, I have realized that I need to change. Untether my happiness from external factors. Prioritize my well-being (physically, mentally, and emotionally) over everything else. I am now the center of my universe. And I plan to keep it that way.

Just over a year ago, I had written that India’s response to the then “novel” pandemic was one to be appreciated - swift and decisive. [1] Of course, the migrant crisis was yet to unfold. The fact that the government with every fucking thing at its disposal could not make arrangements for the safe transport of its citizens while common men like Sonu Sood rose to the occasion and showed that it was possible was the first indicator of the things to come. Since then, little changed about India’s response. The virus evolved, mutated, adapted. Our COVID strategy remained the same - more lockdowns, more extensions. We sacrificed the economy claiming to value human lives above it. But that was just virtue signaling. The first wave was bad, but it was still manageable. We started seeing a faint light at the end of the tunnel as 2020 drew to a close. We had room to breathe. And to prepare. Every other nation was reeling under far deadlier second and third waves of this pandemic. But India’s situation was improving. Rather than take this welcome break to fortify our defenses and chalk out a more responsive plan to tackle an ever-adapting enemy, the government did NOTHING. ZERO, ZILCH, NADA. Just more virtue signaling. And then the elections started. And all pretenses of caring about the common person were dropped. The “Honorable” PM of India and the equally “venerable” HM showed off pictures of massive rallies in Assam and Bengal at a time when cases started rising again. The world’s largest religious gathering, the Kumbh was allowed to be held, with 5 million-plus in attendance. Just to appease the Hindu vote bank. We had 3–4 months to ramp up our medical infrastructure. To stockpile on beds and masks and PPEs and oxygen. To augment our vaccine manufacturing capacity. We knew India would need close to 1–1.5 billion doses to reach herd immunity. And we knew that the Serum Institute could only produce 70–100 million doses per month at full capacity. And yet nothing was done. April of 2021 has been the worst month in recent Indian history. At least in my living memory. We have seen more than 4 million new cases in the last 3 weeks. We have broken the daily COVID case record multiple times in the last few days. Every day, the numbers go up. Today 350,000. And these are just the official figures. I was talking to a friend of mine who has spent his entire life in Prayagraj. The official numbers being reported from the city are 1000–2000 cases per day. But the ground reality is starkly different. He told me of tens of cases coming from every locality. Of people dying but not getting a hospital appointment. Of another friend who drove all the way to Kanpur for Oxygen. The official Indian figures are easily 3–4x of the reported. In the last few days, I have heard of multiple deaths and infinitely more hospitalizations. ICU beds, Remdesivir, Favipiravir, nothing is available. And even if it is, it is being marked up 20–100x and sold via the fucking parasitic middlemen and brokers. And our government and law enforcement are too powerless (or too complicit) to take any action on it. Citizens have set up processes to disseminate information quickly. On Twitter, Insta, FB, 90% of the posts are people begging for plasma, for oxygen, for ICU beds. And the government representatives are silent. And this is just the start. The critical cases we are seeing today were infected 2–3 weeks back. Our active caseload has tripled since then. The next months or two are going to be the bleakest time in recent Indian history. Far more deaths, far more desperation, far more grief. And all of this is on the hands of the people who were elected to prevent such a thing, the chief among them our self-proclaimed “Pradhan Sevak”. Remember, "The bells will toll, and they will toll for thee."

Question: What is your view on the idea that boys should do all housework and not girls?
Answer: To start off, I will confess that I have never heard this particular statement. That does not mean that the question has a false premise, just that it is not a mainstream opinion. When you have 7.5 billion people, even the craziest of ideas will have proponents. But let’s take the question at its face value and decode the utter absurdity of making such sweeping generalizations. Firstly, whenever one makes a statement that discriminates between two sets of people (by gender, race, religion, etc), a quick litmus test to see if that claim is “equitable” is to reverse the roles. Would it be acceptable if I were to say, “girls should do all housework and not boys”? Obviously, this has largely been the case historically across cultures and regions, but we are making progress on this front. And if I did make the above preposterous statement, the fourth-wave feminists would be out in full force outside my house, with their shining pitchforks and their flaming torches. By that logic alone, the original statement is discriminatory.  Now let’s look at it from a different perspective. In a household, who should do the chores? The answer is quite simple. Assume a household that consists of a married couple. One of them is working a job, the other one is not. Considering that being a homemaker is also a full-time role (although unpaid and mostly unappreciated), the one not working an external job should logically pick up all the housework. But that does not mean that the other person should not do anything and make the homemaker tend to them and clean up after them. But the responsibility of cleaning the place, doing the laundry and the dishes, shopping for groceries, tending to the garden, cooking meals, etc. is on the homemaker. But there’s another caveat here. The “working” partner (and I put it on quotes for a reason) gets weekends and holidays off, but the role of a homemaker knows no such luxury. So it is then logical that both the partners pitch in during off days.  People sometime ask why one should do the household chores when most of them can be “outsourced” now. Especially in households where both the partners are working, it makes economic sense to hire a help for the chores. Question: What do you think about the decision to bring OTT streaming platforms (like Netflix, Amazon Prime, etc.) and digital/online news media under Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) in India? How will this affect the content?
Answer: This move is akin to the creation of the universe. “In the beginning the Universe was created. But when the government enters the equations and tries to play the moral mediator, it becomes a very slippery slope. Remember when The Satanic Verses was banned by the Indian government because it supposedly “hurt the sentiments” of Indian Muslims? This is just the same but on the opposite side of the spectrum. If Hindus are offended by the content on Netflix, they are free to not watch it. The government should not be in the fucking picture at all. The need of the hour is to remove archaic censorship laws, do away with insane slander/libel rules, and uphold absolute freedom of speech. Question: Cred has raised 450 million dollars so far with the zero revenue in year 2019, then why do investors still invest such hefty amount in such startups?
Answer: Investors invest based on future potential and not historicals. Cred seems to have a very clear idea of what it wants to do. It started off as a seamless way to track and manage your credit card payments. And they enticed their early users with amazing offers. I knew people who got high-quality headphones and other stuff in exchange for paying their credit card bills on Cred. And that got me interested too. However, over the last few months, as they have acquired more and more customers, such lucrative deals have vanished. They now boast more than 3 million users with credit scores above 750.[1] Their target audience is the well-to-do, aspirational, urban Indian youth. Despite the lack of any cool freebies, I still use Cred because of the convenience. Cred is slowly evolving into a curated premium online shopping experience. If you look at their catalog, you will see brands you have never heard of. They have done a fabulous job of listing products from niche, luxury brands. The brands themselves are usually new startups which get good exposure to their target market segment (the Cred userbase) and Cred can clearly differentiate themselves from other marketplaces that sell anything and everything like Amazon, Flipkart, Paytm Mall, etc. Cred has successfully managed to find and capture a niche market demand. And they are doing a great job executing their strategy to near perfection. The same is reflected in their valuation and investor sentiment.

Question: What are your thoughts on banning crackers only during Diwali? What are different ways to handle situations better during Diwali?
Answer: I see it as akin to asking people to drive carefully during the rains. Accidents happen all year long but are far more likely when the roads are wet and slippery. Yes, firecrackers are used during New Years’ and Christmas and weddings etc during the year, but considering that India is 80% Hindu, the contribution of firecracker pollution during Diwali is the highest. There is repeated historical evidence for this from the last few years. But we never learn — As Delhi flouts cracker ban, air quality dips day after Diwali. The AQI for PM 2.5 pollutant stood at 460 in Pusa, 475 in Patparganj, 450 in Lodhi Road, 491 in Ashok Vihar, 500 in Jahangirpuri and 442 in the IGI airport area. An AQI between 101 and 200 is considered moderate, 201-300 ‘poor’, 301- 400 ‘very poor’ and 401-500 ‘severe’, while the AQI above 500 falls in the severe plus category. With many Delhiites ignoring the cracker ban in the city, on Saturday night, the AQI was recorded as 414 — the worst AQI in the city since 2016 on Diwali. On Friday, it dipped to 339 — in the ‘very poor’ category. For the norther part of India, this situation is exacerbated even further due to the winter season that lends itself to the creation of deadly smog (smoke + fog) and the fact that this is also the time when the farmers in Punjab and Haryana burn their stubble to prepare the fields for the next harvest. There was also a paper published that tracked the pollutant levels over an 8-day period before, during, and after Diwali — Page on ejournal.unam.mx The results clearly show that pollution levels spike considerably during the festival. Finally considering that this year we are already fighting a pandemic that severely impairs breathing, saying no to firecrackers should have been the only logical choice. India is already the #5 most polluted country in the world — World's Most Polluted Countries in 2019 - PM2.5 Ranking. And there has never been concrete policies to combat the same. Firecrackers should be closely regulated. Green crackers should eventually be made the only option. For festival days, there should be a specific time when people are allowed to burst firecrackers and there should be cracker-free zones, especially near hospitals etc. Private events should need to seek permission to use them. And we should extend this to everything — vehicle emissions, factory emissions, crop burning, loud horns, single-use plastics, dumping chemical wastes into rivers, etc. But yes, Diwali is a good starting point since it severely impacts the air quality for days.

A neighbour comes to see what the ruckus is about, and the mother is gleeful as she tells him that these are investors, rushing to bank on ‘Chintu’, their elementary school son who has built an app. The neighbour is visibly jealous. Haria’s video pokes fun at the cinematography, the acting, along with self-deprecating jokes about how he has “wasted six years of his life” not learning how to code. It was uploaded on his channel, called Just Jihan, on Sunday afternoon, and Haria was pleased to see that it seemed to be doing well. But when he woke up from a post-lunch siesta, he was in for a shock: The video had been taken off YouTube for copyright violations, presumptively because it used footage from the advert itself. His channel had got one strike; with three strikes, the channel is taken down entirely. If you search for links about the two companies on Twitter or Reddit and follow-through, most of them will lead to the following. But that is just one side of the story. The other side has Byju’s and WHJ creating multiple fake accounts across social media platforms to flood the portals with fake positive reviews and content to drown out the actual criticism. If you look at the reviews of the app on App Store, you will find a common pattern across the reviews. Question: What are the alternatives of BYJU's?

Question: What disturbed you today?
Answer: I wrote an answer about how BYJU’s silences all of its criticism across social media platforms — Deepak Mehta (दीपक मेहता)'s answer to Why do you hate BYJU's? I also wrote about it on LinkedIn and on Twitter. Around 8 hours ago. An hour ago, I received a call from a random number. I was on another call so I declined. I received the following WhatsApp message. I called them back and had a 30 min discussion. The person on the other end was a senior Byju’s employee who told me he had read a critical piece on Byju’s on Quora and wanted to discuss it. I asked him what he wanted to discuss and he said he just wanted to put forward their side of the story. He went on about Kanthaswamy Balasubramaniam’s post and how it seemed “malicious” to them. Their social media team “analyzed” it and saw that “almost all upvotes” were from Tanzania and other countries. I asked them if they analyzed the tens of thousands of upvotes and the profiles and checked their location and he said yes (which seems quite the impossible feat). I told him that it was still not acceptable that they got it deleted. He responded that they do not have such power and they just reported it. I told them that a single report is unlikely to have triggered the deletion and if what he was saying was true, there was possible mass-reporting from Byju’s employees. He maintained that it was not the case. We also discussed the issue of Dr. Malpani (the VC whose LinkedIn profile was deleted after a string of critical posts about Byju’s) and he said he was in touch with him too and swore they had nothing to do with his account being deleted and that they simply “reported” his content. Finally, we touched on the viral Reddit post where one of their sales managers was abusing a junior associate. He said he was aware of it and they had taken corrective action as soon as they were notified. He accepted that there were issues pertaining to workplace toxicity but they have been addressed. I reiterated that the crux of the issue here is different — how and why did they try to scrub that video off of Reddit. And he maintained the same stance that they did not. After half an hour of hearing excuses, I told him that the fact that he somehow got my number from someone in my social circle, and called me unsolicited within less than 8 FUCKING HOURS of my post being up was a blatant breach of privacy. He said that it was not his intention. I retorted — IT’S 930 PM. And that he had no business calling me up. He could have commented on my posts on the respective social media platform. But he had ABSOLUTELY NO RIGHT to get my number and call me at dinnertime. He went back to the same excuse of trying to “share their side of the story”. And I told him in clear words that his action was just strengthening the case that BYJU’s has an active social media army that tracks all content that is critical of them. I asked him why they do not leverage social media to counter anything that they think is not factual or is actually slander/libel. His excuse was that they are not a very social media savvy company (LO-FUCKING-L). Imagine the biggest EdTech startup in the world claiming that they are not social media savvy! I ended the call asking him to introspect his action today. And to communicate the same to the larger firm. The way to deal with criticism is not to silence it, but accept it and take corrective action. The way to deal with “fake news” and “misinformation” is to disseminate the truth through their own channels instead of calling people in the dead of the night without their permission. I hope it got through. But all of it has left a bad aftertaste. The suddenness of everything. The massive fucking OVER-REACTION about a bunch of posts upvoted/liked by some 3–4k people. The fact that his voice was quivering during the entirety of the call. The lack of convincing responses to queries (“we simply reported them, don’t know how their accounts/content got deleted”, “we don’t do mass reporting”). And I felt a bit scared TBH. I told him that I have been writing for almost a decade now. And I have been critical of a lot of people, corporations, ideologies, political parties, etc. But never across my 4000+ posts have I ever experienced something like this. If the folks over at BYJU’s read this (and I know they will), think about what you are doing. I shared the same advice with your representative on the call, and I will reiterate. “Look inwards. Figure out what you are doing wrong. It is easy to feel on top of the world when you are excelling at everything. Skyhigh valuations, 100%+ YoY growth rate, prestige, etc often go to your head. But none of them will survive if your corporate culture is rotten. One person saying something bad is an isolated incident. 2–3 people saying it might be a coincidence. Thousands of people talking about it points to an actual issue. There are multiple anonymous posts on Twitter and Reddit that all share the same testimony — it’s not about an amazing EdTech firm, but a revenue-hungry company that has sidelined its original mission and the well-being of its employees in the blind pursuit of growth”.

Question: The past year was so tough. I am trying to fight back but sometimes I feel like giving up. I feel like I am stuck in a void. Sometimes I want to feel and think nothing for a few minutes, to rest a bit. I am 23 but feel 53. Can someone help me?
Answer: I call this the quarter-life crisis. 23 is about that age when there is a lot of commotion, too much uncertainty. You are likely just finishing up your Master’s, deciding on whether or not to embark on the Ph.D. journey, or finally getting the hang of your job. As such, you are either thrown out from the comforts of college life or trying to make a life-changing career choice or simply coming to terms with the monotony of being an “independent, responsible” adult. The friends you knew and spent your days around are now scattered all over the globe, each wrestling with their own set of challenges. You suddenly do not have an emotional safety net anymore. If you are single, you are probably thinking about finding your soulmate. If you are committed, you are anxious about if things will work out and how will you cope if they don't. I had the same nagging anxieties 7 years ago. I had just graduated and was trying to make it on my own. It was weird living in a new city where I didn’t know anyone except for my girlfriend and a few friends, but even the latter I didn’t see as much as I wanted to. I wasn’t really sure what my long-term career aspirations were. I had a sizable education loan to repay and a younger sister’s education to take care of. I had also just introduced my girlfriend to my family and then my family to hers. Things did not go as planned. A few people I knew were doing far better than me and the constant envy made things worse. But you probably have it even worse. 2020 is a fuck-all year and I wouldn’t give two hoots if humans collectively decided to just ignore it for posterity. I can only but try and empathize with people who have lost a loved one, or their jobs due to this pandemic. It’s heartbreaking to see young people’s meticulous plans being tossed aside because companies rescinded their job offers. Being locked away at one’s home, away from all human contact and without any knowledge of how long this will continue is sure to take a toll on even the most mentally resilient folks. But just remember 4 simple words — This Too Shall Pass. Sooner or later, this will be over. You might feel as if you are entangled in a web. But the more you get frustrated, the more you flail around in desperation, the tighter the web gets. In order to unravel it, you need to think it through. Focus on one strand and work your way patiently through the interlinkages. If you are riddled with multiple problems, prioritize. Tackle them one at a time. Some things might be in your control — work on them. Some might not be (at least right now) — be patient. What happened to me in 23 happened again last year. But this time I was a bit wiser and a tad more prepared. I shared my experience of dealing with trying times like these at the onset of this year (Deepak Mehta (दीपक मेहता)'s answer to What is that one advise that you would give me for a happy life?), way before things went even more downhill. But it has helped me cope through this travesty of a year, and I hope it helps you too. I had a pretty rough 2019. Like a real bad one. There were times when all I could think of was how to get through the day. Nothing seemed to be working out. It felt like I had consumed copious amounts of the exact opposite of Felix Felicis. Like a Bizarro version of King Midas, everything I touched seemed to crumble and collapse. 2019 was like a year-long, practical exposure to the infamous Murphy’s law. But then, I decided that instead of focusing on everything that was going wrong (which was a lot), I’ll channel my energies elsewhere. Concentrate on stuff I could actually do something about. Stop overthinking. Here are the 3 things that helped me during these tumultuous times. #1: The Serenity Prayer I was applying to new jobs. I could work on my application, do extensive follow-ups, maintain an active tracker, pep up my resume. But I could not control the firm’s final decision. I could not control their utter lack of response. So, I chose to focus on the former. #2: The endless wisdom of the Bhagwad Gita "कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन। मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥" The shloka, in essence, advises one to focus on their efforts and not the outcomes. The former is in your hands, the latter not. In a world, where success is contingent on myriad factors, there are times when you can do absolutely everything correctly, yet fall short. As such, your only “duty” is to “do”. To persist. If (and you eventually will) you fall, get up, dust yourself, and start again. When I truly realized this, the time previously wasted contemplating what would happen, was better utilized in actually working towards the goal. I also found solace in this wonderful line from Winnie the Pooh. #3: The 4.167 rule A day has 24 hours. Each hour represents 4.167% of a day. You spend ~40% time at work. ~30% on sleeping and the routine stuff. Then there is family. And friends you need to talk to. Your social media life. Things you “have to” do — reading, writing, travelling, socializing. In all of this, there is one thing that gets lost — “you”. After a full day of trying to meet every single one of your commitments, you are left with nothing to spare for yourself. I decided to change that and block one hour for myself before sleep. Nothing infringed on this sacred 4.167% of the day — no work emails, no phone notifications, no self compulsions. I spent this time however I wanted — watching random youtube videos, just lying around thinking, getting an extra hour of sleep, making myself a meal, going for a late night stroll. There was no routine or plan. I just did what I felt like doing in that moment. And it helped me rid myself of the entire day’s lethargy.

Question: What do you think about the claims that Qutub Minar is actually "Dhruva Stambh"?
Answer: Like many monuments built during the Mughal era, there is a high chance that the Qutub Minar too was either built on top of an existing structure, or from the ruins of other Hindu temples and monuments. I have detailed it in an earlier answer — Deepak Mehta (दीपक मेहता)'s answer to Is Qutub Minar built over premises of a plundered Hindu temple? Firstly, Qutb ud-Din Aibak was a notorious iconoclast, and the same has been documented extensively by historians. [1] [2] After a string of earlier conquests, Mu'izz ud-Din Muhammad Ghuri annexes northwest Bengal in 1204, but then his luck runs out and he is assassinated in 1206. Qutb ud-Din declares himself an independent ruler, thus founding the Delhi Sultanate, c.1206. To celebrate, he builds (or continues building) a Jama Masjid, on the site of the old Lal Kot fort (renamed by Prithviraj, after himself, the "Qila Rai Pithaura"). He destroys temples that he finds on the site, and uses pieces of them as building material; local Indian craftsmen who are hired to for the work also make their own contribution to the design. This is not the first or the last time that a religious site in India is destroyed/remade; in almost every case (including this one), the motive seems to be political rather than religious. Ibn Batuta, the famed traveler, noted that the site where the Minar was built was previously a temple. [3] In the first official history of the Delhi Sultanate, Taj-ul-Maasir, Poet/Historian Hasan Minazi noted that when Aibak conquered Delhi, “its vicinity was freed from idols & idol-worship; and in the sanctuaries of the images of the gods, mosques were raised by the worshippers of the one God.”. The book was translated in an abridged fashion by Henry Eliot who included it in his book “The History of India as told by its own Historians”. [4] He recounts, with pride, the iconoclasm and brutality of Aibak. Prior to conquering Delhi in 1193, Aibak had conquered Meerut and Minazi notes that he again converted major temples to mosques. And again in Benaras. And in Ajmer. In Benaras itself, Nizami claims that Aibak “destroyed nearly one thousands temples”. Finally, in 1924, Vol. 22 of the Archaeological Survey of India was published, and it featured detailed analysis of the Qutub Minar. [5] P.S. Hindu and Jain imagery can still be found there.

Question: What expression do you hate?
Answer: “starting a family” As someone who has been married for almost 5 years, this is the most irritating question I am asked, the assumption being that starting a family is the same as having kids, which is offensive, to say the least. My wife and I have been together for 13 years. But because we have chosen to not have kids, does that invalidate all those years? I believe we have evolved past that point where family referred to a man and a woman rearing kids. In the broader sense of the word, “family” described the people you care about and love and vice-versa. These are the ones you choose to spend time with. The ones you can bank on to provide emotional support during times of need. And that could be anything. A couple is a family. A gay couple is a family. A man and his dog are a family. Two friends living together are family. 5 men, a duck, a bear, and a lizard, raising an adoptive horse daughter are a family.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why is it necessary to have a kids after marriage?
Answer: It’s not. There are 7 billion people on planet Earth and there is no longer an imperative for humans to ensure the propagation of the species by having kids. Having and raising kids is a huge responsibility. I was just talking to a friend who is pregnant and I marveled at the mental resilience of women to go through the toughest human experience — pregnancy. Carrying a kid in their womb for nine months, going through a whole range of physical, and often irreversible changes, and finally the insanely painful process of childbirth is something that men can only admire from afar. But even that is just the tip of the iceberg. You are now entrusted with the upbringing of a tiny human. The next few years until your kid goes off to college are no longer yours. And by the time that happens, you are nearing your twilight years, no longer possessing the energy to totally enjoy your life. If both the partners have flourishing careers, a kid usually means that one of them (mostly the women) has to make a sacrifice at least for the first 4–5 years. And the financial cost of raising a kid is not to be overlooked. Considering the rising cost of healthcare and education, by the time your kid becomes an independent adult, parents often spend tens of lakhs over the course of the two decades. Opinion | Know the cost of raising a child to plan in advance As per rough estimates, it costs between ₹1.5 crore and ₹2 crore to raise a child—from the day it is conceived to the time it takes off on its own. More women are choosing not to have kids, and society can't cope. The Australian Bureau of Statistics says that sometime in the next decade, the number of couples without children will overtake the number of couples with. That means more women are choosing not to have kids. It is perfectly fine for a couple to choose to not have kids. And there should not be two ways about it.

Question: What goes down as the greatest prediction in sports history? Why?
Answer: In 2008, during the quarterfinals of the Roland Garros, Nicolas Almagro was about to lose to Rafael Nadal, the man who had conquered the last 3 titles. After a brutal return by Nadal for his 5th game of the second set, Almagro’s frustration and admiration for his rival came out in the form of a beautiful compliment. "Va a ganar Roland Garros 40 años seguidos. Va a tener 65 años y va a seguir ganando Roland Garros. A los 65!! "He will win Roland Garros 40 years in a row. He will be 65 years old and he will continue to win Roland Garros. At 65 !!” Needless to say, that was a hyperbole. But more than a decade later, Nadal is still going strong. He has won 13 of the 16 last RG titles. And all of them have been in an absolutely dominant fashion. It is absolutely possible for him to continue his reign on clay for another 4-5 years and end up with more RG titles than Sampras’ total grand slam wins.

Question: How viable is the idea of having "covid positive only allowed" restaurants, flights, movie halls, and pretty much any of the services? How will it be received?
Answer: That would be a very stupid idea. COVID is not a death sentence. If you contract it, there are high chances that you will recover in a couple of weeks if you do not have any existing conditions that can get complicated by the new viral infection. All you need to do is to go to a doctor, isolate yourself to protect others, take rest, and be patient. In 2–3 weeks, you should be almost fine and dandy. You SHOULD NOT be working or going out. COVID-only halls or restaurants would not be feasible. It takes far longer to open a new restaurant or convert one to this specific purpose. And even if you are able to, then what? Do you hire cooks who are COVID positive? Waiters? Movie hall staff? What happens when in 2 weeks they recover? Are you going to find new workers? How are you going to ensure that ALL of these people will follow proper precautions when they are out in public? Will you request a COVID-only Uber? Should companies change their overall operating strategy because a bunch of nincompoops can’t stay at home for a couple of weeks? Let’s not even talk about airlines. Are you going to ensure that all airport ground and air staff at both the source and destination are COVID positive? Would you trust an unwell pilot to take you through the air at thousand miles per hour in a pressurized metal container? People need to grow the fuck up. Make sacrifices for others. Behave like a community. Put the greater good over one’s own petty ideas of “freedom”. The world does not work in isolation. And it is high time that all seven billion people acknowledge that they “share” this planet and learn of their responsibilities alongside their rights.

Question: Why are rural products like earthen, clay products, etc. very expensive in online shopping sites like Amazon and Flipkart while they are so cheap if you buy directly from potters/farmers?
Answer: Because consumers are lazy. Simple as that! When you buy from an online retailer, you are also paying to keep that company profitable. You are also paying for the middlemen who sell to that company because the company is not going to directly transact with thousands of individual artisans. You don’t want to go out and expend effort to find the actual artisan and buy from them. You want to stay in the comfort of your home and order from your smartphone. You want to get the package handed to you at your residence. And you also want the luxury of being able to return the item if you don’t like it. All of that costs money. When my wife and I were traveled to Ooty and Madurai, we stopped at a government-owned local artisan shop. There were these gorgeous sarees that they were selling and the price was less than half of what they cost at stores and on online platforms. In the second season of the Amazon series, Laakhon Mein Ek, there is a scene where the local artisans are elated over a big order that came through. The value of the order is INR 30,000. And they have to deliver 2,000 pieces. So INR 15/piece. And their product? Beautiful life-size paintings. The local artisans are simple folks, untouched by extreme capitalist greed. They do not know how to “maximize their profits” or “market their products”. They get ripped off by the middlemen. The famous Pashmina Shawls from Kashmir fetch anywhere from INR 30K-100K. But the people who make it get just a fraction of it.[1] “On an average, we are paid Rs 10,000 per shawl, which takes almost two months to three months to complete,” he said. Like him, around 200 people in Dralbal and neighbouring Batwina village are engaged in handicrafts like Sozni art of pashmina shawl. Women also do this work in winters, earning a meagre Rs 30 per day. So if you truly want to get them cheaper and at the same time ensure that your money is going to the people who are actually doing the work and not to greedy middlemen leeches, just go out. Figure out what the local handicraft industry in your state offers. Find government outlets that support them. Talk to locals and figure out if you can directly get in touch with the artisans and buy from them directly. You will save 50–60% on the cost and the artisans would make 50–100% more than they would have. Win-win!

Question: Hawan in every Hindu ceremony is polluting India. Why don’t we ban such outdated and cheap practice?
Answer: IF before WHY. You’ve simply assumed that hawans are polluting. Which is a logically correct assertion to make since there is burning of wood and smoke. But it is always better to check one’s intuitions and assumptions. Firstly, hawans are not bonfires. It isn’t just a bunch of wood being burned. The hawans used in Hindu rituals include a lot of herbs and natural ingredients that are added to the fire over the course of the ceremony. Due to the presence of these, the “smoke” actually works as a great disinfectant. There was a 2007 study that confirmed it.[1] We have observed that 1 h treatment of medicinal smoke emanated by burning wood and a mixture of odoriferous and medicinal herbs (havan sámagri = material used in oblation to fire all over India), on aerial bacterial population caused over 94% reduction of bacterial counts by 60 min and the ability of the smoke to purify or disinfect the air and to make the environment cleaner was maintained up to 24 h in the closed room. Absence of pathogenic bacteria Corynebacterium urealyticum, Curtobacterium flaccumfaciens, Enterobacter aerogenes (Klebsiella mobilis), Kocuria rosea, Pseudomonas syringae pv. persicae, Staphylococcus lentus, and Xanthomonas campestris pv. tardicrescens in the open room even after 30 days is indicative of the bactericidal potential of the medicinal smoke treatment. We have demonstrated that using medicinal smoke it is possible to completely eliminate diverse plant and human pathogenic bacteria of the air within confined space. And even if this was not the case, there is no evidence that, a) hawans are widespread in India — I have only seen it done twice in my life, or b) there is any substantial impact of the same on air pollution.

Question: Why do banks take almost 3 times the money you borrowed for a home loan? Isn't this a bad thing?
Answer: One of the most fundamental tenets of Finance is the “Time Value of Money”. Simply put, because of inflation, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow. If I pay you $100 today and you give me back $100 exactly a year later, I will have “lost money” since I could have instead invested that in a safe bond and earned $3–4 in returns. This is also why prices of commodities increase with time, as do people’s salaries. You can see how the price of a Hershey’s bar has changed over the years.[1] Or the price of Oreo cookies. Of course, companies sometimes get more efficient at producing or there are realized benefits of globalization, so the prices go down too. The same applies to banks that loan you money too. If you just return the principal over 15–30 years, the bank will lose money. So, you have to pay them interest too. And this interest has to be higher than the returns on safe investments like bonds, etc. because the bank has to make a profit to pay its employees and other costs, and also the fact that some people default on their loans, and the bank needs to pass this risk on to the rest of the customers.[2]

Question: Why are greek gods so cool and indian gods and American gods etc are not?
Answer: Why are greek gods so cool and indian gods and American gods etc are not? Because you have no idea about “Indian” gods. I may be biased here, but arguably the “coolest” god in all of mythology is Shiva, The Destroyer. The Destroyer goes by many other names, primarily Mahadeva (The Great God), Rudra (The Angry One), Nataraj (The God of Dance), and Neelakanth (The One With The Blue Throat). Here is someone who is the literal depiction of masculinity, a towering figure sporting matted hair, ashes smeared on his body, and adorned in tiger skin that barely covers his physical form, all the while “chilling” in the snow-clad Mount Kailasa, deep in meditation. In this usual form, Shiva is a gentle god that is “easily” pleased with due penance and is liberal in granting wishes. He has a third eye that, when open, would annihilate the material world. (Shiva Purana, Page 140) His hair house the mighty Ganga, so that when she descends from the heavenly plains to Earth, the sheer might of her waters doesn’t destroy it. (Shiva Purana, Page 196) In his hand rests one of the most powerful weapons in Hindu mythology, the Trishula (trident). And again, in his hair, rests the mighty moon. Wrapped around his neck is Vasuki, the king of all serpents. And his throat houses the halahal poison, the most potent one that emerged during the churning of the cosmic seas and was so potent that gods and demons started to faint just from the fumes. They sought help from Brahma who redirected them to Shiva, and the latter simply consumed the poison and stored it in his throat, turning it blue. Even this depiction of Shiva is cooler than 99% of all gods imagined. But it is when the Destroyer gets angry when things become infinitely more interesting. One of the most famous tales is that of Sati’s self-immolation that led to Shiva going truly berserk. Sati’s father Daksha held a huge feast to appease the gods but did not invite Shiva, who he thought was not worthy of being worshipped, because he did not “look” like a God. Enraged at this, Sati destroyed her material body. (Shiva Purana, Page 421) Hearing this, Shiva plucked two strands of his hair, of which emerged Virbhadra and Mahakali, two utterly destructive forces. (Shiva Purana, Page 422) Virabhadra then proceeded to destroy the entire yagna, decimate all gods protecting Daksh, and decapitated the latter to appease his lord. And Virabhadra is but a fraction of Shiva’s power. For the end of the universe, Shiva will perform his tandava nritya (cosmic dance). Just the imagery of an enraged Shiva, dancing away while the universe around him disintegrates into nothingness is awe-inspiring. But there must be a balance, even in mythology. So, we have the Goddess Mahakali, who was the other creation from Shiva’s hair (as per the Shiva Purana). But according to other scriptures, mainly in Shaktism she is the progenitor of the universe, the source of all power. Shiva has a deep blue throat, but Goddess Kali is all blue. With blazing eyes and a red tongue that contrasts her dark complexion, she truly presents a formidable image. Around her neck is a garland made up of the skulls of the demons she has perished. Her “skirt” is nothing but the arms of the same demons. In one of her hands is the severed head of a demon, in another a scythe. She holds the same trident that Shiva does. But her rage is infinitely more potent. Here she is, standing atop the body of the Mahakal himself, the only way she could be appeased.

Question: How do you ensure that you're happy in such a gloomy year (2020) with people dying, losing jobs and when you hear death and loss all around?
Answer: Happiness is a choice. Here’s a bunch of kids from the slums in Uganda dancing. You can see the joy in their faces. They don’t have the latest iPhone or expensive clothes. They are not going on an expensive vacation to an exotic land. And they don’t care. The rich Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol was wealthy beyond measure, and equally miserable. 2020 will go down as one of the worst years in recent human history. But that doesn’t mean a person cannot keep up their spirits in these trying times. Almost a million people have died from COVID. And by the time it is done for good, many more will perish before their time. I am lucky to not have lost anyone I know till now. I find solace in that. I still have a great job and do not have to worry about money like many others have been forced to. I am grateful for it. We’ve weathered the worst of the storm (hopefully 🤞 ) and the sun will soon shine again, bright as ever. I look forward to the day. I am healthy, of body and mind. I don’t have to fight the invisible demons that plague millions. I am aware of my privilege. And yet, there are times when the going gets really tough. Locked away in your house, you might find yourself slowly suffocated by this never-ending misery and the slowly tightening grip of an endless cycle of waking up, surviving, and going to sleep. In such moments, reach out to the ones you love. See their faces, feel the comfort in their voices. Ask them how they are. Take a break and immerse yourself in something that you love. Nourish your soul. Treat this travesty of a year as a challenge. One that will not defeat you. Count your blessings before you complain. And help those who need it. You will find there is little time left for despair. Don’t chase the butterflies.

Question: What is your view on Arvind Kejriwal? Can he fill up the opposition vacuum created by Congress and be a possible challenger to BJP in the upcoming 10-15 years?
Answer: Absolutely. Arvind Kejriwal is an able administrator who has proved himself as the CM of Delhi. His meteoric rise in Indian politics was the result of a disillusioned Indian diaspora seeking the next wave of Indian politicians — educated, honest, and able. Had he not fucked up with the entire resignation drama in 2014, he would have enjoyed far greater support now and would have extended AAP’s footprints outside of NCR, primarily in Punjab, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, etc. And he continued to make gaffes on gaffes, making absurd sensationalist statements on social media, playing both victim and savior as the narrative suited him. All the while his party started crumbling, with his most prominent aides leaving for good. His PM ambitions were out in the open and it looked like he had abandoned Delhi for good. In 2019, he joined arms with the same corrupt breed of politicians (SP, BSP, TMC, etc) that he had vowed to get rid of when his sun was rising. However, in the last year or so, he has toned down. You can now see him more on LinkedIn, sharing timely updates about the government’s work, like the CEO of a company, instead of meandering on Twitter. He has taken a more mellow approach to his public persona and has been focusing on doing some solid work in Delhi. If this welcome change is a permanent one, I can see himself wooing more and more younger voters in the future. By 2029, he would have served almost 3 terms as the CM of Delhi, which is a likely scenario considering that both INC and BJP failed miserable in 2020, and they absolutely deserved the thrashing they received, relying on entertainers rather than leaders to helm their parties in the NCR. However, in order to truly go national and establish AAP as a pan-India party, Mr. Kejriwal would have to do one crucial thing: delegate. He will have to nurture the next generation of AAP leadership, delegate work to the top brass to plant the AAP seed across states, and slowly nourish it. He will have to let go of his “Superman” ego and accept that he can’t do everything alone. If he does, then in the next 10 years, he will have the administrative experience, the honest perception, and the support of millions of young people who are fed up with the traditional crop of politicians — corrupt, illiterate, and power-hungry.

Question: Why don't we have vertical screens in cinemas?
Answer: The human Field of view is about 210 degrees horizontally and 150 degrees vertically. This is because we have two eyes, horizontally placed. This implies an aspect ratio of about 4:3 (horizontal:vertical). That is why most movies and TV shows and photographs etc used to have a 4:3 ratio until very recently. Also, in reality, except for skyscrapers and other tall structures, most of the world is horizontal. You go out and you look “around”. Our necks are made to allow for easier sideways movement rather than upwards and downwards. If you are going to the movies, you would not want to get neck cramps. Also, there are very few situations where a vertical or portrait mode might be better suited for the story. Unless there are a couple of Kaijus or Transformers engaged in an interesting arm-wrestling match, there is little use for a vertical screen.

Question: What are some best lines of poetry?
Answer: I will limit this piece to one poem / snippet per author and will focus on both Hindi and English poetry as I am fond of both. #1. Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening — Robert Frost The woods are lovely, dark and deep, But I have promises to keep, And miles to go before I sleep, And miles to go before I sleep. I love the scenery associated with this poem. I close my eyes and imagine myself to be the central protagonist of the poem - wearing a long black overcoat and a grey hat, riding a black horse with white stripes, on a long and tiring journey as a lone ranger, stopping at those beautiful woods, just looking around, trying to absorb the beauty of everything. But then, like the weary traveler, I am reminded of all I have to do and bid the woods adieu, rather reluctantly. #2. हो गई है पीर पर्वत — दुष्यंत कुमार मेरे सीने में नहीं तो तेरे सीने में सही, हो कहीं भी आग, लेकिन आग जलनी चाहिए। (If not in mine, so be it in your heart, It really doesn’t matter where, but a fire needs to start.) Dushyant’s verses pump you up. They goad you to stand up and take charge. To “be the change you want to see in the world”. They remind you that a revolution is not defined or limited by a person. In Batman’s words, “But as a symbol, as a symbol I can be incorruptible.” #3. All That Glitters — JRR Tolkien All that is gold does not glitter, Not all those who wander are lost. Tolkien’s words perfectly encapsulate the real world, which is all shades of grey, a far cry from the attempts to see it in pure black and white. Evil men do good things too. Good ones have sinned in their past. Hard work is not always rewarded. The corrupt and evil often do not pay penance for their deeds. Appearances are deceptive, and we should never judge too soon. #4. Hope Is The Thing With Feathers — Emily Dickinson Hope is the thing with feathers — That perches in the soul — And sings the tune without the words — And never stops at all. Ms. Dickinson’s ability to conjure up stunning imagery purely with words is mesmerizing. I’ve never heard a more anthropomorphically accurate representation of hope — a bird that sings right till the end unimpeded by every other negative feeling. It is the one thing that keeps people going when everything else seems to be against them. #5. If — Rudyard Kipling If you can fill the unforgiving minute With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run, Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it, And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son! Good advice needs to be simple. And actionable. These four lines from Kipling illustrate the importance of focusing on the now. On the small steps that eventually make up the journey. On keeping your head low and plodding on instead of worrying about the grand scheme of things and despairing even before you begin. #6. Tonight I Can Write — Pablo Neruda Tonight I can write the saddest lines. I loved her, and sometimes she loved me too. Nothing hurts more than love that exists solely in the past. #7. Still I Rise — Maya Angelou You may write me down in history With your bitter, twisted lies, You may trod me in the very dirt But still, like dust, I'll rise. Maya Angelou captures both the angst and the indomitable human will in her words. Although her works focused on the plight and the fight of black people, it is applicable to anyone who has ever been oppressed but refused to back down. #8. Love and Misadventure — Lang Leav When words run dry, he does not try, nor do I. We are on par. He just is, I just am and we just are True love is silent acceptance. #9. I Would Still Ask For More — Rabindranath Tagore I would ask for still more, if I had the sky with all its stars, and the world with its endless riches; but I would be content with the smallest corner of this earth if only she were mine. If ever there was a more flattering love song, I know not of it. Tagore builds up a simple premise — of a man never content with what he has, asking forever for more — and then turns it over its head in the last line, cleverly comparing his lover as being greater than his neverending desire, more than the riches of the world combined. #10. Maud Muller — John Greenleaf Whittier Of all sad words of tongue or pen, the saddest are these: 'It might have been. Regret is more powerful than failure. #11. Around The Corner — Charles Hanson Towne Around the corner I have a friend, In this great city that has no end, Yet the days go by and weeks rush on, And before I know it, a year is gone. A critique of the fast-paced life where we don’t seem to have time for the ones that matter until they are no more. Zen Pencils has turned this into a beautiful comic.

Question: What steps are required to take India's economy back on track after the decline of 23.9% in GDP?
Answer: The precipitous fall of 23.9% in Q1 GDP of India is due to its over-reliance on manufacturing, construction, mining sectors that require physical presence. [1] GVA of mining shrank 23.3 per cent; manufacturing 39.3 per cent; and construction fell 50.3 per cent. Together, these 3 sectors account for ~30% of India’s GDP (3%, 8%, 19% for mining, construction, and manufacturing respectively). A large portion of the Services industry was also severely affected due to the strict lockdown, namely tourism and hospitality and transport which contribute about 15–18% to the GDP. Occupancy in hotels declined by over 80% during Apr-Jun, with incoming visas suspended and inter-state travel clamped down on.[2] The months of April and May saw a complete lockdown across the country, with partial relaxations starting in July. August saw even more relaxations with offices opening and inter-state movement being resumed. Now malls, metro services etc have also been resumed. As such, the road to recovery would have to focus on the most severely affected sectors: However, all these measures are short-term. India also needs a long-term strategy to ensure that 2021 can make up for the losses in 2020 and 2022 onwards can be a sustainable growth story. This is going to be the biggest challenge in front of the Indian government, policymakers, and businesses for the next 18–24 months and we need a holistic approach.

Question: Should gender be included in the design of COVID-19 response strategies?
Answer: Yes. Drugs work differently for men and women due to innate biological and horomonal differences.[1] Because women have a larger storage of fat than men, any medication that is "fat soluble" (dissolves in fat before going to the brain) will be distributed differently in a woman. This impacts several medications used in psychiatry – including antidepressants, anti-anxiety medications and antipsychotics – because most of them fall into this category, says Philip Muskin, MD, professor of psychiatry at Columbia University Medical Center in New York City, and chair of the American Psychiatry Association's scientific program committee. It's not known why, but women tend to respond better to certain antidepressants and antipsychotics than men. For example, women do better than men with the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like Zoloft, with verapamil for bipolar disorder, and also tricyclic antidepressants like Tofranil, according to Heather Whitley, PharmD at the University of Alabama School of Medicine in Tuscaloosa. Another difference between women and men is digestion. Women tend to produce less gastric acid than men do, resulting in slower digestion of foods. Because of this, medications that need an acidic environment to be absorbed, like the antifungal ketoconazole for example, may not be as effective in women. Also, drugs that require an empty stomach for absorption, like the antibiotic tetracycline, may not work as well if women don't wait long enough before taking it after a meal. Estrogen, for instance, can have an inhibitory effect on the way a woman's liver breaks down medication, Dr. Muskin says. Muskin correlates the liver to a giant oil filter. "Everything we eat goes through there and liver's job is to filter out toxins," he says. "The body thinks medications are toxins." Most of the drug tests are done on men because having women subjects is a “little tricky” due to their menstrual cycles and the off-chances that they get pregnant during longer trials which could adversely affect the fetus.[2] “I think it was well-intentioned at the time that women be excluded from drug trials because of the unintended effects on a fetus of a drug that hadn’t been tested for safety yet.” Also, women’s menstrual cycles were seen as a complicating factor in drug trials. Generally, researchers want to keep as many variables as they can the same, to get a clearer picture of what effect a drug is having. Fluctuating hormone levels can affect how drugs are absorbed by the liver, said Tannenbaum, so it was simpler to just test on men, who didn’t have this issue. It even goes back to lab rats. “The majority of drug development research is still done in male-only animals,” she said. Aside from questions about hormones and the estrus cycle in research animals, there were more practical considerations — like ending up with more rats than you started with. So for decades, women weren’t adequately represented in drug research, she said. “Fast forward 10, 20, 30 years from the 1960s and what happened is all of the big drug trials, in this case for the cardiac drugs and other drugs, were having trials where very few women were included.” Covid is no different. For example, in Italy, the fatality rate for men was almost 50% higher than women, across age groups.[3] However, in India, the reverse is true.[4] Indian women who contract Covid-19 are at a higher risk of dying than men, a recent study of cases until May 20 has found – 3.3% of infected women died of the disease compared to 2.9% of men. The above could be due to innate social gender constructs in India — women are more malnourished than men, they often ignore (or are made to ignore) their health issues, and it is entirely possible that a lot of female cases are simply not being reported. Then there is the dark reality that with the lockdowns and the global sense of dread, there has been a sharp increase in gender-based violence, most of it from men unto women. [5] During the first four phases of the COVID-19-related lockdown, Indian women filed more domestic violence complaints than recorded in a similar period in the last 10 years. But even this unusual spurt is only the tip of the iceberg as 86% women who experience domestic violence do not seek help in India. Considering all of this, the fact that women and men have had historically different roles and women in most places have been more disenfranchised than men, already adds to the gender divide in clinical trials, leading to underrepresentation of women and consequently, the lower efficacy of drugs on women. As such, all holistic response strategies need to take into account the medical, social, and economical differences across genders in order to be truly equitable.

Question: Why can't the Indian government afford to ban all the things related to China at one go?
Answer: China and Chinese companies are so deeply ingrained in the world economy that this will be a futile, nigh impossible venture. Just look at their two largest companies — Tencent and Alibaba Group.[1]And how they have created a diverse portfolio of Indian investments. Shall we just ban Paytm, Flipkart, Zomato, Swiggy, Ola, BYJUs, etc? Who’ll deliver your food? Who’ll get you a rented cab? Are you ok with just Amazon being the sole e-Commerce website in India (remember, Myntra is owned by Flipkart too.) What happens to the mid-range smartphone market? And consequently, to the “Digital India” push if you ban OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi? Remember that Indian brands like Micromax have not been able to deliver quality and initiatives like Freedom 251 were a national scam. Chinese firms have invested over $4 bn in Indian startups. Chinese tech investors have put an estimated $4 billion into Indian start-ups. Such is their success that over the five years ending March 2020, 18 of India’s 30 unicorns are now Chinese-funded. TikTok, the video app, has 200 million subscribers and has overtaken YouTube in India. Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance rival the U.S. penetration of Facebook, Amazon and Google in India. Chinese smartphones like Oppo and Xiaomi lead the Indian market with an estimated 72% share, leaving Samsung and Apple behind. There are three reasons for China’s tech depth in India. First, there are no major Indian venture investors for Indian start-ups. China has taken early advantage of this gap. Alibaba’s 2015 investment in 40% of Paytm, a digital payments platform, paid off barely a year later when in November 2016, the government of India demonetised its large currency notes and simultaneously promoted a move to a cashless economy. Paytm benefitted from Alibaba’s superior fintech experience, which it applied to India seamlessly, making it a dominant player. Banning games and utility apps are fine. They will not cause many inconveniences to the people. But banning entire corporations, especially where there are no other global or local alternatives is not feasible. India is a small trade partner for China, but China is a major trade partner for India. China is India’s #1 Import Source and #3 Export destination.[2] However, for China, these numbers are insignificant.[3] Indian imports make up only less than a percent of its total, and exports to India less than 4%. Although the trade deficit between the two nations is decreasing, it is still substantial.[4] India's trade deficit with China fell to USD 48.66 billion in 2019-20 on account of decline in imports from the neighbouring country, according to government data. Exports to China in the last financial year stood at USD 16.6 billion, while imports aggregated at USD 65.26 billion, the data showed. The trade deficit between the countries was at USD 53.56 billion in 2018-19 and USD 63 billion in 2017-18. The main imports from China include clocks and watches, musical instruments, toys, sports goods, furniture, mattresses, plastics, electrical machinery, electronic equipment, chemicals, iron and steel items, fertilisers, mineral fuel and metals. However, with proper strategic planning, India can substantially reduce its dependence on China in the long-run. Let’s take steel as an example: One might ask then, why does India both export and import steel? We are obviously producing enough to meet internal demands (exports>imports). The answer lies in the “quality” of steel. India’s major steel import is “value-added”, high quality steel, especially for the auto sector. To produce such high-grade steel, the industry requires, a) cheap raw material (iron ore) b) cheap power c) cheap land d) cheap financing Indian steel industry is really uncompetitive.[8] The Indian steel industry is often regarded as uncompetitive globally. In 2016, World Steel Dynamics ranked India second in terms of cost of conversion of iron ore to steel, after Ukraine. Indian mills were found to be more cost efficient in converting iron ore to steel than their counterparts in China, Japan or Korea. Most Indian integrated steel producers ranked within the top 35 steel mills globally. The answer to the dichotomy can be found in a report by the National Institution for Transforming India (NITI Aayog).19 The report explains a USD 80–100 cost difference in the table below: Almost 30–40% of the cost disadvantage comes from higher financing costs. Steel is a capital-intensive sector. Nearly INR 7,000 crore is required to set up 1 tonne of steel-making capacity through the greenfield route. Naturally, the cost of financing any expansion or new steel capacity is usually through borrowed capital. And in India the cost of finance is extremely high compared to the cost of finance in developed countries such as China, Japan and Korea. This adds about USD 30–35 USD to the final cost of steel. Moreover, steel demand is cyclical. So, during a downturn, the return on investments gets eroded. From 2004–2011, steel demand increased at a fast pace. This prompted most steel makers to expand existing capacities. However, the Indian steel industry faced a severe downturn between 2014 and 2016. This eventually resulted in many steel makers facing bankruptcy proceedings in 2018. The industry, in fact, is yet to resolve all the bankruptcy cases. Today, financial institutions have become wary of lending to the sector. In conclusion, therefore, a large share of the challenges that the steel industry has faced since 2014 can be traced to the extremely high finance costs or cost of borrowed capital. Although India’s Reserve Bank has lowered the policy repo rate five times and by 135 basis points in 2019 alone, the cost of capital in India still remains significantly high and Indian steel makers continue to face a relative disadvantage vis-à-vis their competitors from the developed world. The government red-tape, lack of proper infrastructure, and outmoded logistics and transportation facilities add a lot of non-essential costs to the tally. In terms of logistics, our iron ore deposits are usually inland, meaning that only railways is capable of transporting the raw material to the plants. Add to that the fact that frieght services in India usually are higher to cross-subsidize the loss-making passenger services, and you have another set of extra costs loaded on. This is just an example of how inefficient planning, bureaucracy, and sub-standard infrastructure can make domestic products non-competitive with imports. Unless the Indian government and the relevant ministries take a long-term, strategic view of the essential industries, we will have to depend on imports to meet demand. However, if done right, we can become a self-dependent economy for almost everything except oil.
