Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What are the best examples of "never give up" on your dream?
Answer: I wrote this a couple of years back. And it fits the bill here too. Towards the twilight years of CS 1.6, a new team from Ukraine entered the global competitive scene and took it by storm. In 2010, less than a year after formation, NaVi (Natus Vincere, meaning “born to win”) won 3 of the biggest competitive tournaments at the time making it the first team to do so. They also broke the record for the highest amount of prize money won in a calendar year. And finally, 4 of their 5 players were ranked in the Top 20 players list by HLTV. (#1 Markeloff, #4 Starik #5 Edward, and #19 Zeus; *Top 20 players of 2010: Introduction* (Top 20 players of 2010: Introduction)) They had a bright future ahead of them and were being touted by some of the greatest players of the time to be the next band of superstars. However, as fortune would have it, 2012 saw one of the biggest changes in the Counter Strike landscape with migration of players, teams, and tournaments, from the earlier 1.6 version to the new Global Offensive (CS:GO). While the crux of the game remained the same, there were a huge amount of changes done to the graphics, maps, movements, weapons. As such, even the best in the world found it challenging to come to terms with it. A lot of 1.6 legends retired from the game, paving the way for a new generation. Navi embraced the change too, however reluctantly, towards the end of 2012. For about 8 months they struggled to achieve anywhere near the same level of dominance they used to in 1.6. And then, a second blow came in the form of Markeloff and Edward leaving the team in the mid of 2013. From then, the team lingered in the mid to low ranks of the game, winning smaller regional competitions but failing to impress at the major ones. They tried various new players but couldn’t find the right fit. By the end of 2014, they finally had a new stable roster - Zeus, Edward (who returned), Seized, Guardian, and Flamie (the 3 new faces). 2015 finally saw them displaying the same ferocity as they did in 2012. They reached the finals of their first ever Major tournament (the most prestigious CSGO tournaments, sponsored by Valve), but lost to one of the best teams in the world at the time, EnvyUs. A second place finish wasn’t bad. 5 months later, they again made it into the finals of their consecutively second Major, but lost again, this time to a rising dominant force in the making, Luminosity Gaming (which got brought by SK Gaming, and is now MiBR). But this isn’t the story of Navi. Nor that of Markeloff. This is the story of Zeus. The man who made himself a promise and kept it. In 2016, the long-standing captain of Navi left the organization. There were changes made to the game by Valve which allowed the team coaches to also guide players during the game and gave them more ammo to work with. A lot of teams, replaced their IGL (in-game leaders) or captains with individually stronger players since the role of IGL could now be done by the coach. So Zeus left. Despite a scintillating career spanning over 6 years, with a couple of years of slump, the man left with but one regret. He hadn’t won a major. Till that time, more than 30 people from 6 teams had the right to claim a Major title in their list of achievement but Zeus was not one of them. He went on and joined a small Russian team with probably just one internationally recognizable name. Gambit eSports soon made it to the finals, and won a bunch of decent tournaments. However, the real test came in July of 2017 in the form of PGL Major Krakow. Gambit had a great start, winning all 3 of their group stage games in convincing fashion (16–10, 16–6, 16–11). In the quarterfinals, they were met by the juggernaut of Fnatic, arguably the most dominant roster of all time in all forms of CS. They prevailed 16–14, 16–12 in a Bo3. The semis were the toughest challenge yet. Astralis, the best team in the world at the time. They prevailed once more, making it to the finals. Just one step away from their dream. The finals started rough with Gambit losing the first map a devastating 16–4. However, Gambit came back strong and won the next 2 maps courtesy some great team plays and some spectacular moments of brilliance by individual players like Hobbit and Dosia. The mighty Zeus finally held the major trophy in his hands. With a new rag-tag team. While his former team that had kicked him out was eliminated in the group stages But this is not the full story, either. A year back, while he was still in Navi, but was likely aware that he would be kicked out soon, he made a promise to himself. And that is the story of how perseverance pays off and why you should not give up on your dreams.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Should I just buy a lot of gold instead of investing in stocks during these uncertain trends in the markets due to Corona virus lockdowns?
Answer: That depends on your investment horizon. [1] If you look at the last 100 years, the stock market beats gold squarely, clocking 450x returns against gold’s 84x. (blue is the stock market index, orange is gold) But obviously, 100 years is not a feasible horizon for any sane person. If you look at the last 3 decades, which is closer to the expected retirement saving horizon for a normal person, the stock market still beats gold 2x. Things get murky however, if you consider just a 20-year horizon. Gold outperforms the stock market 3:1. But again, the last 2 decades saw the 2009 financial crisis. If you start in 2009/10, you will see that the stock market is the better bet. Gold rarely tumbles like the stock market, it is a far safer bet. In fact, during times of financial duress like the one right now, it actually gains since people flock to safer investments like gold and bonds. On the other hand, the stock market is characterized by its extreme volatility. You take more risks in terms of wild fluctuations, but you also reap greater rewards, as should be the case. In fact, in the last 7 years, investments in gold have been a disastrous decision, returning 0% returns. Finally, the golden (lol) rule of investing is to diversify — invest in stocks, bonds, real estate, gold, and other commodities. Even in the stock market, make sure you cover as many sectors as possible.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What is the reply for those who say that "kindness is weakness"?
Answer: What an utterly sad way to live, isn’t it? To believe that the ultimate aim of the miraculous human life is neverending competition, ruthless aggression, and unflinching self-centeredness. Kindness is not weakness. It takes a moment’s indiscretion to frown at someone, but a lifetime of knowing them to smile when you see their face. It takes one tiny mistake coupled with a quick temper to scold a child, but a saint’s patience to forgive them and teach them why what they did was wrong. It takes nothing to remain silent at atrocities, but the heart of a warrior to stand up to them. Bishnu Sreshta had just retired from the Indian army and was on the train back home. He had served his country for years, and no one could have asked more of him. But as the fates would have willed, there was one last test. The train was soon overtaken by 40 bandits who looted the passengers. Bishnu remained calm. Wealth is material and there is a fine line between bravery and stupidity. But when the same bandits started harassing a young girl in front of her own parents, the pleas of whom resounded throughout the compartment, Bishnu couldn’t stay calm any longer. He took out his khukri, a curved trademark knife of the Gurkhas, and slashed his way through the mob. On any logical scale, this was a stupid decision. One man with a knife against 40 vagabonds armed to the teeth. But this wasn’t just Bishnu’s warrior spirit goading him, it was his humanity. He looked at the hapless girl and saw someone who couldn’t defend herself. “The girl cried for help, saying ´You are a soldier, please save a sister´,” Shrestha recalled. “I prevented her from being raped, thinking of her as my own sister.” “Fighting the enemy in battle is my duty as a soldier; taking on the dacoits in the train was my duty as a human being,” said the Indian army nayak. What he did was a dually supreme act of courage and compassion. He was not there to prove his might in battle. He was just another human being who decided to stand up for others. Bishnu’s kindness was his strength. Imagine meeting someone who hates you for who you are. Someone who actively campaigned for killing you and your “type” just because they saw you as inferior to them. How would you feel? Angry? Vengeful? Compassionate? Daryl Davis is a black musician, who has led an incredible life. Over the course of thirty years, he has met, talked to, and helped more than 200 members of the vile, hateful Ku Klux Klan — Talking About Race with the KKK. It takes a great deal of courage to face people whose hearts are corrupted by hatred, even more so when that hatred is directed at you. It takes unflinching patience to talk to them and to understand their point of view. It takes commendable compassion to help them realize the faultlines in their worldview and to help them reform. In time, Davis attended Klan rallies. He was clear that he vehemently disagreed with the group and its ideology. But he would also shake their hands and pose for photographs. He explained his logic: “The most important thing I learned is that when you are actively learning about someone else you are passively teaching them about yourself. So if you have an adversary with an opposing point of view, give that person a platform. Allow them to air that point of view, regardless of how extreme it may be. And believe me, I've heard things so extreme at these rallies they'll cut you to the bone. Give them a platform. You challenge them. But you don't challenge them rudely or violently. You do it politely and intelligently. And when you do things that way chances are they will reciprocate and give you a platform. So he and I would sit down and listen to one another over a period of time. And the cement that held his ideas together began to get cracks in it. And then it began to crumble. And then it fell apart.” Eventually Roger Kelly quit the Ku Klux Klan. "He no longer believes today what he said," Davis explains. "And when he quit the Klan he gave me his robe and hood, which is the robe of the Imperial Wizard." Twelve other Klansmen did the same. Eva Kor did something similar. She was a survivor of the Auschwitz horror and a beloved Quoran (RIP). During her octogenarian years, she met Oskar Groening, a former SS Sergeant, complicit in the murder of hundreds of thousands of Jews. But she did not hate him. Instead, she embraced and publicly forgave him — Why I forgive the Nazis who murdered my family. From the photograph they appear as if old friends. The woman on the left dressed in a trouser suit of cobalt blue leans down to hug the bespectacled elderly man with white hair and a woollen vest seated in front of her. They hold hands and press cheeks close together. Except this image was taken last year in a courtroom in the German city of Lunenburg. The man was Oskar Groening, the former SS Sergeant known as the book-keeper of Auschwitz, who was accused (and later found guilty) of being complicit in the murder of 300,000 people. She was Eva Kor, an 81-year-old Hungarian Jew and survivor of the camp where her mother, father and two older sisters were all gassed to death. But she survived Auschwitz – and then Dr Mengele, who later fled to South America where he died in 1979. Last April, Eva travelled to Germany to give evidence in the trial of his former colleague and, despite suffering so much at Nazi hands, publically forgive his sins. Her words show how brave and powerful her soul was. “Why survive at all if you want to be is sad, angry and hurting? That is so foreign to who I am. I don’t understand why the world is so much more willing to accept lashing out in anger rather than embracing friendship and humanity.” It is convenient to live for yourself. To devote your life for personal growth. More money, more power, more influence. But try living for others. It is easy to ignore the woes of someone you encounter on the road. But try stopping and listening to their story. It takes a single finger to topple a deck of cards. But try building one for a change. True empathy, kindness, and compassion is a virtue only the brave can cultivate. It entails looking at people as human beings, with their own demons and their own battles. It needs an unwavering belief in the inherent goodness of all. It requires patience. It demands action. We don’t live in caves anymore; we don’t have to be aggressive, super-macho, warmongers.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What are your thoughts on the Japanese concept of 'Ikigai'?
Answer: It’s absolutely beautiful. And a powerful yet simple way to always strive for improvement. As a kid, you start off by finding “what you love”. These are your hobbies and dreams, you enjoy doing them. Slowly, you drop some of them off. “You are no good at XYZ”, you are told. And you believe it and try and find things you are good at. After all, most people’s childhood is just a never-ending comparison with others who are “better at this” and “excellent at that”. Your hobbies get stowed in a corner and you try and discover “what you are good at”, aka your talents. Later, when you are about to graduate, you realize that a lot of your skills aren’t marketable. You might be good at painting, but you realize that it is a very idiosyncratic market where the chances of success are infinitesimally small. So you once more filter your skills and try and find something that will help you earn a living wage, something “you can be paid for”, or skills. As you grow older, you read news about people who are changing the world. The teenager who just received a Nobel Peace Prize, or the billionaire building floating extraterrestrial cities. You feel unfulfilled, not knowing what your true calling is. You can’t provide anything “the world needs”. But in all of this, you never realize that you can have it all. Yes, it will take a long time. And unwavering persistence. Lots of failures and dejection. And periods of utter misery. But you can have it all. I love writing. It is something that I discovered about a decade ago. I worked on it for years to the point where I am now good at it. Voila!, I have discovered my passion. I also have other skills that I am really good at — crunching numbers, analyzing data, creating novel solutions. And I utilize them at my job. I am good at what I do and I get paid for it, so I have my profession too. But honestly, I have no idea how to combine the two of them as of yet. I have a few thoughts but there isn’t much progress there. Despite what I preach to others here, I too fall in the trap of lethargy frequently, making excuses for not working to convert my passion into a full-time profession. Once (hopefully) when I have that, I will try and find my true calling. To see how I can take the intersection of these three things and use it to make the world a better place. The pursuit of my Ikigai will be a long one, but I am going to persist. And I believe that all of us should do the same (see, more preaching!). Take the example of Bill Watterson, one of the most famous cartoonists on the planet. Bill had found his passion at a young age. He loved drawing and aspired to be a cartoonist, much like the people he idolized, foremost of them being the creator of Peanuts, Charles Schulz. He pursued his passion and created his own profession. After a couple of other stints, he finally struck gold when he created his magnum opus, Calvin and Hobbes. He could now make a living utilizing what he was good at and what he loved to do. And then slowly, he developed his calling too. Watterson’s stubborn denial to merchandize CnH was a testament to his beliefs against diluting something good just for more money. Some very good strips have been cheapened by licensing. Licensed products, of course, are incapable of capturing the subtleties of the original strip, and the merchandise can alter the public perception of the strip, especially when the merchandise is aimed at a younger audience than the strip is. The deeper concerns of some strips are ignored or condensed to fit the simple gag requirements of mugs and T-shirts. In addition, no one cartoonist has the time to write and draw a daily strip and do all the work of a licensing program. Inevitably, extra assistants and business people are required, and having so many cooks in the kitchen usually encourages a blandness to suit all tastes. Strips that once had integrity and heart become simply cute as the business moguls cash in. Once a lot of money and jobs are riding on the status quo, it gets harder to push the experiments and new directions that keep a strip vital. Characters lose their believability as they start endorsing major companies and lend their faces to bedsheets and boxer shorts. The appealing innocence and sincerity of cartoon characters is corrupted when they use those qualities to peddle products. One starts to question whether characters say things because they mean it or because their sentiments sell T-shirts and greeting cards. Licensing has made some cartoonists extremely wealthy, but at a considerable loss to the precious little world they created. I don't buy the argument that licensing can go at full throttle without affecting the strip. Licensing has become a monster. Cartoonists have not been very good at recognizing it, and the syndicates don't care. And more than two and a half decades after the comic ceased to be published, its legacy lives on. It is one of the most beloved comic strips of all time, packed with precious life lessons — The Impact of Calvin and Hobbes. Watterson would often load his comic strips with some subtle satire or critique about the educational system, public polls, or just life in general. The comic captivated children, but for the adults reading them, they would have their perspective changed. Upon re-reading them you’d learn something new every time making this series truly everlasting. Often times the true beauty of Calvin and Hobbes would be the conversations Calvin would have with his stuffed tiger. Ethically baffling questions were proposed, with the answers and meanings to others discerned through the dialogue they would have. Often times this would be had while they traversed the woods on their way to the Yukon, camping out in their backyard, simply trying to go to sleep at night while thinking about friendship (perhaps as a distraction to ward away the terrors of the night). It’s these things that go on in a young child’s mind that often goes unsaid because it never really needed to be brought up by a six year old. Watterson expertly crafted such short little stories that chronicled hundreds of memories in the life of one fictional boy and his tiger; which then impacted tens of thousands of readers across the entire world. All because Watterson was willing to ask meaningful questions through an art form. It is then no surprise that Mr. Watterson had a fulfilling life. And that is something we all can, and should, aspire for.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How do MBA colleges calculate their average package, and how can they promise 100% placement each year? If this statistics is true, then why does India suffer from a high level of unemployment?
Answer: There are a few inherent issues with the question assumptions. The gravest one is that MBA placements are somehow a good indicator of the health of the economy. India, with almost 80% of its workforce, is a predominantly informal economy [1]. Then there is the fact that only 4.5% of Indian population has completed their graduation[2]. Assuming that even 30% of the graduates go for higher education, the share of post-graduates (including MBAs) is less than 1.5%. As such, MBA placement statistics have zero predictive power regarding the overall employment scenario. Every year, about 5–6 million people enter the workforce in India[3]. Assuming that India has 30-odd good B-Schools, and the average batch-size is 500 students, we have just 15,000 fortunate people graduating from a top-30 MBA college annually. This is 0.3% of the total new workforce. The issue of jobs is because of a vicious cycle of poverty, poor educational standards, and an inability to attract foreign investments. 95% engineers in India unfit for software development jobs — this is quite the harsh reality check about the quality of education in India. There are a lot of us, and not enough good schools and teachers. Teachers get paid dismally, so it is not a lucrative career choice. And the cycle continues. When you have a large number of subpar graduates, the top companies only hire the best of the lot. Then there is the issue of government inefficacy and corruption that has prevented India from becoming a manufacturing powerhouse despite having the largest pool of untapped, cheap, skilled labor — Why India or Vietnam Can Never Replace China As The World’s Manufacturing Hub?. We are trying to change this perception, but there is still time for any concrete outcomes — India Looks to Lure More Than 1,000 U.S. Companies Out of China. India needs to create 8.1 million jobs annually, and that is no mean feat. This will require focused, concurrent efforts across farming, education, manufacturing, and public policy to incentivize new Indian startup and to lure existing foreign brands to come to India. We will need to accelerate efforts to promote the Indian tourism industry which remains woefully under-tapped, and again for a myriad of reasons. I wrote an answer about it 5 years ago, and it still rings true — Why does India lag behind in attracting international tourists? What should we do to improve the situation?. We have made some good progress recently with the simplification of the tax structure and the improvement in ease of doing business, but corruption, under-skilled resources, and lack of a cohesive transformational agenda still remain huge roadblocks to be tackled.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What are some corporate lessons one can get from Mahabharata/Bhagwad Gita/Ramayana categorically?
Answer: Never force others (competitors, suppliers, partners) into a corner. In Mahabharata, there are two incidents that highlight this. First, when Shishupal was insulting Lord Krishna, he was given 100 chances in line with Krishna’s promise to his mother. The lord tolerated his misgivings but when he belittled Krishna once more, committing his 101st sin, he was promptly beheaded. Second, when the Pandavas came back after having served their 13 years of exile and demanded their kingdom back, Duryodhana refused. Krishan then offered to let bygones be bygones if only the Kauravas gave their brothers only 5 villages. Blinded with greed and drunk with power, Duryodhana refused again. 5 villages in a nation as huge as Bharata were nothing more than a blip, but Duryodhana could not even do it. What followed was an all-out war that erased both the clans. A similar corporate story is how Lamborghini forayed into premium cars.[1] Lamborghini was a tractor manufacturer that was doing really great. With the money, the owner, Ferruccio Elio Arturo Lamborghini, bought a Ferrari, but was not pleased with it. He suggested some changes to Ferrari but was turned down. So he took it upon himself to build a superior car. And did so. Then you have the time when the Blockbuster supremos laughed at Netflix.[2] The meeting went further downhill from there. Randolph says it was one of the lowest moments for the company: “You fly to Blockbuster, try and sell the business, and they laugh at you.” The only option left was to defeat Blockbuster, and Netflix stayed afloat by doing painful layoffs, figuring out overnight delivery of DVDs, and preparing early to move into streaming. When you start insulting others just because you can, you are slowly pushing them to the brink. If you force someone into a corner, they have little left to lose and they will retaliate with all their remaining might. Sometimes you have to sacrifice a battle to win a war Everyone knows the story of Ghatotkach — Bheem's son. The only reason for Krishna asking Bheem to call upon Ghatotkach was not to annihilate the Kaurav army, but to force Karna to use the Vasavi Shakti (a deadly divine weapon) that one cannot escape from alive. He made this to ensure that Karna could not use it on Arjuna, the key to winning the war. Hence, by sacrificing one brilliant warrior, he ensured his victory. Sony did this to win the format war. It bled profusely on the sales of PS3 which all came with its trademark Blu-ray discs. It was competing with Toshiba’s HD-DVD format and decided to take the losses on the PS3 sales to entrench its technology and create consumer demand from scratch.[3] Sony wasn’t ready to do anything less than decisively win this format war. Like Thomas Edison’s wax cylinders, Sony signed exclusive content deals with 20th Century Fox, Walt Disney Pictures, and Sony’s own Columbia Pictures. Blockbusters like Spider-Man were only available in HD on Blu-ray. Toshiba also signed major studios to exclusive deals. As a result, market adoption of HD stalled. Consumers weren’t ready to commit to one format or the other if they couldn’t get all the movies they wanted. No one wanted to invest in a 21st century equivalent of Betamax. Some believed that a hybrid player would eventually come out, but Sony had other plans. While both HD-DVD and Blu-ray players were still priced more than $800, Sony put a Blu-ray drive in their new, third-generation PlayStation console. Blu-ray allowed for much larger games than the Xbox 360 could offer with DVD media. More importantly, at US$499 the PlayStation 3 undercut every other player (including other Blu-ray players) by hundreds of dollars. Sony lost money on sales of the PlayStation 3; by some estimates more than $300 per unit. However, getting Blu-ray players into living rooms vastly changed the production of home entertainment. One by one, film studios moved to Blu-ray. Warner Brothers, Universal Pictures, and finally Paramount Pictures all announced they would stop producing HD-DVDs. How to motivate your employees The entirety of Bhagwad Gita is a prime example of a motivational speech. When Arjun's conscience is being haunted by the thought of killing his own kin, ancestors, and gurus, Krishna delivered the philosophical epic called Bhagwad Gita. He made Arjun see things in a different light. He realigned Arjun's incentives to extract the maximum potential from him. The curious case of Arjun and Duryodhan: Keeping all stakeholder's happy When Krishna offered Duryodhan the first choice between him and his army, he played a beautiful game. He did not take any gamble. He knew both Arjun and Duryodhan perfectly and hence, knew the choices they would make. He played what is known as the Strictly Dominant Strategy in Game theory. By doing so, he got what he wanted; so did Arjun and Duryodhan. Pandava's Secret Exile: Two birds with one stone Pandava's stay at Virat's palace was not only meant to hide them but also, in the process, to make powerful allies for the war that Krishna had foreseen. Without the Virat army, Pandava's manpower in the ultimate war would have been reduced by one-seventh.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How does shiridi Sai Baba answer our prayers? I have been begging him for a solution since 7 yrs of my marriage. I have got nothing but more and more trouble. I know this is my karma, but why doesn't Baba help me get through this
Answer: The root cause of a lot of our woes is that we seek the locus of control externally instead of looking inwards. No one is going to solve your problems for you. People will give you advice. Friends and family will comfort you. Faith in god or a higher power will provide you solace. But unless you resolve to take charge of your own destiny, nothing will move. Your demons won’t go away and you will be left blaming everything, apart from yourself, for your misery. You’ve had marital problems for 7 years now. That is almost 10% of your entire life. Have you sat back and wondered why is it so? Is it a core compatibility issue? Or is there a gaping hole in your communication and expectations? The wise Kabir Das said, “मोको कहाँ ढूंढें बन्दे, मैं तो तेरे पास में।” | “Why do you search for me elsewhere, I am but within you!” I am an atheist. But I still understand why people choose to believe in a higher power. There are times when the going goes so tough that you need someone to look up to. To have someone to complain to and seek help from and something to assure you that things will be alright. It is but a psychological trick to find that extra bit of assurance and the strength needed to tackle the demons plaguing you. God, whomever you pray to, is akin to a cheerleader. They provide you the morale boost to keep going when everything seems bleak. But they cannot play your game for you. God is like the ones standing on the sidelines and edging you on during the final leg of the marathon when your legs refuse to move an inch. Their voices and their cries of encouragement allow your body to extend beyond its limits and provide you with that last-minute adrenaline boost to cross the line. But they cannot run the race for you. God is like the wind in your sails that propels your boat. But you need to take charge and man the sails and steer yourself to reach your destination. They cannot take over the boat for you. In the end, you can only ask god for serenity, wisdom, and strength. But the onus of getting up and taking charge of your life is in your own hands.

Question: What are some opinions about the new map of Nepal?
Answer: The Indo-Nepal confrontation on the disputed areas in Uttarakhand and Sikkim is a tale as old as time. The current border demarcations have been in effect since the British Raj. Nepal is indeed right in claiming that “as part of the original Sugauli treaty, any region east of the Kali river is part of Nepal”. However, if we are to talk about and accept history then we should do it in its entirety. After the Treaty of Sugauli, there were more geographical changes done by the British. The issue here is that the Kali river originates somewhere in the middle. (See the tiny blue line) As you can see anything east of the river (except for the first couple of kms) is anyway part of Nepal. What Nepal is claiming now is that the portion north of the origin, and henceforth westward till Kuti village as part of Nepal. This again was addressed 200 years ago. To address this, in the 1830s, the British government clarified that the entire drainage area of the Kali river was part of British India. There is historical documentation to support this, and consequently, refute Nepal’s current claims. There is also an 1879 map that shows the frontier further to the east, following a ridge that runs down from near the Tinker Pass. Trade was a great obsession in the British colonial mind, and presumably Britain realigned the border to gain exclusive control over trade across the Lipu Lekh Pass and the traders using it. Whatever the sequence that led to this new border being imposed or agreed, or whatever date it occurred, maps prepared in Nepal during the Panchayat regime are identical to the post-1860 maps in showing the border as following the line of the river that flows down from below Lipu Lekh. Again, this indicated an acceptance, whether consciously or not, that the traditional trail to the pass fell exclusively on the Indian side and that the border agreed as part of the Sugauli Treaty was no longer valid. Also unhelpful to Nepal’s case is that the China-Nepal Boundary Treaty, formally signed by King Mahendra in Beijing on October 5, 1961 makes no reference at all to Lipu Lekh. The opening lines of Article 1 state: “The Chinese-Nepalese boundary line starts from the point where the watershed between the Kali River and the Tinkar River meet the watershed between the tributaries of the Mapchu (Karnali) River on the one hand and the Tinkar River on the other hand.” (Emphasis added.) This roughly corresponds to the border shown on the 1879 map and the one claimed by India today. The Nepal government published a map in 1960 with a similar boundary line. Article 3 of the China-Nepal Boundary Agreement of March 21, 1960, required the two countries to exchange maps and to set up a joint committee to start the process of delineation and demarcation. Presumably the map Nepal submitted was similar to the one openly published. In short, Nepal’s current claims hold no water. If we go far back, no present-day boundaries make sense. India could lay claim to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar. But it doesn’t.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: If you have been poor and made it out of poverty, what was your biggest culture shock coming out of poverty?
Answer: We weren’t destitute by any measure, but there were times when the line between where we were and utter penury blurred. When I was five, my father and mother decided to move away from the small village we called home. They knew it would be tough, and, like the “creation of the universe”, this decision would make a lot of people very angry. They didn’t care though. The village did not have roads. Or electricity. Or good schools. No one from there had ever graduated. Had they remained back, my best chance would have had been to enlist in the armed forces too. And that is what a lot of people told him, unsolicitedly so. I mean, we are Indians after all. “Don’t do this. Instead, focus on saving so that you’ll be able to buy a house when you retire. You are risking everything. And for what? It’s not like your kids are prodigies.” But they had decided. We had a pseudo-nomadic lifestyle for the next twelve years. Five cities, and as many schools, and more than twice the number of houses. During our first year, I distinctly remember asking dad about his salary. He told me it was 5000 per month. I remember because I calculated how much it would be per day. “Just under 170 rupees”, I concluded. For the little me, it was still a huge amount. But he had four mouths to feed, including an infant. And he was not supposed to bring his family with him during that stint, but he did because I had to start school and he was not willing to set me back a year. So, there we were. Living in a small, one-room kitchen that cost 1200 a month. Dad would “smuggle” out of the cantonment area at night to spend the night with us. He would be gone early in the morning before anyone woke up. They say that bad luck never comes alone. So, he contracted Tuberculosis, which was an absolutely deadly disease back then. The treatment was expensive for us, but luckily he found a doctor (I should actually say a saint; because that dude definitely was) who ran a charity clinic and didn’t charge anything except what the medicine cost. Even then, he would sometime give him the free samples that he would receive from pharma companies. Those years were absolute hell and even a young me was able to comprehend that to some degree. When instead of having some money left at the end of the month, you have some month left at the end of the money, you are driven to some extreme measures. I vaguely recall seeing mother take some money that was offered to the gods to pay for groceries when things reached a breaking point. I have a faint memory of father pretending to fast every now and then so as to curtail food spending. I remember both of them requesting the landlords (who again, were good people) extension on the rent payment because the school fees were due too and the salary hasn’t come yet. My parents rarely spent on themselves. Dad would buy himself a new pair of shirt and trousers probably once a year (and that too, the cheapest, decent quality he could find). Mom did the same. Things eventually got better (thankfully!). But those moments stayed with me. While heading off for my undergrad, I bought just two pairs of jeans — the basic navy blue and black. Unbranded. Cost 300 each. I was careful while spending any money in college. It wasn’t until my last year when I had saved some decent sum from my internship in the first semester that I allowed myself some leeway. Now I’ve been working for over 7 years, making what my father made in a year in half a week. Through all of these years, I have noticed one peculiar behavior — impulse shopping. You don’t really need it but it catches your eye, so you buy it. You won’t probably use it for more than a week, but “hey, it’s on sale!”. SUCH A GREAT DEAL, EH? People buying stuff just because it looks cool, or they saw it in a movie or tv show, or they want to impress others at a party, is just something I don’t understand. Why buy something that you don’t need? Why give in to your base emotions and hoard and want and envy others? Why buy something branded when you could get the same thing without the label at 20% of the cost? Eludes me.

Question: Rahul Gandhi is asking government to distribute money directly to bank account instead of packages like AtmaNirbhar Abhiyan. What do you think about this suggestion? What is actually good for country, free money or packages like this?
Answer: Rahul Gandhi was about to “come of age”, but this statement has shown that he is still, at the very least, 6 months away from it. But despair not, India Today will surely publish another OpEd letting us poor mortals know that Rahul has resurged, rebranded, risen from the ashes of old, soon.[1] The INC was very vocal till a week or so ago, demanding that PM should be bold in declaring economic package of 5-6 pc of GDP. Even Nobel Laureate, Dr Abhijit Banerjee, in his discussion with Rahul, reiterated the same.[2] “A lot of us have been saying that we need a stimulus package. That’s what the U.S. is doing, Japan is doing, Europe is doing. We really haven’t decided on a large enough stimulus package. We are still talking about 1% of GDP. The U.S. has gone for 10% of GDP,” Dr. Banerjee said. Earlier, Dr. Rajan talked about Direct Transfer to the poor people to give them liquidity and to push consumer demand.[3] Mr. Rajan, who took part in the first of a series of dialogues planned by the Congress on the challenge posed by the pandemic, estimated that India needs to spend about ₹65,000 crore to take care of the vulnerable sections like the migrant workers. Of this, more than half has already been achieved through DBT — Direct Benefit Transfer of Rs 36,659 crore since beginning of lockdown Using the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) technology platform, more than Rs 36,659 crore has been transferred through direct benefit transfer (DBT) to the bank accounts of 16.01 crore beneficiaries since the start of the lockdown, in the wake of the outbreak of Covid-19, the Controller General of Accounts said on Sunday. It should definitely be amped up, as the lockdown has continued for far longer than anticipated earlier. There should be at least another set of payments done at the earliest, and payments to poor people in red and orange zones on a monthly basis until all restrictions are eased. Also, the World Bank has pledged $1 bn for the Indian poor, of which $750 mn would come immediately and be disbursed through the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana (PMGKY).[4] “This new support will be funded in two phases—an immediate allocation of $750 million for fiscal year 2020 (FY21 in World Bank parlance) and a $250 million second tranche that will be made available for fiscal year 2021 (FY22)," the World Bank said in a statement on Friday. The first phase will be implemented through the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana (PMGKY) announced by the central government in March. “It will immediately help scale up cash transfers and food benefits, using a core set of pre-existing national platforms and programmes such as the Public Distribution System (PDS) and Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT); provide robust social protection for essential workers involved in covid-19 relief efforts; and benefit vulnerable groups, particularly migrants and informal workers, who face high risks of exclusion under PMGKY," the World Bank said. Generating demand is one side of the entire equation. You need to also protect vulnerable industries. You need to balance the issue of rising NPA versus the inability of consumers to pay their loan EMIs currently. You have to balance the amount of stimulus and inflationary consequences. The FMs proposed reforms for the agricultural sector will have longstanding benefits by providing price protection, eliminating middlemen, and the overall deregulation.[5] “The Modi government has converted crisis into an opportunity in agriculture marketing,” said Ashok Gulati, chair professor at Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations. “The last three points announced by the finance minister on APMC reforms, contract farming and essential commodities are big, and will help farmers and consumers in the long run. They will also make the supply chain efficient.” While the first tranche was more focused on MSMEs, the latter ones have addressed the broader Indian economy, including farming, manufacturing, defense, retail.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What do you think about Allahabad High Court's judgement on the use of speakers during Azaan? Will the case go to the Supreme Court?
Answer: It’s absolutely spot on, isn’t it? The judgment reads[1] : "It cannot be said that a citizen should be coerced to hear anything which he does not like or which he does not require, since it amounts to taking away the fundamental right of other persons...No one has got the right to make other persons captive listeners" "no person has right to take away the right of others" "use of microphones certainly takes away the right of the citizens to speak with others, their right to read or think or the right to sleep." This is something very fundamental that every person should be aware of. We DO NOT LIVE IN A BUBBLE. Our lives intersect that of countless others. There are 7 billion-plus people on the planet. And you share with them the common public goods — water, air, land. You are free to do anything on your own property unless it affects others. Imagine someone building a house on the land they purchased. They should be free to do anything, right? Well, ALMOST. Consider a situation where they decide to cover their entire house with glass. The reflection from the glass now enters your bedroom. Or it damages your car. (And this has actually happened — 'Walkie-Talkie' skyscraper melts car). In that case, their freedom to do what they please on their piece of land interferes with your right to sleep peacefully in your room and damages your property. They have encroached on your personal space and need to back off. The same is the situation here. Mumbai has a population density of 30,000 people per square km. Imagine if a Mosque’s loudspeakers have a range of 500m, their net catchment area would be about 0.8 square km. That means that the loudspeaker is being heard by 25,000 people, most of whom do not want to. Now amplify the situation with hundreds of Mosques in Mumbai itself. I had to recently reject a nice apartment I was about to finalize. The apartment was in the vicinity of 4 separate Mosques and the azaan calls in the mornings lasted 30–40 minutes. Between 4 to 5 AM in the morning. This should not be allowed. Your Liberty To Swing Your Fist Ends Just Where My Nose Begins There is no reason any establishment (religious or otherwise) should be allowed to use loudspeakers and disturb the larger population. Banquet halls have strict guidelines on how loud they can be and till what time they can play. Despite this, I have had to listen to and eventually call 100, on the one near my place because they absolutely were not adhering to the laws. The same should apply to everyone, everywhere. Good going, Allahabad HC! Hope this is soon implemented all over India.

Question: [DC] If a human was raised on Krypton before it exploded of course would they be a Superman? What powers would they posses?

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why do Tesla’s Elon Musk calls Covid-19 lockdown restrictions fascist?
Answer: I just finished the book, “Winners Take All: The Elite Charade of Changing the World” by Anand Giridhardas. The main crux of it is that everything the rich and powerful do, even something as laudable as charity, is aligned with their core interests. Companies only want to change the world, if there is something in it for them. Alibaba only wants “to make it easy to do business anywhere” so that they can sell to every single of the 7 billion-plus people. Google wants “to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful” so that they can sell ads and make money. Coke wants to “refresh the world” so they can sell as much of sugary corn syrup drinks as they can. Elon is no different. He just wants what is best for him and his business. Despite the COVID shutdown in China in Q1 2020, Tesla production did not suffer much — Tesla kept global sales and production up despite coronavirus-related shutdowns Tesla delivered 88,400 vehicles in the first quarter of 2020, according to the release. That’s down from its best sales quarter ever at the end of 2019, where Tesla delivered around 112,000 vehicles. But it’s not nearly as low as the 63,000 the company shipped one year ago in the first quarter of 2019, and it beats out most estimates from Wall Street analysts as well as those from some of Tesla’s biggest supporters. However Q2 won’t fare as good — Tesla Producing Only 50K Cars In Q2? This article is from a month ago and Tesla units were only expected to remain closed till May 4 initially. Then there is also the fact that he has a direct, vested interest in maintaining production levels and, consequently, the stock price of Tesla above a certain threshold — Tesla's Musk nears $750 million options payday ahead of results Monday’s rally put Tesla’s market capitalization at $145 billion. Importantly for Musk, its stock market value reached a six-month average of $96 billion. Hitting a six-month average of $100 billion would trigger the vesting of the first of 12 tranches of options granted to the billionaire to buy Tesla stock as part of his two-year-old pay package. Each tranche gives Musk the option to buy 1.69 million Tesla shares at $350.02 each. Taking Monday’s Tesla closing stock price of $798.75 as an example, Musk could sell those shares for a profit of $758 million.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Should we ask the rich to donate to the poor or blame the poor for their own misery (poverty)?
Answer: Neither. We should aspire to become a society that is not plagued by such obscene levels of income and wealth inequality, where governments are not bought by the rich and the powerful who make rules to suit themselves, where the basic needs for every citizen are taken care of and there is some semblance of equal opportunity. The poor aren’t poor only because they are somehow inferior in terms of their ability to make money. They are poor because they were born into poverty for no fault of theirs. They are poor because they can’t afford to get a good education. They are poor because their entire days are spent grinding for two square meals while the uber-rich literally eat gold. They are poor because the odds are heavily stacked against them. No person is an island. People are a product of their genetics, their upbringing, the opportunities they receive, the challenges they face. Sure, capitalism and free markets are great. But only if they are truly free. What we see in today’s world is a corrupted form of capitalism where firms receive billions in bailout[1]but the poor have to scramble for unemployment “benefits”[2]. Where every tragedy is another opportunity for those who already have enough[3]. Charity by the rich is a way for them to feel good about themselves. The spirit of “giving back” is warm and chocolaty. It absolves them of the visceral feeling of guilt that sometimes haunts them. The tax breaks are a cherry on the top too. What we need is to fix the system. To work towards a world where the needs of many justifiably outweigh the greed of the powerful few. And when we get there, this question will be moot.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why is "#BoycottBigBasket" trending on Twitter?
Answer: Big Basket recently responded to a user on the platform. This might sound an innocuous statement but read on. There are two ways animals are killed for meat in India — Jhatka and Halal. The former is when you behead the animal in one swift stroke and is the preferred way to slaughter an animal for meat for Hindus, and more importantly for Sikhs. The latter is when you slowly slice the jugular and carotid first, allowing the blood to drain out, and is the way Muslims prefer their meat. Now there are arguments on and against both sides — Jhatka people say that theirs is the more humane way to kill, Halal proponents say that theirs ensures that all toxins are first drained out so the meat is healthier. I really couldn’t care less about either. But the larger issue here is that Halal is a form of economic boycott against all others.[1] The requirements for meat to be considered Halal are: These requirements indirectly shun any meat slaughtered by Hindus or Sikhs. Again, I don’t really care. People should have options. People can choose to buy from who they want to. But “corporations” are not people. Big Basket stated that “all of their meat is Halal”. Basically, they only buy from Muslim meat sellers. The same was the case with McDonalds last year. Imagine the amount of meat McDonalds and Big Basket purchase. Now understand that Hindu or Sikh meat sellers are indirectly blacklisted by these megacorps because they only buy Halal. They could very well have kept both choices. Want a halal burger? Yes, we have that. Want to buy Halal meat from our online store? Yep, that’s an entire category in itself. But no, they didn’t. They just went with the easiest option because they didn’t think anyone would care. But this is absolutely discriminatory. Boycotting an entire section of the society is not acceptable. Freedom of choice goes both ways. And that is why #BoycottBigBasket is rightfully trending.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Will WFH be successful in India?
Answer: Absolutely yes. And this is not just specific to India. The ongoing epidemic has just showed that Indian companies’ insistence on coming to office on the pretense of productivity, data security, compliance, discipline, etc. were just words. HCL, Infosys, and TCS have posted statements that even after this pandemic ends (hopefully soon), a large part of their workforce will continue to work from home. Prior to 2020, Infosys allowed employees to avail WFH for 9 calendar days every month[1], and it was one of the few firms to do so. Accenture also had quite the flexible WFH policy. But these were exceptions. WFH was usually treated as a privilege and not a more productive alternate. TCS only allowed WFH in special cases. The concept/policy as a whole was non-existent. Even globally, the situation was similar — Why work-from-home doesn't work -- in India and elsewhere. My current employer is subject to very stringent compliance and data protection policies. As such, most of the people working on client projects have to sit in a secure area, with some clients even demanding that smartphones should not be allowed in the working bay. This was before COVID struck. As of today, 99% of our projects are running as usual without any compliance issues or any drop in productivity and/or quality. Clients who were absolutely anal about these restrictions have had no choice but to surrender to the new world order. The same is likely the case with most employers. Indian corporate world has some really fucked up metrics and presumptions — people are lazy and won’t work dedicatedly from home, the longer someone is in office, the more productive they are, WFH is more like a day off. All of these baseless assumptions have been challenged and thrashed by the current litmus test. They say “necessity is the mother of invention”. The COVID epidemic has just been the decisive push to endorse what should be common sense. If you allow employees flexibility, they will be more engaged. If people don’t have to commute 2–3 hours every day just to reach office, they will be more focused and productive. If half of your workforce on any given day is working remotely, you can save 50% of your establishment costs.

Question: How can a realist be happy?
Answer: Truth be told, only realists can truly be happy. Optimists just live in their fictional worlds where everything is just perfect. When they snap back to reality (oh, there goes gravity!), they either resign to gloom and haplessness or ignorance. They chase an impossible dream and when that clashes with the stark, sub-optimal reality, they find themselves proposing ideal solutions to complex, multi-faceted, practical problems, solving none of them. Pessimists usually linger in their bubble of negativity, looking at everything with distrust and misplaced anger. They never have a solution (even ideal, impractical ones), but just more problems and more questions. Their contribution to the world is usually zilch. Realists reconcile both the extremities. They accept what is given to them and try and make the best of it. They look at the bad things and try and change them. They look at the good in the world and they rejoice in it. They concur that the world is riddled with diseases and inequalities and wars and famines, that we are better than we were but worse than we could potentially be, that a utopia might never come but we will darn sure get as close to it as possible before the human race perishes. They spend their lives bettering themselves and the world around them. After a long day, an optimist goes to bed dissatisfied — thinking about everything they could have done more. A pessimist falls asleep ruminating in their bottomless anger, having done nothing. A realist rests at peace, knowing there is more to do, but satisfied with the littlest of progress they have made that day.[1] [2]

Question: Is the Indian government hiding real statistics of the spread of the corona virus?
Answer: The COVID data in India is shared by the state governments and aggregated by the ICMR (Indian ̧Council of Medical Research).[1] This implies that the onus of checking the veracity of data lies with the respective state governments. Then there is the challenge of identifying and dealing with asymptomatic cases, which make up more than 80% of India’s overall cases.[2] In the absence of sufficient infrastructure to tests every single one of the 1.3 billion Indians, asymptomatic cases flow under the radar, silent but deadly. Towards the end of April, Banerjee announced that tea stalls and local paan shops would be kept open in safer areas of the State. Even buses were allowed to ply in the eight districts of the State which had not recorded COVID-19 cases yet. Question: The pollution level of the main rivers and the environment of our country is improving unexpectedly due to the lockdown. Will the Modi government be able to keep it pollution free, even after the lockdown ends?
Answer: The rivers are cleaner than they have ever been in years because of the lockdown. There was no special effort by the administration. The only change is that humans are indoors and that industries are not operating — Ganga is much cleaner now but it will take more than a lockdown for people to be able to drink from India’s holiest river. But as soon as the country resumes normal, this ephemeral, welcome improvement would be undone too. Industrial pollutants are no longer being dumped into the rivers, and they are the biggest reason behind the pitiable condition of some of the largest Indian rivers — Grossly polluting industries more than doubled in 8 years: SOE in Figures One of the reasons for this is the substantial increase in the number of grossly polluting industries (GPI) between 2011 and 2018. There has been a 136 per cent increase in the number of grossly polluting industries over the period, according to the State of India’s Environment (SoE) In Figures, 2019. Around 84 per cent of the GPIs were found to be located in four states — Uttar Pradesh (1,079), Haryana (638), Andhra Pradesh (193) and Gujarat (178). GPIs are industries that discharge more than 1,00,000 litres of wastewater and/or hazardous chemicals into the rivers, and include pulp and paper mills, distilleries, sugar mills, textile units, tanneries, thermal power plants, the food, dairy and beverage industries, chemical units, slaughterhouses, etc. The waste they dump looks like this. At the same time, domestic pollution is a factor too. Households near the banks of the rivers dump their waste into the rivers directly — ‘Over 60% of urban India’s sewage enters water bodies untreated’. We need to invest in proper sewage disposal and treatment infrastructure. Finally, there is the issue of cremation of bodies alongside the Ganga shores. Most of the time, half-burnt bodies are just dumped into the river. Along with flowers, incense, clothes, plastic, etc. This needs to stop now. Like most problems, this too would require efforts from both the public and the government. The former has to change its ways and move away from tradition and history and acknowledge the harsh reality of the present. The latter has to make the necessary institutional changes, regulatory reforms, and invest in elevating public awareness about the issue.

Question: Has the corona virus leveled the playing field in economic terms?
Answer: Nah. Capitalism doesn’t work that way, bruh! You can’t make the world a better, less unequal place. The only goal of unfettered capitalism is to funnel money to the top, so that the rich can get richer, fund election campaigns and buy elected representatives, so that they can get the laws tweaked to their benefits, accelerating the process of them getting richer, while they stow away their money in tax havens, or turn them into capital gains to leverage a lower tax rate. But don’t worry. They’ll do charity to help the poor. And then deduct it to further lower their tax liabilities all the while flaunting their good deeds on social media. Jeff Bezos probably loves the Coronavirus. After all, it has made him richer by more than $30 bn. At the same time, Amazon workers are fighting to remain safe — 'Jeff Bezos values profits above safety': Amazon workers voice pandemic concern. The pandemic has been good to billionaires around the world, with American billionaires getting richer by a whopping $282 billion. All the while, 30M Americans are now out of a job, needing to file unemployment claims. Harvard recently received a 9 Million stimulus (which they rejected after backlash, appropriate considering that Harvard has over $40bn in assets under management and is obviously not strapped for money). Concurrently, they were also firing all of their contract dining and catering workers, another decision they recently reversed after public backlash (I see a trend here.) While governments across the globe are bailing out dying businesses, they are still paying dividends and fat salaries to their top honchos — £400bn paid in dividends by UK companies before coronavirus crisis / U.S. companies criticized for cutting jobs rather than investor payouts. Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd (RCL.N), Halliburton Co (HAL.N), General Motors Co (GM.N) and McDonald’s Corp (MCD.N) have all laid off staff, cut their hours, or slashed salaries while maintaining payouts, according to a Reuters review of regulatory filings, company announcements and company officials. Even for something as basic as getting access to healthcare, there is no “level playing field” — Need a Coronavirus Test? Being Rich and Famous May Help If nothing, we can look back and learn from History. The Spanish Flu of 1918 and the Black Death of the 14th century were huge setbacks for income equality — https://www.ifn.se/wfiles/wp/wp911.pdf Taking both a short- and a long-term perspective, Herlihy and Cohn (1997) analyses the effects of the Black Death in Europe. Along the lines of Robbins (1928), their results suggest that the drop in labour supply increased wages in the agricultural sector, while land rents dropped. Moreover, the study suggests that wages remained persistently high, in turn inducing a change in the economic structure in the long run, where labour was substituted by capital. Herlihy and Cohn (1997) also hypothesise that major pandemics will cause an increase in wealth inequality and claim that the Black Death skewed the distribution of wealth compared to an earlier situation when property was much more evenly distributed. In a recent study, Alfani (2010) explores the consequences on economic structures of the severe mortality crisis caused by the 1630 plague using detailed documentation available for the city of Ivrea in Italy. Testing the Herlihy and Cohn (1997) hypothesis, the results indicate that the plague decreased inequality in the short term, but increased inequality in the long run. Cohn and Alfani (2007) suggest that it was primarily the unskilled immigration to the city to fill the gap in the urban population that fuelled the rise in economic inequality in the long run. Question: How should we plan for our MBA now, with Covid19 causing a terrible economic impact?
Answer: I think Rohit has absolutely nailed it in his answer. What you are seeing now as in the market is pure panic. I mean, companies are laying off employees after just one month of muted or no operations? It seems like a knee-jerk reaction to me. However, the current pandemic will also have some long-lasting effects on all sectors, and consequently on the job market as well. The 2009 crisis was catastrophic for the graduating classes. And the 2020 situation will likely be equally bad — Poets&Quants | This Year’s MBA Job Market: How Bad Will It Get? At the top ten business schools, MBA employment rates at graduation dropped an average 21% from 2007. At the next 15 highly ranked schools, the drop was even steeper: 23%. At Harvard Business School in 2009, nearly one in four grads failed to have a job at graduation, as the employment rate fell to 76.8% from 94.3% two years earlier. At Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management, the employment rate for MBA grads slumped to 68.1% from 91.9%, a 25.6% decline in jobs. However, the hardest hit will be the people graduating right now, or next year. By 2022, we would already have weathered the worst of this storm. I will even venture as much to say that 2022 might be a better-than-average year for job prospects. Once this economic downturn fizzles out, a lot of weak companies would have closed shop. Most of the remaining ones would be running on minimal human power possible. But like after every trough, there is a crest, so will the market rebound once this is over. A lot of new startup ideas will germinate. Mature firms will look to pursue growth once more instead of focusing on minimizing their risk exposure. All in all, if this pandemic is truly contained by the end of 2020, we might be looking at a strong rebound which will benefit the 2022/23 classes the most. Anyway, it might not be the best time to be in the job market. Growth will be muted, both in terms of your profile and the money. There will be a constant risk of lay-offs if you are in a cash-heavy organization in an industry severely impacted by the lockdown. So, it might be prudent to take this opportunity to go back to college and acquire some new skills. A lot of colleges have waived off GMAT and GRE requirements considering the situation, so you can take a shot — Some graduate schools are waiving GRE test requirements because of COVID-19. After all, if you had planned to play outside and it started raining, do you still persist or go back and study while it pours?

Question: Which movies of Irrfan Khan will you remember the most?
Answer: I moved to Mumbai in 2013 — eager, and a little anxious, for the next phase of my life. My college life was behind me, having left behind two beautiful campuses in Ahmedabad and Goa. The fun and frolic were over, and I was now expected to be a fully-functional adult. I had always hated change. And crowds. But I had also always tried to hide my fears and apprehensions. Mumbai seemed scary, a neverending human mass, moving seamlessly despite no visible space to maneuver. I used to always just close my eyes and whisper “All is well” when things started to get overwhelming. A few months passed. Having settled in, my girlfriend (who is now my wife) and I decided to go to the mall to shop for her upcoming birthday. Having accomplished the goal we set for, a spur-of-the-moment decision to watch a movie was taken. When we reached the ticketing counter, there were two shows scheduled — one for the latest Housefull flick with a long, winding line of waiting customers, and a smaller one for a movie titled “Lunchbox”. Neither of us had heard about it. I had only seen Irrfan in Billu Barber till then. But tired and impatient, I bought the tickets. The next 2 hours were one of the best cinematic experiences of my life. We both came out of the theatre — solemn yet serene. Something about the simplicity of the movie, the lack of forcefully inserted songs and dance tracks, the mesmerizing performances of Irrfan, Nimrat, and Nawaz, and the overall, indescribable, feel of the entire movie lingered with me for a long time. I came back, and wrote a review of the same (though I did a pretty substandard job of it) — Deepak Mehta (दीपक मेहता)'s answer to What is your review of The Lunchbox (2013 movie)? 7 years hence, somethings have changed, but some haven’t. The movie is still very close to my heart, but Irrfan has grown on me, in an absolutely delightful way. One of the last 40 days of quarantine was an Irrfan Khan marathon for the wife and me — we watched/re-watched Angrezi Medium, Qarib Qarib Single, and Karwaan. It was a much-needed respite from the absolute travesty that 2020 has been. It was a love-story told that was spared the colorful, flamboyant lenses of the usual Bollywood romance flicks. And it was a love story without par. And it helped ease me into the beautiful pandemonium that is Mumbai. I recently posted the letter Saajan (Irrfan’s character) writes to Ila (Nimrat’s), as a final goodbye towards the climax of the movie on my Instagram story. A friend of mine, whose wife and mine were roommates for many years, replied to it. Turns out, it was the first movie they watched together in Mumbai too. Mumbai for me is special. Despite being home to everything I abhor, it has somehow made permanent residence in my heart. It is not so much a city as it is a living, breathing organism. A microcosm made up of the people that dwell in it. Forever entwined with their destinies. A lingering presence in all their stories. I will remember the city long after I would have moved on. But it will still persist in my memory. And, in the future, whenever I think about the City of Dreams, I would go back to this very movie that has defined the city for me.

Question: Do you believe a lot of lives have been saved due to Coronavirus lockdown which are lost in huge number in road accidents across India?

As of now, the COVID19 crisis has taken about 1,100 lives. [3] There has also been a reduction in the number of murders. Neeraj Kumar, who is in charge of a crematorium on the banks of the holy Ganges river in Uttar Pradesh state, said victims of crime were also not being brought in. “We used to get at least 10 accident-related bodies every day and many related to murder cases. But after the lockdown, we’re only receiving natural death cases,” Kumar said. The site used to perform up to 30 cremations a day but in the month since March 22, only 43 people had been cremated, Kumar said after leafing through the crematorium’s record book. While strict lockdowns may have deterred some criminals, the lower rates might also reflect difficulties in reporting deaths, officials said.

Lunchbox In what has been one of the closest movies to my heart, a love-story mercifully spared the colorful, flamboyant lenses of the usual Bollywood romance flick, Irrfan plays the role of Saajan Fernandes, a middle-aged man who finally finds himself falling in love with a woman, played by the equally versatile Nimrat Kaur, whose lunchbox, prepared for her husband, was accidentally delivered to him instead. Her attempts to prepare delicious food every day go unnoticed, until the day of the reckoning. It is an incredible film. The two primary characters never meet. Except for the end, when they decide to. Nirmat reaches the restaurant, anxious. She waits but Irrfan doesn’t turn up. The next day, she sends an empty lunchbox to him and he explains his side of the story. Dear Ila, I got the lunchbox today, there was nothing in it. And I deserve that. Yesterday, you waited in the restaurant for me for a long time. But before that, that same morning I forgot something in the bathroom. I went back in to get it. And the bathroom smelled the same, exactly the same as it used to be after my grandfather had been to the shower. It was like my grandfather had been there. But he had not. It was just me. Just me. And the smell of an old man. I don’t know when I became old. Maybe it was that morning, maybe it was many, many mornings ago. And maybe if I had forgotten something in the bathroom before, I would have found out sooner. Life kept on going and lulled me with its motions. I kept rocking back and forth as it threw me left, and then threw me right. And then before I knew it…. No one buys yesterday’s lottery, Ila. I came to the restaurant while you were waiting. There you were - fidgeting with your purse, drinking all that water. I wanted to come up and tell you all this in person but I just watched you wait. You looked beautiful. You are young. You can dream. And for some time, you let me into your dreams. And I want to thank you for that!

Question: Will foreign businesses start to invest more in India post-Covid-19?
Answer: Maybe, maybe not. But if we do not act soon, the opportunity will already be gone. And the warning signs are already here — Indian economy in danger of being left behind in post-COVID world, warn experts. The exodus of companies shifting their manufacturing bases from China should have been the perfect opportunity for India to capitalize on. After all, both economies offer similar advantages in terms of labor costs, economies of scale, low cost of production, and skilled labor. However, “According to a recent study by Nomura, out of 56 companies shifting base from China, a mere three companies preferred India, while 26 decided to relocate to Vietnam. Taiwan was chosen by 11 firms and Thailand by 8 companies.” That is a dismal success ratio. And the culprit is the snail’s pace at which we function. The Indian government is mulling a strong boost to Make in India post the COVID-19 lockdown — Govt’s Covid-19 Revival Plan Includes Major Focus On Make In India. There is literally no reason to wait that long. In fact, the lockdown should have given enough time for the Ministry of Commerce to have a special committee come up with an actionable plan to leverage the opportunities in the market. On the other hand, Vietnam has already done so couple of weeks back — Vietnam Issues Incentives to Counter Impact of COVID-19 Impact. Vietnam had also emerged as the top beneficiary of the US-China trade war, another opportunity India was unable to capitalize on — Vietnam Is Becoming The Big Winner In The China Trade Wars. All this while, the Indian government’s push for single-brand FDI, the lucrative corporate tax reduction in the last year, and improvements in the Ease of Doing Business, have not yielded results anywhere as commensurate as expected. But all hope is not lost — 1,000 foreign firms mull production in India, 300 actively pursue plan as 'Exit China' mantra grows And this is what scares me the most. Indian bureaucracy and red-tape are infamous for still being hungover from the License Raj. I hope that this changes. That the Ministry of Commerce takes cognizance of how incredibly rare this opportunity is. That the global sentiment about India and Make in India is strong. That we have never been better poised in terms of infrastructure and our human capital to become the next economic powerhouse. I hope.

Question: Isn't it better for all the countries to buy lots of oil now since the cost of oil has dropped drastically and store it for future use?
Answer: Crude Oil and Oil Futures prices recently dropped to historic lows, with futures venturing into the negative price territory. The crux of the reason behind this was the excess of oil production vs demand as the ongoing pandemic has drastically reduced demand for oil as commute, transportation, and industries worldwide are shut down. Technically, negative Futures prices do not make sense. Any asset, however worthless, cannot have a negative financial worth. So what is going on here? The answer lies in the fact that Oil is a commodity that requires huge storage charges, a subset of the Cost of Carry. Imagine you have a barrel of oil at your disposal. If you bought it for $30 and it is currently trading at $10, you can wait for a few months if the prices are low right now. However, that assumes that your costs will remain the same. But if you were to incur $10 in storage cost every month, oil prices would need to be above $50 two months later, if you want to break-even and avoid any losses. As the time horizon increases, your costs (and subsequently losses) will too. That is why some traders were willing to “pay” you to take the oil off their hands. They are just sure that by the time the futures contract would be profitable, they would have incurred far more in losses than the amount they are paying you right now. So, no. It is not a good strategy for countries to hoard oil right now. For example, India’s storage capacity is only 39 million barrels, which is very low compared to other nations — India misses a trick due to lack of oil storage capacity While India has a storage capacity of 39 million barrels, China’s total capacity is at 550 million barrels and Japan’s at 528 million barrels, ensuring a supply of over 190 days in the event of a supply disruption. Though India approved construction of two new caverns in 2018, as part of its phase two expansion, in Chandikhol in Odisha (4mt) and Padur II in Karnataka (2.5mt), work is yet to commence on these projects. While building these caverns has a budgeted cost of around ₹15,000 crore (as of 2018), filling them would cost at least an additional ₹20,000 crore. Globally, Oil storage is running at almost full capacity — Global oil storage fills to the brim despite leap in costs / World’s Biggest Oil Storage Firm Says Almost All Space Sold The world is estimated to have 0.9-1.8 billion barrels of spare storage capacity - equal to 9-18 days of global supply of 100 million barrels per day (bpd) or 90-180 days to accommodate supply exceeding demand by 10% or 10 million bpd. Commodity data firm Kpler estimates the industry is using around 71% of its global storage capacity and has 1.8 billion barrels of free space. UBS estimates on-land free space at 0.9 billion while Bernstein puts it at 1.6 billion barrels. But even if traders in their search for storage are willing to pay high prices, technical restrictions limit the amount available. “Every installation will eventually have a working maximum,” Alexander Booth, head of market analysis at Kpler, said. Operational limitations can prevent full utilisation. Also, light crude cannot be stored with heavy crude, and the quality of jet and gasoline can deteriorate when they are stored. Not all storage is conveniently located and can involve the additional costs of longer shipping routes.
