Question: Will India see regular lock downs in the future, as there is every chance of re-occurrence of the virus?
Answer: Absolutely. We’ve already seen one example of a strong second-wave of infections in Singapore, despite having what was touted to be a “model response” to prevent the spread of the virus — COVID-19 Leadership Lessons From Singapore: Be Ready, Be Bold, Be Decisive. Singapore started screening Wuhan passengers as early as Jan 2. NOBODY knew that we had a future pandemic on our hands back then, but Singapore wasn’t taking any chances. By the end of the month, all passengers were being screened, there was an official travel advisory in place, preparations were being made by turning available infrastructure into quarantine centers. By Feb, the citizens were provided face masks, and everyone who had recently traveled to China was told (not asked) to self-quarantine themselves for 2 weeks with strict penalties for non-compliance. Testing kits were developed by the end of the month. Ministers and officials at all levels have been working in perfect tandem and have effectively contained this travesty. Unfortunately, a bit of haste in uplifting restrictions has plunged the country into a second wave of infections, far stronger than the first — Singapore had a model coronavirus response, then cases spiked. What happened? So what went wrong? The answer appears to lie in overlooked clusters of cases among migrant workers living in cramped dormitories and an underestimation of the speed at which those infections could spread through a city where lockdown measures had not been put in place. Many of the new clusters have been connected to Singapore's vast migrant worker population, in particular those workers -- most from South Asia -- living in cramped dormitories, who appear to have been overlooked in the initial wave of testing. Multiple dormitories have been quarantined and the government is ramping up testing for all workers. It's unclear whether those infections were from migrant workers coming in from outside, or if the virus was circulating among the largely-untested population for some time. What is evident is that the conditions that workers live in made effective social distancing -- or "home" quarantine -- next to impossible, making it easy for the virus to spread. In India, cases have been growing despite the lockdown. The rate of increase is slow compared to most nations, but cases are still doubling every 12 days.[1] And this is despite a stringent, nationwide lockdown that is currently in its 6th week. Once the restrictions are lifted, there is a high chance of a rebound. After all, most infectious outbursts have seen multiple waves.[2] Epidemics of infectious diseases behave in different ways but the 1918 influenza pandemic that killed more than 50 million people is regarded as a key example of a pandemic that occurred in multiple waves, with the latter more severe than the first. It has been replicated – albeit more mildly – in subsequent flu pandemics. Other flu pandemics – including in 1957 and 1968 – all had multiple waves. The 2009 H1N1 influenza A pandemic started in April and was followed, in the US and temperate northern hemisphere, by a second wave in the autumn. Germany and China have also seen a second wave, though thankfully smaller. A small rise late last week in the number of infections in Germany – another country credited with handling its outbreak well via extensive testing and tracing – has also drawn attention, even as the country moved to loosen restrictions. And despite China’s apparent success in bringing the outbreak in Hubei province under control, there has been an increase in cases in the country’s north. The CDC chief has already warned that the US might see a second, even stronger wave in Autumn, and coupled with the flu season, it will be a double catastrophe.[3] "There's a possibility that the assault of the virus on our nation next winter will actually be even more difficult than the one we just went through," CDC Director Robert Redfield told the Washington Post in an interview. "We're going to have the flu epidemic and the coronavirus epidemic at the same time," he said, and the combination would put even greater strain on the nation's healthcare system than the first outbreak. Scientific studies have suggested that the entire world might need to follow social distancing well into 2022, and that governments will have to be on constant vigil until a vaccine is developed.[4] Under current critical care capacities, however, the overall duration of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic could last into 2022, requiring social distancing measures to be in place between 25% (for wintertime R0 = 2 and seasonality; fig. S11A) and 75% (for wintertime R0 = 2.6 and no seasonality; fig. S9C) of that time. So, it is likely that the next 2 years are going to be an absolute clusterfuck of a time, and that humanity as a whole will be permanently changed due to this. As such, countries like India, with pockets of highly dense populations, will need to be constantly on the lookout. This would imply that even a few dozen new localized cases in an area should be dealt with swiftly and without mercy. We could very well see multiple instances of lockdown in cities like NCR, Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Ahmedabad, Lucknow, etc. Fuck you 2020!

Question: What is your take on Arundhati Roy's comment on Coronavirus that 'situation in India is approaching in genocidal'?

Here’s a proper rebuttal if you’d like to read — Only Arundhati Roy sees a genocide of Muslims in India - India Narrative Author and activist Arundhati Roy is not a senior citizen yet, but she has been showing many a sign of senility for quite some time. Ten years ago, she and only she found that the murderous Maoists rampaging in the killing fields of Chhattisgarh were actually “more Gandhian than any Gandhian.” Since then, she has become even more delusional: now she, and only she, sees genocide in India. No prizes for guessing the culprit right: the Narendra Modi government, which is liquidating the Muslims. Her verdict is unambiguous: “the situation is approaching genocidal.” “I think what has happened is Covid-19 has exposed things about India that all of us knew,” she told a German TV channel DW. “We are suffering, not just from Covid, but from a crisis of hatred, from a crisis of hunger.” She went on to elaborate hatred in the time of the coronavirus. “This crisis of hatred against Muslims comes on the back of a massacre in Delhi, which was the result of people protesting against the anti-Muslim citizenship law.” It was a curious massacre in which one-third of about 50 victims were non-Muslims, including a police constable and an Intelligence Bureau officer. Never willing to let facts derail a conspiracy theory, she went on with her rant, claiming the government was using the coronavirus to wipe out Muslims: “The whole of the organization, the RSS to which Modi belongs, which is the mother ship of the BJP, has long said that India should be a Hindu nation. Its ideologues have likened the Muslims of India to the Jews of Germany. And if you look at the way in which they are using Covid, it was very much like typhus was used against the Jews to get ghettoize them, to stigmatize them.” It is a well-known fact that it was the rashness of the Tablighi Jamaat that has brought grief to not just Muslims but also the other sections of society. To the Muslims, for the Tablighis have spread the coronavirus among Muslims more than they have among non-Muslims. Aljazeera reported (How Tablighi Jamaat event became India's worst coronavirus vector) on April 7, “Of about 4,400 Covid-19 positive cases in India, nearly a third are related to the religious gathering at the Markaz, as the Jamaat headquarters is known.” Aljazeera is a Qatari news channel, not an RSS mouthpiece. And it is not exactly pro-Modi. The same report also said, “#CoronaJihad trended on Twitter, with many ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders calling the religious gathering ‘corona terrorism’—a term many said hinted at the Islamophobia of the governing party.” It is astonishing that in this day and age, with the ubiquitous media and social media, nobody (other than Roy) in a country of 130 crore—or, for that matter, anywhere else—has noticed that something as serious as a genocidal situation in India. “Genocide,” says Encyclopedia Britannica, is “the deliberate and systematic destruction of a group of people because of their ethnicity, nationality, religion, or race. The term, derived from the Greek genos (‘race,’ ‘tribe,’ or ‘nation’) and the Latin cide (‘killing’), was coined by Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-born jurist who served as an adviser to the US Department of War during World War II.” The backdrop was that of the Holocaust when Hitler’s murderous thugs tried to racially purify Europe by physically eliminating impure peoples like the Jews and gypsies. Lemkin said that the key component of genocide was the “criminal intent to destroy or to cripple permanently a human group. The acts are directed against groups as such, and individuals are selected for destruction only because they belong to these groups.” As many as six million Jews were slaughtered in a planned manner. The entire operation, ‘final solution,’ was carried out with characteristic German efficiency. That was genocide. As I mentioned earlier, Roy wrote (Outlook, March 29, 2010), “As far as consumption goes, it’s more Gandhian than any Gandhian, and has a lighter carbon footprint than any climate change evangelist. But for now, it even has a Gandhian approach to sabotage; before a police vehicle is burnt, for example, it is stripped down and every part cannibalized. The steering wheel is straightened out and made into a bharmaar, the rexine upholstery stripped and used for ammunition pouches, the battery for solar charging.” A few days later, the “Gandhians” carried out the bloodiest attack on the troopers of the Central Police Reserve Force, murdering 76 of them. Ten years earlier, Roy mistook the thuggish Maoists for the disciples of Mahatma Gandhi; now she is hallucinating about a genocide. Maybe the lockdown has taken a toll, for there is evidence that mental health issues are rising all over the world. I wish her well; she should take ample precautions. Like sanitizing hands. I wish the mind could also be sanitized in a similar fashion; this would help her overcome hallucinations. Get well soon, Arundhati Roy.

Question: Wouldn't it be good for the economy if the Indian government nationalises properties of temples, churches, and Waqf boards?
Answer: Don’t nationalize; there should be a total separation of state and religion. But start treating all such religious institutes like any other corporation. This would entail paying income and property taxes as applicable. Although some services provided by religious institutes have been brought under the ambit of GST — food tariffs, sale of CDs, books, etc — the tax on income is still not applicable. If you have religious trusts earning hundreds of crores a year, you need to pay taxes just like everyone else. Salaried individuals pay taxes on their income and then pay GST on stuff they buy. Such huge religious institutions should be mandated to follow proper accounting principles and be taxed under corporate law. The Tirupati temple[1] alone earned more than 2800 crore in 2018 as income. Assuming a paltry 20% profit margin, it would have netted 500–600 crore in profits and should ideally have paid 150–200 crore as tax. An article in Deccan Herald[2] noted that the state had 171 temples earning more than 20L (and hence under the ambit of GST). It seems even gods cannot exempt themselves from GST, as 171 temples in Andhra Pradesh above Rs 20 lakh income have come under the new tax regime. There are 23,834 temples in the state, of which 45 temples come under the Rs 1 crore income category, 63 temples up to Rs 25 crore and seven temples with more than Rs 25 crore annual income, including Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), the country’s richest. Sum up and you get ~Rs 4000 Crore as the total income. Assuming 20% EBITA, the total taxable income should have been Rs 800 Crore, leading to about ~250 Crore in taxes. Andhra is home to about 4% of Indian population. Assuming uniform distribution of temples as per population, the total tax collection would have been 25x, or about Rs 6000 crore. Add Gurudwaras, Mosques, and Churches, and the government can net up to Rs 10,000 crore annually.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: You are from IIMA, have a great marriage, are extremely smart? Are you satisfied with your life? Do you think you have arrived in life
Answer: I am content, but not satisfied. And while they are synonyms, there is a subtle difference — contentment is being happy with where you are in life and all that you have achieved, satisfaction is the gratification you feel once you achieve a goal or desire. The former is active and a content person still strives to be better every day. The latter is more complacent and passive in nature. I am absolutely at peace with my current stature. I no longer feel the need to seek external validation, or the urge to compare my life with those of others. And in all of this, I am always aware of everyone who has contributed to my journey — my parents, family, wife, friends, teachers, colleagues, and every single person who has said the tiniest bit of encouragement when I was down. However, I also realize that there’s so much more out there — to learn, to achieve, to experience. I maintain a lot of lists. The act of enumerating and categorizing things allows me to clear and organize my haphazard thoughts. And none of them are anywhere near completion. I want to read twice as many books as I am. I yearn to visit every beautiful place on the planet. Talk to new people. Reconnect with old ones. Skydive. Learn a musical instrument. Put out a podcast. Develop something. Start a company. Go sailing. Write a book. Master woodworking. Run a marathon. Experience the northern lights. Spend a winter in the arctic. But I am not going to tie my happiness or sense of self-worth to any such goals. Aspirations are great until they dominate every waking second of your life. Happiness is within.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Do you believe in janm kundali?
Answer: The concept of “janm kundali” or horoscopes is rooted in the unscientific belief that the time and place of one’s birth, and by extension the alignment of stars and planets at that moment in time, somehow determines their life trajectory. This entire idea is hogwash. Firstly, it runs contradictory to the concept of “free will”. If the events and the ultimate destination of an individual are already charted the moment they are born, then their choices should be inconsequential. That would imply that we are nothing more than mindless automatons, inconsequential moving cogs in a piece of gigantic machinery, which is both terrifying and depressing. Thankfully, that is not the case. Individuals make choices on a regular basis. We choose not to kill. We choose to abide by the law. We choose to be generous even if there is nothing in it for us, save for some sense of worthiness. If there were no free will, there would not be any conscious discoveries. No novel inventions. Why take the more arduous path when anything you do leads you on the same path? Secondly, Astrology has not kept pace with modern scientific progress. For example, Hindu astrology, or Jyotisha-shashtra, were developed, at the very least, 1800 years ago. It is fairly unchanged since then. While we have discovered many more planets and moons, found out that the Earth was not the center of the universe and that it revolves around the sun and not vice-versa, and that a vast part of the universe is “invisible”, manifesting in the form of dark matter and dark energy, Indian jyotisha-shashtra still follows the concept of navagrahas, or “Nine planets”. However, these “planets” include the sun, the moon, and two fictional gigantic demons named Rahu and Ketu. The outer planets, Uranus and Neptune are not included, because they were discovered later on. While Science attempts to reconcile all of its older beliefs and assumptions with newer discoveries, astrology ignores it. Thirdly, the entire notion that all individuals can be classified into 12 Zodiac signs, or “Rashis” in Hindu astrology is arbitrarily reductionist. That should imply that the world can be divided into 12 groups of roughly 600 million people each and all of these 600 million people should share some commonalities. But then you have billionaires and geniuses that share the same “classification” with people born in utmost destitution or ...

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What do you think about people who never wish to marry? Do you think they are doomed (since you are married)?
Answer: There is a simple, singular thought-shift that could make the world a far more loving, encompassing place if everyone adopted it — the acceptance of personal choice. All of the 7.5 billion people on planet Earth should be absolutely free to choose what to do with their lives — the way they dress, their career choices, their lifestyle, and the philosophies they follow. With one simple caveat, of course — your actions and your choices should not be to the detriment of others. Speeding might give you an adrenaline boost, but it also endangers others on the road. It is ok to eat anything if there was no risk of it snowballing into a global pandemic. Eating endangered animals, similarly, adversely harms the overall ecosystem and might lead to the extinction of the said species. I am even ok with substance abuse, but then addicts often go on drug-fuelled rampages destroying lives and property. That is unacceptable. That said, the choice of partaking in the institution of marriage, thankfully, does not suffer from any such unintended consequences. As such, it should be absolutely no one’s business if someone decides to be a lifelong bachelor. Yes, there is the question of loneliness in old age. But again, most developed nations have a sturdy system of old-age homes where people can develop camaraderie in their twilight years. The concept of monogamous marriages is quite frankly outdated. We live in relatively far peaceful and prosperous times. The law can be reworked to take care of the legalities involving polygamy, polyandry, open relationships, and the entire multitude of possible domestic and amorous relationships. As we keep on evolving, we would need to make peace with a world order that changes rapidly and welcomes departures from the norm.

Question: Why is the Indian government saying Zoom is not a safe platform?
Answer: Because it isn’t. The global lockdown has forced people, institutions, universities, and companies to resort to video conferencing apps. At the forefront has been Zoom, which has seen its userbase grow exponentially in 2020 — Zoom’s daily active users jumped from 10 million to over 200 million in 3 months Even before the MHA issued this advisory, a lot of other authorities have banned the use of Zoom. As you can see, there seems to be a global consensus that security and privacy concerns abound Zoom, the buzz of the town. So, what are these issues? All of them are public concerns, but it looks like the app wasn’t ready for such a huge boost. And it was not designed with security at the center of the focus. And the folks over at the company have taken notice, promising to work on the issues unearthed. However, we did not design the product with the foresight that, in a matter of weeks, every person in the world would suddenly be working, studying, and socializing from home. We now have a much broader set of users who are utilizing our product in a myriad of unexpected ways, presenting us with challenges we did not anticipate when the platform was conceived. These new, mostly consumer use cases have helped us uncover unforeseen issues with our platform. Dedicated journalists and security researchers have also helped to identify pre-existing ones. We appreciate the scrutiny and questions we have been getting – about how the service works, about our infrastructure and capacity, and about our privacy and security policies. These are the questions that will make Zoom better, both as a company and for all its users. We take them extremely seriously. We are looking into each and every one of them and addressing them as expeditiously as we can. We are committed to learning from them and doing better in the future.

Question: If the coronavirus has a 97% recovery rate, then what's with all the hype?
Answer: Firstly, COVID19 does not have a “97% recovery rate”. It was the case with China, but EU and US and a lot of other countries are seeing far greater fatality rates. This is the current status of the outbreak. The fatality rate right now is closer to 6.7% (148,728 deaths out of 2.2 mn cases). However, this data includes China. Also, China today revised the death toll by almost 50%, raising eyebrows everywhere. So, China’s death rate is also closer to 5.6% right now. And if you look at specific countries, the death rate is far higher than the average. Those are scary figures. Finally, these numbers are understated. Because we are taking total cases and comparing them to total deaths. Even if the cases do not increase from this moment on, the deaths will. Some of the patients still suffering from the disease will not make it. If you look at the current stats once more, there are about 56,000 critical cases. Assuming they do not make it through, the revised mortality rate would be (148,000+56,000)/2,200,000, or about 9.2%. Now assume that this infects everyone in the world. It would imply more than half a billion deaths. There are about 40 people in my close family. And another 20 or so close friends of mine. If the “law of averages” holds up, it would mean that 5 of them would die from this disease. I can’t even comprehend that, let alone ignore and label it as “hype”. It is easy to ignore deaths when it is just a statistic. But not when it is someone you know. Every death represents the loss of a HUMAN BEING. Of many years of potential wasted. Of the pain and lifelong grief of many more who loved the departed dearly. Remember, “The Bell Tolls For Thee!” No man is an island, Entire of itself. Each is a piece of the continent, A part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less. As well as if a promontory were. As well as if a manor of thine own Or of thine friend's were. Each man's death diminishes me, For I am involved in mankind. Therefore, send not to know For whom the bell tolls, It tolls for thee.

Question: How have the wealthy convinced everyone to socialise their risks for the past few decades?
Answer: There are two types of compensation in the business world — salary and equity. The former gives you a steady stream of income and you are not affected by erratic market movements. The latter gives you ownership of the company, and accordingly, the perks and the dangers if the company soars or crashes. The Risk-Reward tradeoff is key to efficient markets. However, the rich rarely suffer, do they? Amid the current market turmoil, companies are laying employees with little discretion. Normal people are expected to save for a rainy day. They are told to get a second job if one does not suffice. When the government pays them because they were laid off, or suffered an injury, its called “benefits” or “handouts”. But multi-billion dollar behemoths have started screaming “save us!” in less than two months since the global pandemic reared its ugly head. Companies (at least in India) are terminating employees, sending them on forced “unpaid leave”, or just slashing salaries by 25%-50%. Note that, if there is a bumper year, employees don’t get the benefits of the same. “Trickle-down economics” was one of the greatest illusions ever. But somehow, if operations are disrupted by even a couple of months, routine employees are the first to get axed. Look at this guy. His net worth is currently about $140 bn, an amount unseen in the modern day and age. This is after the most expensive divorce settlement that cost him $35 bn. Currently, the company he started, which is one of the 4 trillion dollar corporations in the world, is asking for public donations so that they can pay sick leaves for their employees and contractors. This came after the fact that a few weeks ago, Whole Foods, a company Amazon recently acquired, asked its employees to “donate sick leave to their colleagues who might need it” — Whole Foods CEO Suggests Employees Donate Sick Days to Each Other as Way to Get Through Coronavirus Outbreak And then you have the wealthiest university in the entire world, Harvard. Harvard, through years of fees and donations and alumni contributions, has amassed over $40 bn, that is managed through its Asset Management arm. Even a moderate 5% annualized return on it would yield it $2bn every year. And yet, as the epidemic rages on, it decided to lay off its dining staff — Harvard, Boasting $40 Billion Endowment, Lays Off Dining Hall Workers Due to Coronavirus. And it also received $9 mn from the Fed as “relief” — Harvard Nets Nearly $9 Million in Coronavirus Aid from Federal CARES Act | News | The Harvard Crimson Finally, you have companies like American Airlines, Boeing, and Delta. They, and other players in the aviation industry, have spent tens of billions buying back their own stock in recent years, spending over 96% of their total profits on it — U.S. Airlines Spent 96% of Free Cash Flow on Buybacks Imagine a person using 96% of their savings to buy an expensive house or car. And then asking the government for “social benefits” from the next month as they lose their job. Ridiculous, isn’t it? But then nothing is ridiculous when you replace people with corporations. After all, people just vote, corporations make campaign “donations”. The airlines in the US are receiving over $60 bn in a bailout from the government — Airline salaries compared to stock buybacks show why so many people are angry at the bailout Now, of the 750,000 employees Airlines for America says it represents, these three airlines account for about 320,000 of them, and collectively they would need about $36 billion to pay them for an entire year, and collectively over the last seven years, they've spent about $33.3 billion buying back their own stock. The stimulus bill has about $60 billion set aside for the airlines There you have it, folks. Socialism is evil and must be purged when common folks talk about a universal basic income, or universal healthcare, or free education. But when you need to rescue Umbrella Corp, it is in the “best interest of the economy”.

Question: Will the world still be a same place after coronavirus, or it will change?
Answer: I hope it changes. The COVID19 pandemic should be treated as a warning. Viruses and infectious diseases have been a part and parcel of human history from its inception. However, this truly might be the biggest, most devastating one in modern history. The Spanish Flu outbreak happened over a century ago. Since then, the world has changed so much that it is unrecognizable. We have made advancements in science and technology by leaps and bounds. The first commercial flight took place in 1914, just a few years before the Spanish Flu and today more than 4 billion people fly every year. Globalization. The advent of the internet. The population today is more than 4x what it was a century back. And everything is so interconnected that the entire world has been brought to halt because of one person eating a bat/pangolin. We truly are living in an era of unprecedented connectivity. The world has shrunk and the chances that another “butterfly effect” might just be the ruin of all of humanity have increased drastically. As such, the Novel Coronavirus is indeed “Novel”. We have not seen the likes of it in a long time, and absolutely not in the current setting. So the year 2020 should ideally work as a warning/template/learning opportunity for all federal governments and the global humanity for years to come. There are more. Question: Why is Adityanath Yogi's 'Agra model' being discussed on the corona virus?
Answer: Right now in India, there are 3 models that have proven effective in curbing the spread of the deadly COVID-19 — Bhilwara, Kerala, Agra. Kerala model for entire states, Bhilwara models for small towns and districts with low population densities, and Agra model for densely populated Metropolitans and Tier 1 cities. I have recently written in-depth about the Kerala model and I strongly believe that it is the ideal way for all Indian states, regardless of size, and current status of the outbreak. However, while the Kerala model is “macro” in nature and provides an overarching effective framework for a large state, the Bhilwara model is far more suited for smaller, active “hotspots” within states. Bhilwara was one of the first regions to be severely affected by the viral outbreak. So much so, that it was being touted as “India’s Italy” — Is this textile city set to be 'India's Italy'? The district went into lockdown on 20th March, way before all of India did — Curfew imposed in Rajasthan's Bhilwara district as nine test positive for coronavirus To prevent the spread of COVID-19, the administration has now sealed the boundaries of the entire Bhilwara district. The health department has also started a door-to-door survey through 300 teams in 80 thousand houses of Bhilwara city in hope of identifying suspects and preventing the virus from infecting more people. The district authorities set up 300 teams to do exhaustive door-to-door testing of every single person. They also did due contact tracing of people who might have come into contact with the affected. And after almost a month of absolutely amazing efforts by the district administration, this fucking virus has been almost eradicated in the district — Coronavirus: Want to contain the virus spread? Do it the Bhilwara way Before enforcing a strict clampdown, Bhilwara was Rajasthan’s worst-hit district, with 27 cases, and stood out in the national count as well. However, no new cases have been reported since 2 April, and in fact, 17 have recovered. Two have died due to co-morbidities, while seven are on the road to recovery and 11 already discharged. Finally, the Agra model. Agra had a different challenge than Bhilwara. It did a lot of the stuff that Kerala and Bhilwara did, but the unique challenge was to take care of the dense population. For the same, the city locked down a 3-km radius around the house of the first imported cases at amazing speed. It was absolutely splendid execution — Success of a local shutdown: Centre showcases Agra model of containment A senior official associated with the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, who oversaw the combing operations that followed, said: “The confirmation from the airport tests came at 2 am; we got into action immediately. A 3-km radius around the house was sealed and 259 teams were formed of two members each. We covered 1.63 lakh households in a few days, took about 1000 samples, used S N Medical College as our base. It was an exercise where nothing could be left to chance — a security guard was roped in to supply daily needs to the families.” Each team covered about 100 homes per day; doctors sat at a nearby civil dispensary, and people who showed symptoms could visit them. The Union Health Ministry said in a statement: “The State, district administration and frontline workers coordinated their efforts by utilising their existing Smart City Integrated with Command and Control Centre (ICCC) as war rooms. Under the cluster containment and outbreak containment plans, the district administration identified epicenters, delineated impact of positive confirmed cases on the map and deployed a special task force as per the micro-plan made by the district administration. “The hotspots were managed through an active survey and containment plan. Area was identified within radius of 3-km from the epicentre while (a) 5 km buffer zone was identified as the containment zone.” In these containment zones, urban primary health centres were roped in and 1,248 teams were deployed; each team had two workers, including ANMs/ASHA/AWW, reaching out to 9.3 lakh people through household screening. Additionally, effective and early tracking of first contact-tracing was thoroughly mapped.

Question: Is Kerala better than other Indian states in terms of covid 19 prevention?
Answer: Oh, absolutely! Kerala is showing the way right now for the rest of India on how to fight this dastardly virus. Remember that Kerala was the first state in India to register a case of the COVID19 infection — India's first coronavirus case: Kerala student in Wuhan tested positive. It was also the first state to have a case of a child infection — 3-yr-old from Kerala becomes first child in India to test positive for coronavirus For a long time, it had the highest number of cases in India until states like Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu exploded, with a not so little help from the Tablighi Jamaat. However, over the past few days, active testing by the state government and cooperation from the people have turned the tide around. Kerala’s list of “firsts” got a welcome new entry — India's oldest COVID-19 survivor, wife discharged from Kerala hospital They set up nifty, protected booths to collect samples while maintaining social distancing and appropriate safety measures to combat the spread of the disease. Kasargod, the worst affected district, was high on the priority list for appropriate government measures, with a dedicated 200-bed, 20 ICU hospital set up at astounding pace. They initiated contact tracing well before the TJ fiasco unveiled, enabling people to self-assess whether they had come in contact with someone who was infected — Kerala maps movement of coronavirus patients And finally, the results are coming out. The curve has started to flatten in Kerala and in a day or two, the total recoveries will be more than the total active cases. I literally can’t describe how happy I was to see this weird little graph. The times, they are a-changin’ folks. Just a few more days of patience, cooperation, and persistence. Go Kerala! Kerala, Go!

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Why is Tablighi Jamaat and its followers branded as anti-nationals and terrorists by the Indian media?
Answer: Who said they are branded as terrorists by only the Indian media? They have been called out by many more people and nations. It has been called a “Wolf in Sheep’s clothing” and 80% of extremist terrorists in France have ties to the organization. The US has also confirmed that it is a breeding ground for recruits that eventually join the likes of Al Qaeda — Tablighi Jamaat: Jihad's Stealthy Legions Perhaps 80 percent of the Islamist extremists in France come from Tablighi ranks, prompting French intelligence officers to call Tablighi Jamaat the "antechamber of fundamentalism." U.S. counterterrorism officials are increasingly adopting the same attitude. "We have a significant presence of Tablighi Jamaat in the United States," the deputy chief of the FBI's international terrorism section said in 2003, "and we have found that Al-Qaeda used them for recruiting now and in the past." It has also given rise to many terrorist offshoot outfits, like the Harakat Ul-Mujahideen and Harakat ul-Jihad-i Islami, which have been linked to multiple hijackings and terrorist incidents. Tablighi Jamaat has long been directly involved in the sponsorship of terrorist groups. Pakistani and Indian observers believe, for instance, that Tablighi Jamaat was instrumental in founding Harakat ul-Mujahideen. Founded at Raiwind in 1980, almost all of the Harakat ul-Mujahideen's original members were Tablighis. Famous for the December 1998 hijacking of an Air India passenger jet and the May 8, 2002 murder of a busload of French engineers in Karachi, Harakat members make no secret of their ties. "The two organizations together make up a truly international network of genuine jihadi Muslims," one senior Harakat ul-Mujahideen official said. More than 6,000 Tablighis have trained in Harakat ul-Mujahideen camps. Many fought in Afghanistan in the 1980s and readily joined Al-Qaeda after the Taliban defeated Afghanistan's anti-Soviet mujahideen. Another violent Tablighi Jamaat spin-off is the Harakat ul-Jihad-i Islami. Founded in the aftermath of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, this group has been active not only in the disputed Indian provinces of Jammu and Kashmir but also in the state of Gujarat, where Tablighi Jamaat extremists have taken over perhaps 80 percent of the mosques previously run by the moderate Barelvi Muslims. The Tablighi movement is also very active in northern Africa where it became one of the four groups that founded the Islamic Salvation Front in Algeria. Moroccan authorities are currently prosecuting sixty members of the Moroccan Tablighi offshoot Dawa wa Tabligh in connection with the May 16, 2003 terrorist attack on a Casablanca synagogue. Dutch police are investigating links between the Moroccan cells and the November 2, 2004 murder of Dutch filmmaker Theo van Gogh. They have been noted to be a kind of “gateway” institution for radicalized terrorists in Europe — French Islamic group offers rich soil for militancy The Tablighi are one of the primary forces spreading Islamic fundamentalism in Europe, and many young men pass through the group on their way to an extreme, militant interpretation of the religion. Former members of TJ were responsible for the 2005 London Bombings — Islamic group is linked to London Bridge killer and 7/7 attack The youngest of the London Bridge attackers was associated with an Islamic group with links to a series of terrorist plots. Youssef Zaghba, 22, attended meetings of Tablighi Jamaat while studying in Morocco before moving to London two years ago. The group, which has a strong presence in Britain, has been accused by foreign intelligence agencies of becoming a recruitment ground for foreign extremist organisations. British terrorists linked to it include Mohammed Sidique Khan, leader of the 7/7 bombers who killed 55 people in London in 2005, and fellow attacker Shehzad Tanweer. Both attended the group’s mosque in Yorkshire. And it was the case for the 2006 airline bombing plot that was thankfully foiled — Airline bomb plot: investigation 'one of biggest since WW2' Ali, 28, was born in east London, into a religious family of eight brothers and sisters, with close connections to Pakistan. Even before graduating in engineering at City University in London, he was surrounded by the extremists of al-Muhajiroun, led by the preacher Omar Bakri Mohammed, and the fundamentalists of a world-wide missionary group, Tablighi Jamaat, both of which operated from his local mosque in Queen’s Road, Walthamstow. They are currently being heavily criticized in both Pakistan and Malaysia, two more nations that have suffered heavy COVID19 casualties due to events organized by the TJ in Feb and March — Tablighi Jamaat faces ire in Pakistan, Malaysia. Both Pakistan and Indonesia are Muslim-majority countries, so it is very clear that the TJ does not represent the average Muslim, but is a cult whose main agenda is to brainwash impressionable young minds and fuel extremist terrorism. The organization is a listed “terrorist organization” in Kazakhstan, Russia, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan — Kazakhstan Bans Islamic Group A court in Astana has banned the international Islamic group Tablighi Jamaat. Kazakhstan's Prosecutor-General's Office announced on February 26 that the group had been designated as extremist and all its activities in Kazakhstan were now considered illegal. In recent years, it has been banned in Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. Last year in Tajikistan, several members of the group were sentenced to prison terms of between three and five years. So, no. It is not being branded as terrorists only in India. It should have been done long ago. But better late than never.

Question: Which is the worst op-ed written by an Indian journalist you've ever read?
Answer: This one : The Callousness of India’s COVID-19 Response Written for The Atlantic by a Ms. Vidya Krishnan (we will get back to her later), it just shows how journalism is truly failing with each passing day. The article is just a rant, an outlet for the hatred the author harbors against the current Indian administration. In writing about the lockdown and the Indian government response to it, the author somehow manages to start off by talking about the CAA and NRC protests in India in Jan. I have no idea how that was relevant to the article, but the author did. The country reported its first case on January 30, but authorities steadfastly insisted that cases were one-offs and no local transmission was taking place. I have ZERO clue what the author is trying to say here. Yes, India did have its first case on Jan 30, a student who returned from Wuhan. There were 2 more cases in Feb. And that was it. At the start of March, India still had 3 cases, all imported. By definition, they were one-off, and there was no LOCAL transmission, leave alone COMMUNITY transmission. Even today, India thankfully hasn’t reached the community transmission stage — WHO corrects report, says no community transmission in India. WHO has rectified its earlier statement and said that India has “clusters” of cases but no community transmission. And we all know that one incident, the Tablighi Jamaat congregation in Nizamuddin is responsible for the former — Coronavirus: 1,445 cases liked to Tablighi Jamaat event, total crosses 4,000 But instead of condemning that incident, the author twists it to suit her agenda; for her, calling out the TJ is just another form of persecution of Muslims in India. She then lambasts the government for the short notice and laments that there were no shops open after the announcement. Modi made his speech at 8:00 p.m. on March 24, saying the restrictions would come into force just after midnight and be in place for three weeks. By the time he spoke, shops had closed for the day, catching off guard people who had been repeatedly told not to panic-buy. The next morning, nothing was open in Goa, the state where I live. Elsewhere, such as in Britain, France, and Italy, grocery stores and pharmacies have remained open to provide essential services, but here, they are closed. I live in Mumbai, and all essential stores are open. Medical stores are also selling basic groceries and fresh produce. This is literally what the PM had said — no need to panic, essentials will be available. But it seems like asking for a little patience was too much as the author could not wait even a couple of days. She goes on to highlight the “authorities’ callousness” by quoting a few incidents. Again, the authorities’ callousness has been on display: In one heartbreaking video that went viral, police in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh force young boys to perform frog jumps as punishment for violating the curfew. Another video shows police waiting outside a mosque in the southern state of Karnataka, beating worshippers with a stick as they leave. Similar cases of police brutality have been reported around the country, and social media have filled with messages of people running out of food yet afraid to leave their dwellings, fearful of the police. So, the case where offenders who broke lockdown guidelines were made to do “frog jumps” is “heartbreaking”. And the fact that people congregated for prayers despite clear directions not to do so is not criticized but police meting out punishment is? It’s absolutely insane that someone like her is afforded multiple global platforms to spread the misinformation and channel her own biases. Today, she mocked the PM for wearing a face mask for a virtual meeting with all CMs to decide on extension of the lockdown. India’s COVID response, as per her, is “high on tokenism & low on common sense”. She forgot that the PM is a role model for crores of Indians, and his wearing a mask in a virtual meeting would set a great example for the rest of the nation. His words, his actions, his appeals have power. And we have already seen it when he asked people to clap for the first responders and the medical workers a couple of weeks back. We saw it again when he asked everyone to shut off their lights and India’s power consumption went down by more than a quarter. So yes, he needs to wear a mask even for online meetings. It is an example for people to be followed. Not to mention, the fact that his residence will have other people too. India has the most stringent response to the COVID crisis. With nothing more to say, the lady compared the PM to Lord Voldemort, exposing the vacuousness of her own arguments.

Question: How long can India shut down everything to contain the coronavirus (COVID-19)? Is it even practical?
Answer: The original lockdown deadline is nearing. But based on the 4-hour long meeting between the PM and the CMs of Indian states, an extension of about 14–16 days is almost confirmed. We just have to wait for the official announcement. Had the Tablighi Jamaat incident not thrown a spanner and derailed India’s efforts to curb the viral outbreak, we would have seen the curve getting flatter now. But what is done is done, and we can only prosecute the offenders later and focus on alleviating the situation for now. IMO, a 2-week extension of the lockdown is absolutely manageable. We are still doing ok on the economic front and can take another couple of weeks of a proper shutdown — IIP: India Industrial Production Rose To Seven-Month High In February However, I do not think that the situation will truly be resolved by the end of April. However, we might be able to open up a good chunk of the informal economy. In my opinion, Tier 1 cities and large clusters like NCR and Mumbai will need to be kept under lockdown for another 2–3 weeks in May. The large population density of these cities will mean that even a few active cases could lead to a second wave of infections. However, even in these cities, the governments need to come up with a plan to address the needs of the poor. Food and other essential items must be provided by the state coffers. There needs to also be some sort of monetary compensation directly credited to them to run their household. I am in favor of Mr. Owaisi saying that the poor should receive at least Rs 5000. Remember that we might be in the Endgame already. We have had a few setbacks along the way, but things are still very much under control. With a few asinine exceptions, this country of 1.3 billion has displayed truly phenomenal control in the last 3 weeks. Let us not let that go to waste.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Is the statement 'MBA is not for introverts' accurate?
Answer: Absolute hogwash. I am an introvert, and I successfully completed my MBA program. Of the 400-odd participants, probably just 10% could be truly termed extroverts. Some of the more shy ones registered the most class participation because they put in efforts to read the material before a class and to frame questions that they needed answers to. The same applies for pre-placement talks and networking events. A lot of the people I vibed with were like me, and they have made it in every domain and role — consulting, finance, marketing, product, etc. It is true that the ability to effectively network with batchmates, professors, seniors, alumni, and recruiters is absolutely essential. And yes, the more extroverted ones have it easier than others. However, like almost everything in life, it is a skill that can be learned and nurtured with practice. Introversion is not crippling social anxiety. And deeming an entire program to not be fit for a large group of people with a specific social proclivity is totally nonsensical.

Question: Do you think India's Corona curve would have flattened or went on a decline if you remove the cases due to Tablighi Jamat?

Question: If all other conditions remain the same, can it be said that India will carry a high risk of Covid-19 due to eating habits like direct hand-to-mouth?

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What are good impacts of preventive measures against corona virus i.e. lockdown of India till 14 April by the government?
Answer: One amazing positive side-effect of the lockdown is that the pollution levels in the country have come down drastically — The world's largest coronavirus lockdown is having a dramatic impact on pollution in India In the capital, New Delhi, government data shows the average concentration of PM 2.5 plunged by 71% in the space of a week -- falling from 91 microgram per cubic meter on March 20, to 26 on March 27, after the lockdown began. The World Health Organization considers anything above 25 to be unsafe. The data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), part of India's Environment Ministry, was collated by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). Nitrogen dioxide went from 52 per cubic meter to 15 in the same period -- also a 71% fall. Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and Bangalore have also recorded a fall in these air pollutants. Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: How are you managing social distancing in this pandemic times?
Answer: There are some perks to being an introvert. 😊 Today is the 20th day of the quarantine for me and frankly, it isn’t nearly as bad as I thought it would be. I have ventured out around 4–5 times in this period mostly to get some fresh produce and groceries. My only consistent company is my wife and our neighbors (a couple and their 4-year old). I get up around noon. Spend an hour on the daily morning routine — coffee, news, music, personal hygiene. I then fire up my mailbox to address anything urgent. Then it is time to prepare lunch. And regularly cooking has been quite fun these past days, especially when there are some amazing tunes in the background. Preparing and eating lunch, plus the dishes afterward takes about an hour or 90 minutes, so it is well past 3 pm. I work till 6 pm on weekdays or catch up on a movie or TV series on the weekends. I have finally started on the “new year resolution” that has been with me for over a decade now — to walk/jog. I go out and complete about 30–40 rounds of the building, listening to an audiobook or catching up with old friends. The next 2 hours are spent preparing for dinner. Afterward, we usually catch up with the neighbors over a fun game of Uno or Scrabble. The little one joins in too, making it even more fun. From midnight till the wee hours of dawn, I have about 4–5 hours to myself, during which I can really focus amid the eerie but welcome silence. It’s usually a course, or a book, or just spending time online. There is always a better vantage point for any situation. In the last 3 weeks:

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What would be your strategy to lift the lockdown in India after April 14th? Should it be extended or partially lifted for some sectors/states?
Answer: It definitely has to be a staggered approach. The number of COVID-19 cases in India have been growing sharply. The effects of the lockdown might be visible towards mid-April, but a lot of it has already been undone by the Tablighi Jamaat incident in Nizamuddin. It has literally cut the doubling time for cases by 40%. Considering this, opening up the entire nation on 15th April would just mean that 3 weeks of (almost) everyone staying home were just a futile exercise that delayed the progress of the virus but would do little to lessen its overall impact. Multiple studies have concluded that to be effective, the lockdown should be for at least 7–8 weeks.[1] So, the best way forward from 15 April would be a staggered approach. This is it. I personally am absolutely horrified at the idea of staying holed up at home for another 4–5 weeks. I have already been in quarantine for 19 days now, and there’s another 9 for the original 3-week lockdown to expire. But this is a small price to pay for millions of lives. A model[2] by Armed Forces Medical College, Pune and INHS Asvini, Mumbai predicts that at the current rate, India will have 3 million cases by May. However, a successful lockdown can bring IT DOWN BY 90%. At 3 million cases in May, we will have 30,000+ ICU cases and India has an overall capacity of 70,000. And some of them would be required for non-covid cases too. Implying that, if we don’t do anything, our healthcare system would be absolutely in shambles in a mere two more months. However, a successful lockdown that is able to contain and quarantine at least 50% of the infected cases will see the numbers go down to 300,000 total infected, 10,000+ hospitalizations, and only 2000+ ICU requirements. This would enable our frontline healthcare workers to eventually conquer this fucking plague.

Question: Is there anyone here who thought the coronavirus was no big deal and changed their mind? What made you change?
Answer: 🙋🏻‍♂️ Around the start of March, when the world had not yet descended into total madness, I came across a LinkedIn post about how the Coronavirus outbreak was more mass hysteria than an actual pandemic since it was the first true “social media outbreak”. A lot of things in the post resonated with me — the low mortality rate (~2% at that time), few cases outside China, and the fact that Swine Flu and Ebola resulted in far more deaths. I wrote about it here, urging people to not panic. I did not see the appeal behind panic buying and stocking (I still think that a lot of people have gone horribly overboard with it). When I saw the first person in Mumbai wearing a mask, I chuckled to myself. I have been holed up at my place for 14 days now. There are another 14 to go before the ongoing lockdown in India is lifted. There are almost 2000 cases in India and we have finally reached the community transmission stage, which for a country as densely populated as India is a frightening scenario. And globally, we are almost at a million cases, with 90% of them outside of China. On March 1, there were 3 cases in India, and 87000 globally, with only 8000 or so cases outside of China. What made me change my mind? Data. The exponential growth of cases has continued for 30 days now and shows no signs of stopping. China, Japan, South Korea have contained the outbreak. The curve has started to flatten in Italy. But the US, Spain, Germany, UK, and France are still reeling under an avalanche of new cases every day. And for some nations like India, Brazil, Pakistan, things are only getting started. We live in really scary times. And all I can do right now is to hope that this is over soon.

Question: What is wrong with making everyone happy?
Answer: Two thousand years ago, a man was born. He preached love for everyone. He healed the deformed and fed the hungry. He was a total pacifist and an all-around great dude. Do you know what happened to him? People nailed him to a cross. There are 7 billion people on the planet. All with their unique sensibilities and prejudices. No two people will ever have the exact same opinion of you. Every action of yours, every word that comes out of your mouth, every choice you make, every breath you take (dang!), can and will be used against you in the court of public judgment. If you are shy and quiet, some will think of you as self-involved and/or anti-social. If you are a vivacious socializer, some will deem it attention-seeking. Your honesty will be seen as a lack of empathy. Your zeal as over-confidence. Your charity as gloating. Some people will hate that you are taller than they are. Some will envy you for your wealth, intelligence, success, recognition. You can be a statue standing still and I guarantee you at least one person will hate you because you “don’t give the right vibe!” And some will even backtrack and hate you for doing exactly what they criticized you for not doing. I mean, look at this lady. (Someone, please tell Rohini about the choice between having your cake or eating it, and the fact that they are mutually exclusive) There’s a beautiful Aesop’s Fable that highlights the fallacy of trying to please everyone — “The Man, the Boy, and the Donkey” A Man and his son were once going with their Donkey to market. As they were walking along by its side a countryman passed them and said: “You fools, what is a Donkey for but to ride upon?” So the Man put the Boy on the Donkey and they went on their way. But soon they passed a group of men, one of whom said: “See that lazy youngster, he lets his father walk while he rides.” So the Man ordered his Boy to get off, and got on himself. But they hadn’t gone far when they passed two women, one of whom said to the other: “Shame on that lazy lout to let his poor little son trudge along.” Well, the Man didn’t know what to do, but at last he took his Boy up before him on the Donkey. By this time they had come to the town, and the passers-by began to jeer and point at them. The Man stopped and asked what they were scoffing at. The men said: “Aren’t you ashamed of yourself for overloading that poor donkey of yours and your hulking son?” The Man and Boy got off and tried to think what to do. They thought and they thought, till at last they cut down a pole, tied the donkey’s feet to it, and raised the pole and the donkey to their shoulders. They went along amid the laughter of all who met them till they came to Market Bridge, when the Donkey, getting one of his feet loose, kicked out and caused the Boy to drop his end of the pole. In the struggle the Donkey fell over the bridge, and his fore-feet being tied together he was drowned. “That will teach you,” said an old man who had followed them: “Please all, and you will please none.” So, “What is wrong with making everyone happy?” It’s a pipe dream. And definitely not worth chasing.

Question: How destructive has Covid-19 been for the world economy?
Answer: $3.5–3.7 trillion. The economic impact of the ongoing pandemic can be gauged by the downwards revision of the growth forecasts of the major world economies. #1: USA There are many estimates right now. The predictions range from -2% to -15%. Assuming a very “liberal” 5% drop in GDP in 2020, and adding to it the 2% growth predictions prior to the COVID disaster, US will forego about 7% of projected GDP in 2020. For a $21 trillion economy, that translates to $1.4 trillion. #2: China China has done a great job of recovering from the crisis, but it will still feel the aftershocks of the pandemic — Top China bank unexpectedly slashes 2020 growth forecast amid virus fallout. The growth rate has been slashed from 6.1% to 2.6%, implying 3.5% of foregone growth. For a $14 trillion economy, that is a notional loss of $0.5 trillion. #3: Eurozone Britain, eurozone face 2% recession in 2020 – S&P S&P says a 2% recession for Britain and the eurozone would amount to a loss in real GDP of about 420 billion euros ($460 billion) in 2020 And finally, #4: India Covid-19 impact: Barclays cuts India's GDP target to 2.5%, fiscal deficit to 5% of GDP “We estimate that the cumulative shutdown costs will be around $120 billion, or 4 per cent of GDP," says Barclays. Add them all up, and we get $2.5 trillion in GDP losses in 2020. Considering that the 3 economies and the economic zone mentioned above roughly make up two-thirds of the world economy, we can extrapolate that the total loss to the world economy would be to the tune of $3.5–3.7 trillion.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: After Covid19, how long will it take for the stock market to return to January 2020 levels?
Answer: At the very least a year, assuming the world is able to vanquish this virus in the next 3–4 months. In the worst case, more than double that. During the 2008–09 financial meltdown, global markets crashed by more than 50%. NASDAQ peaked at about 2800 in Nov 2007. On 27 Feb, 2009, it was lingering below 1400. It took another 2 years (Feb 2011) for it to regain the 2800 mark. The Indian SENSEX had a similar trajectory. The peak of about 20,200 in end-Dec 2007, followed by a trough of 8700 in Jan-end 2009. Although it was able to recoup the losses and breached the 20,000 mark again in Oct 2010. The ongoing crisis, even after it is quelled, may have a lingering impact on the overall global economy, with trade restrictions and subdued travel impacting export-oriented (China, India) and tourism-heavy (Thailand, Italy, larger Europe) economies. Also, the overall consumer sentiment might just have been changed for the long-term with people preferring to save instead of spend, in fear of another looming disaster like this. This would again impact consumer-oriented economies like the USA. Also, if the pandemic is prolonged, there will be bankruptcies and massive layoffs, coupled with hoarding and price-gouging, with the potential to plunge global economies into stagflation, which is a really bad scenario. The cost of dealing with the aftermath of the epidemic coupled with lower business and personal incomes will put a dent into the fiscal deficit of large countries, making the road to recovery even harder.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What long-term impacts will COVID-19 coronavirus have on our world? When will we recognize them?
Answer: The COVID-19 crisis has exposed the chinks in the armor of this world and the people. We’ve just been proven, with a drastic example, utterly incapable of handling a worldwide pandemic. The coronavirus strain is ridiculously infectious, but the silver lining is that it is not as deadly as say Ebola. Imagine if it were! 300k infected, >150k dead. And that count is not going to stop anytime soon. We’ve seen how China needs to be held accountable in a world so highly interconnected. Had they taken the required precautions and quarantined the Hubei province at the initial signs of trouble, we wouldn’t have seen the virus go global. During the nascent stages of the now pandemic, China was, as usual, secretive and did squat-all. The first case was on 31 Dec, 2019 in Wuhan, yet it took the government more than 3 weeks (23 Jan) to quarantine Wuhan.[1] It was probably too late. The first known cases in now Italy were detected on 30 Jan, both being Chinese tourists who arrived in Rome on the same day as the declaration of Wuhan quarantine[2]. The same goes for the first cases in Japan — a tourist that returned from Wuhan on 14th Jan[3], in US — a tourist who had visited Wuhan and returned around 15th Jan[4], South Korea — tourists who returned on 22nd[5] . These are the countries that are the worst affected at the moment. Countries that are the worst hit right now, especially Italy and US, downplayed the severity of the virus at the start. Italy took over 3 weeks to shut down major cities like Milan.[6] The POTUS was busy boasting how “the average American” is at “negligible to low risk” from the virus and how “everything is good”. All of this has highlighted the need for Epidemic/Crisis management teams across major world economies, with a high level of autonomy. This needs to be coupled with an international organization like WHO that needs to be given more teeth to shutdown international travel in the early stages of a potential outbreak to ensure it stays contained at the epicenter. Businesses have been stressed, with a lot of them teetering on the verge of bankruptcy, sharply highlighting the need for diversification and for stronger regulations to ensure adequate capital buffers to manage such tumultuous times. The stress tests we have for major global banks in the wake of the 2009 crash need to be customized for other industries to ensure that large firms, at any time, have sufficient capital to continue operations unabated for at least 12 months. If individuals are expected to save for a rainy day, so should companies. They should also seriously evaluate the merits of a dispersed, virtual workforce that can continue operations remotely. This could also serve as a wake-up call for all world governments to rethink medical care as a fundamental right (looking at you USA). People don’t only get sick because of their choices, but also circumstances absolutely not in their control. Nobody should be denied treatment just because they cannot fucking afford a $1000 ambulance ride or a $20,000 diagnostic. Governments would need to massively transform their current healthcare operations — assess overall healthcare capacity, ensure that there is an auxiliary capacity to handle peak time cases, reform epidemic laws, pump more money in medical research, establish infrastructure to handle such quarantine cases, and overall work towards a system where large corporations do not hold all power. Finally, it has truly helped the people realize their priorities (hopefully!) All sports events have shut down or been postponed. Movie releases have been put on hold. Music concerts and art festivals have been canceled. Are you thinking about that? Then why are these folks being paid millions for the sake of “entertaining” us while doctors and nurses and cops get paid shit for their indispensable services? Also, being put at home without the option of paying for and availing help for basic chores like cooking and cleaning, has made people realize that some life skills need to be developed and honed instead of relying on an increasingly on-demand economy.

Question: What is your view on Narendra Modi's speech on the corona virus?

I would have also liked to see some update on businesses acting unethically and preying on people’s fears — hoarding, price gouging, spreading misinformation. Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What is the status and amount of coronavirus testing being done in India?
Answer: Thankfully, as of now, India has been spared the wrath of COVID-19. A lot of it can be chalked up to the proactive measures taken by the Indian authorities early on while Trump was busy calling COVID19 a democrat hoax and Europe was undecided. Dr. Balaji Viswanathan (பாலாஜி விஸ்வநாதன்)'s answer to How is it possible that Mumbai, being such a densely populated region, is still untouched by coronavirus? On Jan 17th, India announced mandatory thermal screening of all passengers from China. Coronavirus threat : Mandatory health screening of passengers from China at 7 Indian airports. This was before even quarantine was announced in Wuhan and just 41 confirmed cases worldwide. You can compare this with UK’s response [London has far more flights to China than Indian cities] 5 days later that was much more limited: UK to monitor China flights as virus precaution. UK’s applied only to just direct flights from Wuhan and not other flights. By the time India had 2 infections, the state that had them declared emergency on Feb 4: Kerala declares coronavirus outbreak as state disaster By the time India had 10 infections, there was a nationwide taskforce on March 4, with a wide range of measures. Government’s multi-step strategy to tackle coronavirus spread in India By the time India had its first death from Coronavirus, all tourists from abroad are stopped: India suspends tourist visas over coronavirus and even citizens are mandated high restrictions: People with travel history to Italy, S Korea need 'negative' COVID-19 certificate to enter India. As of today, there are 137 confirmed cases of the viral infection in India,[1]of which 14 have recovered and 3 have died. However, I have this strong feeling that Indian numbers are underreported, primarily because the volume of daily screening and tests have been astonishingly low. [2] India is conducting only about 90 tests per day, despite having the capacity for as many as 8,000. So far, 11,500 people have been tested. Except for the 3 students who returned from Wuhan in early Feb, the first cases in India were noted at the start of March, just 2.5 weeks ago.[3] Considering that the virus has an incubation period of about a week and that a lot of infected people are asymptomatic, coupled with the tendency of the general Indian populace to not go to the doctor for a “simple cold”, there is every chance that things could go horribly wrong soon. I hope I am proven wrong and the various state governments and ministries continue to take stringent preventative measures. Because if I am not, we might be staring at a crisis within a crisis.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What can you do during 14 days of the Coronavirus quarantine period?
Answer: Amidst the global frenzy in the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak, a lot of people will find themselves socially isolated and quarantined, mostly involuntarily. For people who are accustomed to a hectic life, this might be daunting, especially confined within the four walls of their homes, with no idea what to do. However, such “downtime” can be made productive and leisurely. You could always revisit a childhood hobby, something you abandoned before duties and responsibilities occupied every waking moment of every day. Or you could pick up a new one, something you have always wanted to learn but could never find the time to. There are instructional DIY videos and detailed lessons for beginners on Youtube on almost every topic conceivable. If you want to relax, there’s an inconceivable amount of literature and art online to consume. Download a new ebook to read. Or visit Project Gutenberg to get your hands on thousands of “classic” works that are in the public domain. Hit up your Netflix or Hulu account and watch some good movies. I am going to be exploring more of world cinema and watching movies and shows in languages other than Hindi or English. I just saw Parasite a month ago and I am currently binge-watching Money Heist. You could watch the French classic Amelie, or the painfully funny German tragicomedy A Coffee in Berlin. Non-Indians could explore wonderful Bollywood movies like Udaan, 3 Idiots, Andhadhun, The Lunchbox, Stree, etc. Animation fans, especially from the Western nations could step out of their comfort zones of Disney, Pixar, and Dreamworks and explore the mesmerizing creation of Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli — Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro, The Red Turtle, Kiki’s Delivery Service. You could take this time to think of something new — academicians could publish a paper, techies could develop a new app or a new website, entrepreneurs could just seed the next unicorn. Comic enthusiasts could purchase a DC/Marvel/Comxiology subscription and catch up on the last few years of stories they have missed. The musical souls could finally pen and record a song, who knows there’s the next Ed Sheeran or Taylor Swift, hiding somewhere in their apartment, bogged down by their daily obligations to dedicate time to their art. If you have a great voice and in-depth knowledge about any topic, start a new podcast. It requires minimal set-up and could very well become a great secondary source of income. Working professionals can learn a new subject or complete an online course or certification to boost their profile, to diversify their skill set, or just for the sake of learning something new. I have shared some good resources on my UoQ (University of Quora) space. If you have always wanted to get in shape, you can start forming the habit now — you don’t even need equipment to start training your body — The 7 Best at Home Workouts (No-Equipment Required). People who stay alone could learn how to cook, a skill that is absolutely essential yet forgotten in a world where everything from groceries to gourmet meals is just at the tap of a few buttons. You’d not only be eating healthier, but you will also save a lot of money (once this outbreak dies off, and God! let that be quick). At the same time, cooking, at least in my personal opinion is a great destresser. This list is by no means comprehensive, but you get the idea. Quarantine doesn’t have to be dull and unrewarding. With some planning and effort, it could be a great time to catch up on life or plan what lies ahead.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: What are the worst coronavirus myths roaming around social media?
Answer: One of the scariest things I have been reading all over is people pondering getting infected early. Yep. The “reasoning” seems to be two-fold: early infection will mean immunity later on when the virus is deadlier and the fact that they will get treated right now when the cases are low. But this is a very dangerous line of thinking. Firstly, there is NO evidence that like Chicken Pox, getting infected will build immunity to the virus. Secondly, the time-frame in which people get infected matters. In fact, one of the primary reasons that make COVID-19 so scary is the rate at which it is spreading. Worldwide, the infrastructure is not equipped to deal with such a sudden surge of patients that require utmost care and isolation — Coronavirus cases are pushing Italy's hospitals to the brink. The need of the hour is to “flatten the curve” — i.e. to slow down the spread of the virus so that the “peak number of cases at any point” remain low enough to be handled properly by our existing healthcare infrastructure. Washington Post has done a brilliant piece — https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/corona-simulator/ — providing simulations for multiple situations in a hypothetical town of 200 people. In essence, “JUST STAY HOME AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE, PEOPLE!”

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Which industries benefit from the coronavirus?
Answer: The primary beneficiary of the COVID19 pandemic would obviously be the healthcare sector — hospitals, pharmacies, pharma firms, and insurance companies. Just the fact that the entire world has been given a stark reminder of how fragile our lives are would lead to more risk-averse behavior. In India, the ongoing scare has seen 40% rise in queries for health insurance.[1] “We have seen enquiries on health insurance policies from customers rise nearly 30-40% over the past few days,” said Amit Chhabra, business head, health insurance, PolicyBazaar. “A standard health insurance policy will cover all post-hospitalisation covers. Right now, pre-hospitalisation costs, such as check-ups, are being incurred by the government.” Since people are being forced to stay home, businesses that are primarily online will likely see a boost — social media companies, websites, online shopping, streaming services, etc. A lot of movies slated for summer release are being postponed and some might even move to online streaming services like Netflix.[2] "We are boosting our anticipated subscribership numbers for Netflix's first quarter, primarily due to what we believe is a 'cocooning' effect at hand due to fears surrounding the coronavirus," he wrote in a note to clients this week. "Not only is Netflix's service impervious to the effects of the virus, but because the price is so low, it is impervious to any derivative recessionary effects that may arise as a result," Miller said. Miller now expects Netflix to add 510,000 subscribers in the UCAN market and 7 million international subscribers, bringing the first quarter total to 7.5 million, significantly higher than Netflix's forecast. Then there is the online porn business.[3] For example, on Thursday, Pornhub’s worldwide traffic was 5.7% higher than usual for a Wednesday. Digging into the data more, the site found that “at 2 a.m., traffic was 11% higher than usual, but dipped 9% below average at 8 a.m.” Apparently, 8 a.m. is usually one of the most popular times to visit Pornhub. The site attributes this change to “people who did not need to commute to work the next day stayed up later and slept in longer than they normally would.” And the video game industry. The popular CS:GO just witnessed a massive landmark — one million concurrent players and the Steam service saw 20 million concurrent users.[4] Of course, when you can’t go outside and socialize, you log on to play some games with people.

Name: Deepak Mehta
Question: Did the coronavirus do good things too? If so, what?
Answer: They say, “Every cloud has a silver lining”. The ongoing COVID-19 Pandemic has forced the world to fundamentally reassess its priorities. Companies all over the world are evaluating the feasibility of a large part of its workforce working remotely from home.[1] [2] [3] If this change becomes structural, then once the outbreak has been quelled, we will see a more dispersed, global workforce. It should have already happened with the technology that we have now and the fact that a good number of jobs do not require their employees to be present at a specific location. This would imply less commute for work, lower need for corporate infrastructure, and overall increased employee satisfaction. We might see lowering of real estate prices across metropolitans as demand for both offices and residential properties in industrial hot-beds decline. This would also be a great push for distance learning. We already have avenues to promote learning outside of the classrooms but we haven’t been leveraging the same. There is no reason why someone should have to fly from India to the US to attend a class at Harvard if they can get the same experience on their laptop. I had written a piece about MOOCs and the future of learning, and this outbreak might just breach the glass ceiling and hasten its adoption — Deepak Mehta (दीपक मेहता)'s answer to What according to you is the future of MOOCs? The scare has also pushed people to be more cognizant of their health and personal hygiene. The sudden reminder of our mortality might also encourage people to reevaluate their goals and pursue their passions. Quarantined in their homes, people might just make new scientific and technological breakthroughs. When the Great Plague of London hit, Sir Issac Newton was one of the many who were forced to stay at home. During this time, he made great strides in what would be his theories of gravity and optics and his foundational work on Calculus.[4] Newton left Cambridge returned to his family’s home in Cambridge, where he had long stretches of time to work alone on various questions that had been on his mind. While there, he had a breakthrough regarding the nature of motion and gravity — a narrative you might already be familiar with. But that wasn’t all that Newton accomplished in isolation. According to Brockell’s article, Newton came up with vital early theories of both optics and calculus during this period. The whole world seems to be on a collective vacation, spending more time with their family and pets. It had been hustling and frantically working till now — the stock market had been on a bull run for more than a decade, tourism was at an all-time high, it was pure chaos and pandemonium all around. Now it seems like the planet is taking a breather.[5] [6] (Kaaba) (Venice) Animals are reclaiming the planet. Global warming will slow down.[7] If this trend continues, analysts say it is possible this will lead to the first fall in global emissions since the 2008-09 financial crisis. Even a slowdown in CO2 could buy time for climate action and, more importantly, inspire long-term behavioural changes – particularly in travel. As conferences, air travel, concerts, sports events, etc. get canceled, the overall emissions are expected to go down.
