Question: Is the coronavirus that we are having right now among the worst in human history?
Answer: Not by a long shot. Not till now, and hopefully never. The ongoing Coronavirus/COVID-19 outbreak is deadly, no doubt. But the worst part about it is the nature of its virality — it is spreading at an unprecedented rate, with the number of confirmed cases doubling every 3 days or so.[1] In absolute terms, the stats currently are as follows[2] There are speculations that if a treatment is not developed soon, or if the spread of the disease is not curtailed by governments and the public, eventually ~50% of the world might get affected. The current stated mortality rate of 3%+ seems an exaggeration since a lot of people who contracted the virus (mild infection) likely didn’t get tested and got well, overstating the more serious cases.[3] Assuming a 1% mortality rate, the worst-case scenario would imply about 3.6 bn infected, and 36 million dead. This would be extremely tragic, but would still not compare with the Spanish Flu of 1918. [4] The Spanish Flu infected a quarter of the global population of about 2 billion at that time. Total infected were in about 500 million of which estimated casualties were about 50 million, implying that 2.5% of the global population perished because of it. But we need to remember that a century ago, we didn’t have the scientific temper and the medical advancements we have now. In fact, the world at that time did not even know that the flu was caused by a virus, and in fact, believed it was a bacterial infection. [5] The Spanish flu is frightening because it demonstrates that in a reasonably modern society, a pandemic killing tens of millions of people is very plausible. But that “reasonably modern” society was still much more primitive when it came to medicine and public health than the world of today. If only people follow the medical guidelines issued by health authorities worldwide, go to the doctor at the slightest sign of infection, duly self-quarantine themselves, and just be cautious for the next month or two, we have the infrastructure and the facilities required to treat the infected and the rate of spread would drastically decline.

Question: Which finance certification should I do after MBA?
Answer: #1: CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst) [ https://www.cfainstitute.org/en/programs/cfa/exam ]: [ https://www.cfainstitute.org/pages/index.aspx ]Granted by the CFA institute, the CFA certification is the most popular certification in Finance for those wishing to pursue a career primarily in Financial Research and reporting. Requiring at least 1.5 years of commitment to clear a 3-stage examination, it is highly advised that one be serious about it before enrolling. Cost: ~$2100 (for early-bird registration) #2: FRM (Financial Risk Manager) [ https://www.garp.org/#!/frm ]: Almost as popular as CFA, the FRM certification from GARP (Global Association of Risk Professionals) is spread over 2 tests that can be taken either together or at an interval of 6 months. While CFA is more generic in nature, covering financial statement analysis, corporate finance, economics, wealth management, and derivatives, the FRM is more focused on risk and derivatives. Note that it requires 2 years of experience in the risk domain to be eligible for the charter, but that can be done after the exam too, within the next 5 years. Cost: ~$1100 (for early-bird registration) #3: ERP (Energy Risk Professional) [ https://www.garp.org/#!/erp ]: Another certification, in line with FRM, provided by GARP. This one, however, is tailored to people in the Energy Risk Domain — either with global Oil and Gas firms or within Consulting and Research domains focusing on the energy sector. It is also a 2-part examination, with the format, dates, etc similar to FRM. Cost: ~$1100 (for early-bird registration) #4: CAMS (Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist) [ http://www.acams.org/anti-money-laundering-specialist-certification/ ]: Continuing on the path of greater specialization, we have the CAMS certification from ACAMS (Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists) for professionals working in the domain of Anti-Money Laundering and FCC (Financial Crime Compliance). ACAMS is the leading authority on this. There is only one examination, but there are criteria for eligibility which can be calculated on the website: CAMS Credit Calculator [ https://www.acams.org/cams-calculator/ ]. If you have a Masters’ degree and 2 years of experience in the AML field, you are eligible. Cost: $1695 (for private sector people), $1295 (for public sector) #5: CGSS (Certified Global Sanctions Specialist) [ https://www.acams.org/certified-global-sanctions-specialist/ ]: Another certification from ACAMS within the Money-Laundering domain, but focusing on Economic Sanctions and Screening. A little more niche than CAMS. Cost: $1695 (for private sector people), $795 (for public sector) #6: CFE (Certified Fraud Examiner) [ https://www.acfe.com/become-cfe-qualifications.aspx ]: Provided by the ACFE (Association of Certified Fraud Examiners), this is closely linked to the previous 2, but focuses on Fraud Detection and Prevention. Even people with just a Bachelor’s Degree and 2 years of experience in the Fraud Domain are eligible. Cost: $400 #7: NCFM Modules (NSE - National Stock Exchange of India Limited) [ https://www.nseindia.com/education/content/module_ncfm.htm ]: The 40+ NCFM modules spread over foundation (beginner), intermediate, and advanced cover a wide range of financial topics from the basics of financial markets and the OTC derivatives market, to mutual funds, venture capital, algorithmic trading and other advanced concepts. Cost: ~$100 per certification #8: Vskills Govt. Certification [ http://www.vskills.in/certification/index.php?route=common%2Fhome ]: Vskills is a special, low-cost certification program run by the Govt of India. Although it has certifications for a wide variety of industries (Design, IT, Legal, Marketing etc), the relevant ones for finance professionals can be found here: Accounting, Banking, and Finance: [ http://www.vskills.in/certification/accounting-banking-and-finance ](40+ certifications for Equity analysis, FI analysis, AML/KYC, Portfolio management, M&A, Credit risk, Basel III, IFRS etc). Cost: Most (>90%) certifications are priced in the range of ₹3000–5000. #9: Multiple certifications from IIBF [ http://iibf.org.in/Certificate_exam_schedule.asp ]: The Indian Institute of Banking and Finance offers a host of certificates (Quantitative Finance, Trade Finance, AML/KYC etc) at a very reasonable cost. Cost: About ₹1500–5000 per certification. However, I would recommend going for the JA-IIB (Junior Associate of IIBF) [ http://iibf.org.in/flagshipcourses.asp?tab=1 ]program for beginners. It is their flagship course which covers Principles and Practices of Banking, Accounting and Finance, and Legal and Regulatory Aspects over 3 examinations spread over a month. Once you are done with it, for the CA-IIB (Certified Associate of IIBF) [ http://iibf.org.in/flagshipcourses.asp?tab=2 ] module which is more advanced. Cost: ₹2700 for JA-IIB, and ₹3000 for CA-IIB #10: Free 2-year MSc in Financial Engineering [ https://wqu.org/programs/mscfe ] from WQU (World Quant University) [ https://wqu.org/ ]: WQU is a not-for-profit with an amazing mission — “…to make advanced, quality education accessible to capable students everywhere by leveraging technology at scale to deliver entirely online, tuition-free programs.” They are providing a full-fledged 2-year MSc in Financial Engineering [ https://wqu.org/programs/mscfe ] from the comfort of your home — all it would take is dedication to complete the same. The syllabus is comprehensive and the course ends with a Capstone project to test what you have learnt. Cost: Free #11: CAIA [ https://caia.org/ ] (Certified Alternate Investment Associate): Another great certification (based on review from people who have done it) that covers alternate asset classes for investment. Quite difficult but a must for people aiming for a career in Asset Management, Private Equity, Hedge Funds etc. 2-part examination. Question: ‘Thank God this didn’t start in India’: Jim O’Neill praises China’s coronavirus response. What are your thoughts on this statement?
Answer: Siddharth Kumar's answer hits the nail on the head. China, clearly, has far superior infrastructure to contain and handle the situation and it has shown that. It built a new hospital in less than a week[1]. In India, even the foundation would not have been laid because we would have been waiting for an “honorable dignitary” to cut the ribbon and kick-off the project. They have converted all toll plazas to checking points. India would not have been able to do so. The autocratic Chinese government quickly implemented measures to quarantine entire cities to curtail the spread of the disease. More than 45 million people were effectively locked down[2], theaters shut down[3], whistleblowers’ deaths shushed[4]. In India, any such measure would probably have been hailed by our and the Western media as an infringement of human rights and personal freedom. But, China can do all of that because it is China. It is not a democracy and the government has absolute control. We don’t see the failures of the CCP because anyone who dares to criticize the government “mysteriously disappears” or just jailed.[5] The government exercises total control over its citizens and businesses, public or private. In fact, during the nascent stages of the now pandemic, China was, as usual, secretive and did squat-all. The first case was on 31 Dec, 2019 in Wuhan, yet it took the government more than 3 weeks (23 Jan) to quarantine Wuhan.[6] It was probably too late. The first known cases in now Italy were detected on 30 Jan, both being Chinese tourists who arrived in Rome on the same day as the declaration of Wuhan quarantine[7]. The same goes for the first cases in Japan — a tourist that returned from Wuhan on 14th Jan[8] , in US — a tourist who had visited Wuhan and returned around 15th Jan[9], South Korea — tourists who returned on 22nd[10]. These are the countries that are the worst affected at the moment. Imagine if only China had implemented the quarantine measures two weeks earlier? And this isn’t the first time. The same pattern was evident during the 2002–04 SARS outbreak.[11] The first cases was reported in mid-nov 2002, but China only informed WHO three months later. And yet China is reluctant to clamp down on “wet markets”. This video from Vox explains all of it beautifully.[12] “Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it”. So no, Mr. O’Neill’s statement isn’t entirely correct. Had the outbreak started in India, it might have caused far more chaos and deaths. However, it didn’t. And China has been the culprit for a long time now and needs to be called out, not praised for swift action.

Question: What is the best advice you can give someone who believes he can do a lot of things but has challenges in choosing his career path?
Answer: “Words are wind.” What you think or believe in is of no intrinsic value, at least not to anyone apart from you. The world demands proof. If you are good at many things, DO THEM. Get certified. Go for internships. Execute independent projects. Create something compelling. Not only will the above lend credence to your profile (and you claim of being a jack of all trades), it will also help you refine your focus and help decide which path to take. If you don’t maintain a personal investment portfolio, a job in the investment management industry might not be for you. If you don’t have the patience to sit and develop an app from scratch, then maybe rethink your plan to pursue a career as a developer. If you don’t blog, writing might not be a good career fit. So go out there. Create a great Github profile. Express your creative self on Deviantart. Make good music and upload it on Soundcloud. Show the world your artistic/educational/funny side on YouTube. Publish a research paper. Create a personal website/interactive resume. Take up freelancing gigs. Show the world what you’ve got and back up your words with actions.
